articles.title: Judge says agriculture secretary’s religious emails were unconstitutional
articles.description: Judge says agriculture secretary’s religious emails were unconstitutional AP News Agriculture Secretary’s Christian Messages to Staff Went ‘Too Far,’ Judge Says The New York Times Agriculture Secretary’s religious emails are unconstitutional, judge rules The Washington Post Judge says Rollins’s religious holiday messages likely violated First Amendment The Hill Federal judge blocks USDA secretary's Christian notes to
articles.content: Religious messages that U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins emailed to the agency’s 100,000 employees were unconstitutional, and she must be careful to avoid proselytizing when communicating with workers, a federal judge ruled Thursday. Rollins sent the messages, which included Christian messages and images, from her official email account on holidays such as Independence Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas and Easter. She did not send messages commemorating holidays from other religions. “And so, like the very first disciples to encounter our risen Lord in the Upper Room almost two thousand years ago, this Easter let us too be alive with hope, full of Paschal joy, and confident in the mission each of us has been called for,” Rollins wrote in an April 5 email marking Easter. U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson in San Francisco said the emails violated the First Amendment’s establishment clause, pointing to her position of authority, her use of an official email account and the messages suggesting that Christianity is the shared faith of USDA workers. A USDA spokesperson called the ruling “is a completely unprecedented attempt to muzzle a Cabinet Secretary” and said the agency is considering an appeal. Employees cannot realistically opt out of reading emails from their agency director, and the messages could coerce them to hide their own faith or feel pressure to adopt Rollins’ Christian faith, Thompson ruled. When disseminating religious messages, Rollins must stop if a colleague asks her to stop, “cannot create a hostile work environment through persistent unwelcome advances” and “cannot use official authority to pressure subordinates,” Thompson ordered. Her commands were quoted directly from a USDA policy on workplace religious expression that Rollins herself adopted. Rollins may discuss her faith with interested colleagues, share why her faith is meaningful to her, politely invite co-workers to religious events and express her views in appropriate conversations, Thompson ruled, again quoting directly from Rollins’ policy. Six USDA employees and the National Federation of Federal Employees, a labor union representing 19,000 USDA workers, brought the suit in May.

articles.title: U-M Regents approve 'research computing center' in Ypsilanti Township, which says it will sue
articles.description: Despite fierce opposition from Ypsilanti Township officials and residents, the University of Michigan Regents approved the construction of a research computing center — which opponents say is a data center by another name.
articles.content: Opponents of a planned University of Michigan computing center in Ypsilanti Township demonstrate outside a University of Michigan regents meeting on November 19, 2026.(Tracy Samilton / Michigan Public )Regents of the University of Michigan approved a highly controversial computing center in Ypsilanti Township at their Thursday meeting, by a vote of 7-1.U-M President Domenico Grasso said without the facility, the university risks losing its status as one of the nation's top research institutions."Our current computing capacity is simply not sufficient to meet the demands of modern research," he said. "This is like using a rotary-dial phone, where smartphones are ubiquitous."Grasso said the university plans to set aside $5 million for community development projects in Ypsilanti Township, and to work with township and local leaders to identify shared priorities and ways that Michigan help can help achieve themOpposition to the data center remains undiminished. Ypsilanti Township officials and residents said the university has ignored their pleas to build the center somewhere else. They say it will destroy the quality of life in the township. They also question its necessity. That's because the plan is for University of Michigan researchers to use about 10% of the center's capacity, with its partner, the Los Alamos National Laboratory, using the other 90%.Ypsilanti Township attorney Doug Winters said the university has shown contempt and disdain for local officials, as well as for Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson, who has said she supports a one-year moratorium on new data centers in Michigan.Winters said he has been authorized by the township to pursue "all legal means" to stop the facility from being built. "It won't go unchallenged," he said.Editor's note: The University of Michigan holds Michigan Public's broadcast license.

articles.title: From MAGA stardom to a U-Haul: Lauren Boebert considers her own and GOP’s losses
articles.description: From MAGA stardom to a U-Haul: Lauren Boebert considers her own and GOP’s losses AP News Three MAGA Women Who Defined an Era in Congress Are Exiting The New York Times Boebert: Trump ‘did some things that hurt my voters’ The Hill MAGA Loser Turns on Trump After Humiliating Election Loss Yahoo Lauren Boebert gives a candid interview from a U-Haul van after her election loss The Independent
articles.content: Rep. Lauren Boebert sat in a U-Haul van in the nation’s capital after packing up her congressional office and her “dungeon of an apartment” on Thursday, about six years after she became a MAGA star and one week after voters decided not to return her to Washington, D.C. “I think about it every day,” said Boebert, referring to the midterm elections where American voters sent Democrats to Congress en masse. Boebert spoke via Zoom from the van in one of her first interviews since her loss to Democrat Eileen Laubacher in a district Boebert had won by double digits two years ago. “This could be a referendum on President Trump. It could be the referendum on Congress or the Republican Party,” the Colorado Republican said. Then, lowering her voice, she added, “I think it’s all of it.” “I’m not mad at the president,” she said, but “the president did some things that hurt my voters.” Congresswoman Lauren Boebert reflects on Washington, her campaign and the GOP’s midterm losses. The AP’s Jennifer King reports. Boebert was one of the most vocal and visible members of the “Make America Great Again” movement, making headlines with her right-wing righteousness on television and the House floor from the time she was first elected, in 2020. Her time in D.C. roughly traced the arc of that movement — and its supporters’ more tenuous relationship with Trump of late — through its apogee in 2024 and its more recent midterm losses. As someone who described herself on Fox News as “ultra MAGA” four years ago, Boebert has become less inclined toward definitions. “When Jesus comes back and I’m raptured up, like all these labels are just going to fly off anyway,” she said. “I respect President Trump, I still work with him, I want to continue to work with him. Not for him, with him.” Boebert says she hasn’t changed too much in her six years, besides a few more gray hairs and maybe some “personal growth” on bipartisanship. She said she wouldn’t have done anything differently — besides, she joked, “not gone to the theater.” She was referring to an incident at a Denver theater where she was caught on camera vaping at 2023 performance of “Beetlejuice” and escorted out of the venue, a clip that was replayed in campaign ads against her that she partly credits for her loss. She felt it was an unfair dredging up of a past she’d already “owned up to,” but said there could be “a great number of” unaffiliated or Republican voters who, when it came to the scandal, just said, “‘I don’t care if any of this is true or not, I’m tired of the drama.’” At the time, she apologized for it up and down her former district, which covered western Colorado. She later moved to a more conservative House seat covering the state’s Great Plains, where she won in 2024 before losing two years later. Boebert’s opponent raised far more campaign cash than she did. “I didn’t raise millions of dollars and I kinda refused to,” she said. “Colorado voters know me, and, you know, if they know me enough to get rid of me, then I guess that’s my answer.” Though Boebert has broken from Trump at times — typically on topics other Trump supporters also opposed, such as the war in Iran and the administration’s treatment of the Jeffrey Epstein files — she didn’t lay the blame for her defeat or other GOP losses squarely at Trump’s feet. “I think it’s more all of us. It’s all of the Republican Party,” she said, citing high gas prices, GOP infighting and unfulfilled promises. “We had solutions and we didn’t take action.” Boebert said she doesn’t take her loss as an “L,” and instead sees it as a “launching pad” for the future, one that she didn’t specify but gave a hint toward. “Too many people come to Congress and get rich,” she said. “I am not one of those, and I’m gonna go make some money now.” “The U-Haul is getting started,” she said, her camera vibrating a bit as the nation’s capital outside the van’s window started to move by.

articles.title: Anthropic’s 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO
articles.description: At the upgraded $83/share IPO price, Anthropic's seven founders each pocketed $280 million, while the company nabbed nearly $105 billion.
articles.content: Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO. At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for. Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The company said that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy. However, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The company points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.” With the IPO in the record books, there were a few other interesting numbers worth highlighting. $104.8 billion. That’s really the amount Anthropic raised for its coffers (with a possibility of $117 billion, if the bankers buy all of their allotment of shares). In addition to selling its Class A common stock, it also sold a previously announced $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry. Nvidia bought $10 billion of these Class N shares, Google bought $10 billion, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divvied up the rest. Just for comparison: When Facebook had its then record-breaking IPO in 2012, it raised $16 billion on IPO day. 28% stake to Amazon and Google combined. All told, at the higher IPO share price, Google wound up owning 13.4% of the company. Amazon also now has a big stake in Anthropic because when it previously invested in the AI lab as a startup, it was granted promissory notes that could be converted to equity. It converted a small percentage of them as part of the IPO, leaving it with a 14.6% stake. Had it converted all of them, Amazon could have owned nearly 24%. The two large cloud providers now own 28% of Anthropic, the AI lab says. More than $1 trillion. As mind-blowing as it is to raise nearly $105 billion, giving Anthropic nearly $230 billion of working capital available (along with capital it already had on hand), the company’s need for future capital is still far greater. Anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026. It needs $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030. And it has racked up hundreds of billions of other commitments that are either conditional (and may not happen) or haven’t been priced yet. All told, the company has disclosed a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future. This was a huge IPO. But it is a pricey business to run. articles.title: Make progress reach every child in Papua New Guinea
articles.content: Statement by Dr Veera Mendonca, UNICEF Country Representative in Papua New Guinea, on World Children’s Day PORT MORESBY, 20 November 2026 - “Every child in Papua New Guinea has the right to survive and thrive, to learn, to be protected and to be heard. On World Children’s Day, we mark the adoption of the Convention on the Rights of the Child and renew our shared commitment to make those rights real. This year’s theme is My Day. My Rights. My Future. Children are speaking up. Our duty is to listen and to show them how their voices shape the decisions we make. “Remax Daniel, a Grade 4 student, put it best: ‘We may be small today but our dreams are big. We ask you to walk with us, listen to us and invest in our future. If you build the foundation now, we will build the nation tomorrow.’ Remax dreams of good teachers and safe classrooms, clinics with medicines, clean water in every community, healthy food for every child, and homes where girls and boys can grow up without fear. Every child has a right to these things. It is our job to help deliver them. “This year, UNICEF and the Government of Papua New Guinea mark 40 years of partnership. Together, we have made measurable progress for children. Under-five mortality has more than halved, from about 85 deaths per 1,000 live births in 1990 to 39 in 2024. General education enrolment rose from just over half a million in 1993 to around 2.8 million in 2023. The Government now funds most of the country’s routine vaccines and has committed K26 million in 2026. It has also introduced the HPV vaccine to protect girls from cervical cancer. Together, we contained a polio outbreak, with no new cases reported since October 2025. "This year, the National Parliament made its Committee on Children and Youth permanent and unanimously adopted the committee’s report and recommendations. I commend the Government and Parliament for this leadership, and I salute the health workers, teachers, social workers, child protection officers and village health assistants who bring essential services closer to families, often in the most remote places. “Here at home, some of our strongest allies are the ones closest to families. Churches run many of the country's health facilities and schools and reach communities where few others can. Church leaders, civil society and young people are helping communities stand up against violence and keep children safe at home, at school and in the village. They are also building trust in vaccines, including the new HPV vaccine. They are our core partners, and I thank them for their tireless service to every child. “None of this happens alone. I thank the governments of Australia, the Republic of Korea, Japan, the United States and New Zealand, United Kingdom, Cyprus, the European Union, the World Bank, the Global Partnership for Education, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, UNICEF Australia, and our sister United Nations agencies for standing with the children of Papua New Guinea. I also thank the Member States whose contributions to UNICEF’s core resources and flexible humanitarian funding allow us to act quickly and reach children where needs are greatest. This year, that flexible funding helped UNICEF move early, alongside the Government, as El Niño began to strain water, food and health services. Flexible funding saves time, and for children in a crisis, time saves lives. “But progress has not yet reached every child. Where a child is born still shapes her chances of surviving, learning and growing up safe. Every child’s story should begin with a safe birth and a name on the official record. Yet fewer than half of babies are born without a skilled health worker present, and only 13 per cent of children under five have had their births registered. “Too many children still miss out on the care, education and protection they need. In 2025, less than half of infants received all three doses of the vaccine against diphtheria, tetanus and whooping cough and around 130,000 children have never received a single vaccine dose. Nearly half of children under five are stunted, with potentially lifelong consequences for their growth and learning. 72 per cent of 10-year-olds cannot read and understand an age-appropriate text. And too many children experience violence at home, at school and in their communities, often with no one to turn to. Behind each of these numbers is a child whose future is being decided now. “El Niño is now testing these fragile systems. One in three children is exposed to at least two overlapping climate hazards, and dry conditions are already putting pressure on food and water supplies. I urge the Government and partners to act early: keep safe water flowing in schools and clinics, and give frontline workers what they need to bring vaccination, nutrition support and birth registration closer to the families most at risk. “Ahead of the 2027 national election, I call on all political parties and leaders to put children and young people at the heart of their policies and programmes. Tell families which services you will improve and how you will fund them. Show young people how you will help them gain skills and find decent work. Children like Remax are asking for ‘leaders who listen to children, make good decisions and help our country grow.’ Children cannot vote, but every vote cast in 2027 will shape their future. “More than half of Papua New Guineans are under 25. Investing in their health, learning and skills is not a cost; it is the surest path to the more prosperous Papua New Guinea envisaged in the country’s Development Strategic Plan 2010–2030 and Vision 2050. Children need that investment now. Their health, learning and safety depend on it. “To Remax and to every child and young person in Papua New Guinea: we hear you, and we stand with you. UNICEF will keep working alongside the Government, Parliament, churches, civil society, communities and partners for every child. For me, progress is what children can count on in their daily lives: a school that stays open through a dry spell, a mother who gives birth safely close to home, a baby who is vaccinated and registered, and a young person who can point to a decision that changed because adults listened. "Yumi wok bung wantaim long olgeta pikinini – together, we work for every child.” UNICEF promotes the rights and wellbeing of every child, in everything we do. Together with our partners, we work across Papua New Guinea to translate that commitment into practical action, focusing special effort on reaching the most vulnerable and excluded children, to the benefit of all children, everywhere. Musk's SpaceXSI denies liability in UK lawmaker's lawsuit over Grok images
articles.content: Elon Musk's SpaceX Super Intelligence (SpaceXSI) has denied legal responsibility for fake sexualised images of a British lawmaker generated using its Grok AI platform. In a written defence filed at London's High Court on October 29, the company argued that AI-generated images that are obviously fictitious cannot violate a person's right to privacy. The response came in a lawsuit filed by Jess Asato, a member of Britain's governing Labour Party, who is seeking an order to prevent Grok from creating manipulated images of her.SpaceXSI has denied allegations of misuse of private information and breaches of data protection laws. It has also contested Asato's request for an order requiring it to "implement effective and permanent technical measures" to stop Grok from generating manipulated images of her.'Fictitious and implausible'In its defence, lawyers for SpaceX Super Intelligence LLC said the company had removed AI-generated images of Asato that violated its terms. These included a video showing her "being chloroformed and prepared for a sexual assault".However, the company argued that other images it had allowed to remain online were clearly artificial.They said such content "would be understood by reasonable and sensible persons viewing that content to be AI-generated, fictitious and implausible ... rather than as realistic images".On this basis, the company argued that Asato could not claim a reasonable expectation of privacy.SpaceXSI also denied violating her data protection rights. It argued that it "did not determine the content of the relevant users' prompts".Lawmaker challenges company's defenceAsato hit back at the company's position on Thursday, saying that developers of powerful AI tools must be held accountable for their products."SpaceX SI wants to have it both ways," she said."The company admits it built the AI model, rewrote user requests to add its own graphic details, pulled images from across the internet, and published the results from an account it controls," she said, adding: "Yet it also claims it is a neutral bystander without legal responsibility".Asato has accused the company of designing and training Grok in a way that enabled users to generate sexualised images of her. Her lawsuit alleges misuse of private information and breaches of data protection laws.A test case for AI companiesThe lawsuit is among the first cases to examine whether an AI developer can be held legally responsible for the way its system is designed and the content it generates.The court's eventual findings could have implications for similar cases involving AI-generated content and the responsibilities of companies developing such tools.Grok faces scrutiny across countriesGrok, which is available through Musk's social media platform X, has faced regulatory scrutiny in several countries following an outcry over its use to generate sexualised images of people without their consent.In mid-January, xAI said it had restricted image editing on Grok. It also said it had blocked users from generating images of people in revealing clothing "where it's illegal".However, a Reuters investigation in early February found that Grok continued to generate sexualised images even after the restrictions were introduced. The platform did so even when users explicitly warned that the people depicted had not consented.In July, xAI sued a man in the US, alleging that he had misused Grok to create child sexual abuse material. The case was among the first of its kind brought by an AI company.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: BWL’s newest ewe-tility workers
articles.description: Sheep are munching away at the last of the summer grass in and around a small solar panel farm in Lansing Township. As Michigan’s first such municipal utility sheep subcontractors, […]
articles.content: Sheep are munching away at the last of the summer grass in and around a small solar panel farm in Lansing Township. As Michigan’s first such municipal utility sheep subcontractors, the flock of 125 will soon be trucked away to warm up during the winter, and they’re getting rid of the last bit of the grass. Sheep, it turns out, are the best grass-eaters for solar farms. Egypt Krohn, owner of Dragonfly Downs Farm in Grand Ledge, talks about the use of sheep at a utility site and integrating agriculture with power generation. Mike Ellis/City Pulse Goats are often the go-to grass chew crew. But they’re super-curious and nimble and they’d use the panels as a jungle gym. Cows would use the structures as scratching posts. But sheep? Docile and gentle and easily-transportable sheep are exactly what a utility farm needs. Using livestock can help save money over human mowing crews and curbing some of the gas-powered mowers will help to move the needle on the utility’s environmental goals, said Dick Peffley, CEO of the Lansing Board of Water and Light. “It would take a lot of time and fossil fuel to mow this site and now we’ve got mowers here,” Peffley said, as he was interrupted a few times by the bleating of Snips, a friendly ram who shared the spotlight in front of news cameras. Dick Peffley, center, is the general manager of Lansing Board of Water and Light. Mike Ellis/City Pulse The sheep arrived recently, after the Lake Lansing site was completed this fall. If the sheep are there all year, there wouldn’t be any sign of long grass on the site, said shepherd Egypt Krohn, owner of Dragonfly Downs Farm in Grand Ledge. The solar farm generates about 6MW of power from about 13,000 panels on a site at Lake Lansing Road and Wood Road, on the site of a former gravel pit and disposal site. The ground is now covered in grass except for the large banks of solar panels. The panels help to create a nice shade and shelter option for the sheep, until it gets too cold. They go back to the farm for the winter. Krohn said her sheep require little water, no more than 20-30 gallons a day on the hot days and that fits in a small tank on the back of her truck. The flock is kept there behind a portable electric fence, run itself by a small independent solar array. A solar site in Lansing Township now has a crew of sheep eating the grass. Mike Ellis/City Pulse Krohn said the fence and watering flexibility means her sheep can go just about anywhere, no infrastructure required. And they don’t have a habit of eating wires, which is handy at a utility site. The Lake Lansing Solar site is relatively small at 6MW. Solar accounts for around 10% of BWL’s generation, gas is around half. BWL gets 115MW from the Whitetail Solar array in Washtenaw County and between 10MW and 80MW from three other solar sites in Eaton, Clinton and Shiawassee counties. But its location on Lake Lansing Road in the Lansing Township-Lansing-East Lansing borderlands makes it a prominent reminder of BWL’s green initiatives. And the sheep should provide a little bit of amusement. Peffley said the sheep and the site amounted to a bit of a defying act, pointing to criticism about farmland being turned into solar farms, “We came up with this idea to do the exact opposite here,” he said. “This has always been light industrial, now we’re going to use it for agricultural use.” A solar site in Lansing Township now has a crew of sheep eating the grass. articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed, JD Vance look to meet after campaign attacks
articles.description: Vice President JD Vance and Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed are preparing to meet, the incoming Democratic lawmaker and the White House said, after a bitter campaign season that featured sharp and at-times personal attacks between the two men.
articles.content: WASHINGTON — Vice President JD Vance and Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed are preparing to meet, the incoming Democratic lawmaker and the White House said, after a bitter campaign season that featured sharp and at-times personal attacks between the two men. The circumstances of the would-be meeting were not immediately clear, nor was it certain on whose initiative it was being set. And Vance will ultimately preside over El-Sayed’s swearing-in Jan. 3. El-Sayed said in a Tuesday interview on MSNOW that his team was contacted by Vance’s office for a meeting. Vance’s office said Wednesday that it had contacted El-Sayed’s staff after being told the Democrat sought time with the vice president. Vice President JD Vance speaks at the 2nd Marine Aircraft Wing’s annual Marine Corps Birthday Ball in New Bern, N.C., Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. (AP Photo/Matt Rourke, Pool) The talk of a meeting comes as Vance nears a decision on whether to seek the Republican nomination for the White House in 2028, which has been complicated by voters’ bruising rejection of President Donald Trump in this month’s midterm elections, and as El-Sayed prepares to take office as the nation’s first Muslim senator. Both men have in recent days expressed willingness to attempt to find common ground after their heated criticism — albeit on their own terms. Vance described El-Sayed as “very, very evil” while campaigning for Michigan Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers outside Detroit in August and appeared to question the Democrat’s patriotism. Related: Fact checks, takeaways: JD Vance stumps for Michigan Republicans Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan propels ‘Medicare for All’ debate ‘A beautifully American story’: El-Sayed’s win resonates with Muslim Americans Vance, however, sounded a much more charitable tone about the incoming Michigan senator during a Fox News Channel interview Monday. “If Abdul El-Sayed wants to work with me and the president to make people’s lives better, he’s going to find us very much a willing partner,” Vance said during the Fox segment. It was far from clear how and on what issues the two might cooperate, especially in light of El-Sayed’s chief policy objective, a Medicare for All healthcare system the Trump administration, including Vance individually, has dismissed. But it appeared at least to represent a rare bipartisan olive branch for President Donald Trump’s attack dog in the wake of midterm elections, when Republicans were routed nationally while losing majorities in both houses of Congress, and as Vance looks ahead to his own future.Donate “If he wants to work with us to get money out of politics, put money in pockets and pass Medicare for All, which is what I ran on, I’m a willing partner,” El-Sayed said on MS NOW.

articles.title: Appeals court grants Trump request to halt order restoring Venezuelan TPS
articles.content: A federal appeals court has agreed to keep deportation protections frozen for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan migrants, shortly after the Trump administration filed an emergency appeal to the Supreme Court. The appeals court order handed down late Wednesday means the administration remains free to detain and deport Venezuelans who had previously been granted temporary protected status. Federal attorneys have said some 1,800 are in detention, and about 330 are subject to deportation proceedings. The Supreme Court previously intervened to allow the administration to temporarily end the program for Venezuelans. Congress created the TPS program in 1990 to protect migrants from deportation to countries experiencing natural disasters or civil unrest. The designation is granted in periods of up to 18 months. The Trump administration argues that TPS is a temporary program and that Venezuela no longer meets the requirements for its renewal. During President Donald Trump’s second term, the Department of Homeland Security has terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria. However, in a shift in policy in recent months, the administration has maintained protections for nearly 200,000 Salvadorans and more than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan. TPS was first granted to Venezuelans in March 2021, under Democratic President Joe Biden. The designation was expanded in September 2023 to cover additional beneficiaries. About 600,000 Venezuelans have received TPS protections. The Trump administration’s move to end protections for Venezuelans was challenged in court, and a California-based judge ruled it unlawful. The Supreme Court twice intervened with temporary emergency orders, and later sent the case back to an appeals court after upholding the end of TPS for Haitians in a different case. The U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals had yet to rule when the administration returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday, arguing that a temporary pause would soon expire and allow the restoration of deportation protections. Hours later, though, the appeals court extended its temporary freeze on protections until seven days after it hands down a full ruling. The Justice Department subsequently withdrew its appeal, although federal attorneys could return to the high court later. After the Trump administration terminated TPS for Venezuelans last year, their work authorizations also became invalid. Thousands faced deportation proceedings, detention and removal. Many others chose to leave the country voluntarily. It remains unclear how many Venezuelans who previously held TPS are still living in the United States.

articles.title: Michigan gamers explain why they're taking time off work for GTA 6
articles.description: The highly anticipated video game Grand Theft Auto VI was released on Thursday. Some Michigan gamers are celebrating by taking the day off work to play.
articles.content: The highly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI released on Thursday. Some Michigan gamers are celebrating by taking the day off work to play.(Rockstar Games)Fans of the Grand Theft Auto video games have been waiting for 10 years for a sequel to the critically acclaimed GTA V. Well, now their wait is over. Amid high expectations and high excitement from gamers, GTA VI was released on Thursday. And according to Jeff Grubb, veteran video-game journalist and host of the podcast Game Mess Mornings, the wait was worth it.“So the surprising thing is that it didn't just like meet those expectations across the board,” Grubb said. “Everyone I've spoken to as I play the game through these first 10 hours or so, it does really feel like they went above and beyond.”Grubb said that in a world where the tools to build games are becoming more democratized, big gaming studios have to deliver something special to capture the kind of attention they are getting with GTA VI.“One way that games can stand out is to be more expensive, and to look more expensive, and to have more options than ever before.”Estimates put the cost of game development at over $1 billion, though the developer Rockstar Games has not provided an exact figure. But that investment, Grubb, said, shows in the detailed game play and expansive world building.To celebrate, many Michigan fans of the franchise are calling off work this week to sink their teeth into the immersive world and cutting-edge graphics.“I was leading a stand-up meeting today at work, and I was telling them someone has to cover our monthly business review because I'm off Thursday and I'm taking it off for a video game,” said Wyoming resident Charlie Hunt. “And no, it's not negotiable.” Charlie Hunt will intentionally be playing Grand Theft Auto VI while his kids are at school. (Courtesy / Charlie Hunt )Hunt is 43 years old and a project manager at Steelcase. He’s planning to take Thursday and Friday off so he can play the game while his kids are at school.“I have 7-year-old kids, and I also have a full-time job. And sometimes video games and my kids work really well together. They'll watch me play Fortnite, I'll introduce them to Nintendo games, that sort of thing. But this is a game that's kind of incompatible with my role as a dad.”GTA is a famously violent game. Players steal cars, evade police, and shoot bystanders with high-powered firearms. But for many of the gamers we spoke to, the violence of the game was not the main draw of GTA VI. It was the chance to escape their adult lives for a few hours — and reconnect with a past version of themselves. Ryan Lee bought a new XBox to play Grand Theft Auto VI. (Courtesy / Ryan Lee)“I think it kind of brings me back to when I was younger,” explained Ryan Lee from Saginaw. “So definitely kind of bringing me back to when I was, like, real young, a teenager, and, you know, kind of like that where you don't realize, when you're older, you have to pay bills, go to work every day.”For gas station manager Patrick Dumond, the game also offers him a chance to find refuge from the difficult parts of his job. "I work overnight in a gas station," he said. "So it's a good feeling to go home and be able to pop in a game. ... It allows me to escape from the trials and tribulations I deal with on a daily basis."Lee is also planning to take the day off to immerse himself in the game — something he has never done before.“I actually went on my lunch today to pick up a PlayStation 5,” he said. “I didn't even own one.”The hype around the release of the latest installment has been intense. Originally scheduled to release in 2025, the drop date has been pushed back several times. The delay has only heightened the excitement for many fans.“And the fact that this game has over $1 billion budget, no expense spared, no time spared. I mean, as we all know from the delays,” said Hunt. “I'm just really excited for a luxury experience and seeing what that looks like in 2026 and how I interpret it as a 43-year-old. I mean, I was just turning 30 when the last one came out.”For fellow Wyoming resident Randy Thomas, the game’s release holds a deeper, more personal significance. Randi Thomas (left) was introduced to Grand Theft Auto by her late brother, Louis Thomas (right).(Courtesy / Randi Thomas)“I got introduced by my brother. Actually, we we planned this weekend together, but he passed away on his birthday two months ago,” Thomas said. “And so now I'm kind of just like playing in his honor.”Thomas is also excited for the new storyline of GTA VI. One of the two main characters is a Latina woman named Lucia Caminos, a former inmate in search of a better life. This version of the game will allow players to play as Caminos or her boyfriend, Jason Duval, a former Army serviceman who works for local drug runners. Thomas said she is looking forward to playing a game she loves with a character who’s relatable to her. "So I've always wanted a woman character that has their own storyline," she said. Like the other gamers we talked to, Thomas said the game is also just a chance to escape real life for a little while.“I've been just sitting in grief for these last couple months. And I'm hoping that like just being able to play the game this weekend, I could just disconnect from that a little and really just be excited and have fun, like joyful, giddy, kid stuff.”

The diplomatic choreography was delicate as China's Xi welcomed Putin and Trump to APEC
articles.description: The diplomatic choreography was delicate as China's Xi welcomed Putin and Trump to APEC AP News Top House Democrat questions what Trump accomplished in Xi-Putin summit NPR Stalemates over semiconductors and rare earth minerals appear little changed as Trump heads home from China Yahoo Finance Remarks: Donald Trump Holds a Bilateral Meeting with Xi Jinping of China - Factba.se Roll Call Xi Seeks to Cement Stable Ties
articles.content: SHENZHEN, China (AP) — Like almost all the other leaders, U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin received military honor guards, waving crowds and red-carpet welcomes. But different men were waiting for them at the airport as they descended from their planes. When Trump arrived in Shenzhen in southern China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, Chinese President Xi Jinping was there to greet him personally. But earlier, the welcoming duties for Putin fell to Cai Qi, Xi’s chief of staff and a top member of the Communist Party’s leadership. Does this mean that Trump mattered more to Xi than the Kremlin leader he calls his “old friend”? Not necessarily. APEC’s annual summit and a historic trilateral meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the U.S. showcased some of Xi’s political and diplomatic calculations in his interactions on a global stage. But analysts caution that while optics matter, they do not always signal substantive policy changes. “We shouldn’t read too much into this or conclude that Beijing is pivoting to Washington at Moscow’s expense,” said Dominic Chiu, senior analyst at Eurasia Group. “The difference reflects Beijing’s diplomatic calculation.” When Trump arrived in Shenzhen, the Chinese leader strode down a red carpet to the stairs leading to Air Force One. Enthusiastic crowds waved Chinese and American flags and shook pompoms in unison. Xi and Trump shook hands and even embraced momentarily. A young girl presented Trump with a bouquet of flowers, and the leaders stood at attention, side by side, as a military band played the national anthems. When Putin arrived, there was an honor guard, a short red carpet, Xi’s chief of staff and a crowd waving Russian and Chinese flags. Xi’s personal welcome could be seen as an effort by Beijing to maintain stable ties with Washington, a recognition of Trump’s appreciation for respect and favorable optics, and a gesture reciprocating the American president’s in-person greeting in September in the U.S. at Joint Base Andrews, Chiu said. He added that China’s partnership with Russia is more established, noting that Xi and Putin know each other well and have had more frequent meetings than either of them has had with Trump. “If anything, Xi and Putin likely share a tacit understanding that each of them needs to manage his own relationship with Trump carefully, even if that means accepting a relatively less ceremonial treatment from the other,” Chiu said. Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center, said she does not think the difference in treatment would undermine Beijing’s relationship with Moscow. “China needs the U.S. and Russia for different things. U.S. needs to be managed, while Russia is a partner for China,” she said. “It’s like comparing apples and oranges.” The leaders arrived one by one for the family photo, ahead of Wednesday night’s welcome banquet. They strode through a cavernous atrium to greet Xi. Xi’s expression, a genial half-smile, barely changed as he methodically shook their hands. Trump, by contrast, took his time with the greeting and then turned, pausing for a long moment to pose for the cameras with Xi. The interaction with Putin was much faster — a brief smile from Xi, a turn to the cameras, and then it was done. Just before the group photo, Putin tried to engage Trump but was cut short. Both Trump and Xi seemed to point to a spot where Putin should stand, with Xi’s wife separating the other two leaders. “You had a beaming Xi Jinping in the middle. You had a taller Donald Trump to one side and a much shorter Vladimir Putin on the other,” said Edgard Kagan from the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “For Russians, this is probably a slightly uncomfortable image because it does drive home the very significant difference between Russia on one hand and the US and China on the other.” The language of friendship also featured in the summit’s diplomacy. “You’re my friend, and we have a very special relationship,” Trump told Xi. The American also called Putin “my friend” as they greeted each other Thursday. Between Xi and Putin, the expressions of friendship were mutual. Xi welcomed the Russian leader as his “old friend” at their meeting Wednesday, while Putin addressed Xi as “dear friend” and said the Russians were happy to be “among friends.” At Thursday’s meeting of the three leaders, Xi appeared to give Trump and Putin equal attention. In a room at a villa used for government receptions, they sat at a round table, with Trump to Xi’s left and Putin to his right. “I am pleased to hold a trilateral meeting with President Putin and President Trump here in Shenzhen,” Xi said. China said the leaders agreed to support reforms at the United Nations, where all three countries are permanent members of the Security Council. They also agreed to increase fuel supplies and pursue dialogue to reduce nuclear risks. “Each of them wants to project this image of history in the making,” said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University. “It’s significant symbolically, there’s no real substantive outcome.” Klug reported from Tokyo and Leung from Hong Kong. Associated Press writers Didi Tang in Washington and Huizhong Wu in Bangkok contributed.

articles.description: Expert called MAHA's spending "pretty unusual" for a PAC.
articles.content: In the wake of the Make America Healthy Again movement's midterm wipeout, a top leader suggested the heavy losses came down to being outspent by wealthier, more powerful rivals. But a Stat report on MAHA's own spending in the run-up to the election raises questions about whether the group's priority was ever winning elections in the first place. The dive into the financial documents reveals that the MAHA PAC, led by Tony Lyons, spent more on allies, boosters, meals, luxuries, and its affiliated nonprofit than it did on political candidates. The findings are in stark contrast to an announcement from Lyons in the spring that he was heading a $100 million fundraiser to boost MAHA's clout in the midterms. In reality, MAHA PAC took in $3.2 million. During the election cycle, the PAC spent more than $10.5 million, with over $7 million coming from money it had collected previously.Read full article Comments

articles.title: US Senator-elect El-Sayed says Israel should not identify with one faith or culture
articles.content: US Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-MI) said in a new interview that Israel should not identify itself with a particular culture… US Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-MI) said in a new interview that Israel should not identify itself with a particular culture or religion, renewing questions about his willingness to recognize Jewish national self-determination as he prepares to enter the Senate. Speaking Tuesday at “The Atlantic Summit: Politics, Power, and What’s Next in Washington,” El-Sayed told Atlantic staff writer Jonathan Lemire that Israel should guarantee equal rights to all its citizens but should not define its national identity through its Jewish heritage. “I believe that Israel ought to be a country that upholds equal rights for all of its citizens, does not identify itself with a culture or a faith, and that dignifies the rights of those citizens to live free under its laws,” El-Sayed said. The remarks appear to effectively call into question the principle underpinning Israel’s identity as the world’s only Jewish state and that the Jewish people, like other peoples, have a right to national self-determination in their historic homeland. Israel’s Jewish character is not inherently incompatible with equal citizenship. The country’s Declaration of Independence guarantees equality of social and political rights to all inhabitants, regardless of religion, race, or sex. Arab citizens of Israel, for example, participate in the country’s political system, serve in the Knesset, and hold positions throughout Israeli society. Muslim citizens of Israel oftentimes enjoy more protected rights than in Muslim-majority countries. El-Sayed also declined to endorse a specific framework for resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, suggesting that the eventual political arrangement could involve one state, two states, or another configuration. “There needs to be a free, open Palestinian movement that can, on equal footing, negotiate with Jewish Israelis to think about what the ultimate peace should look like,” the senator-elect said, adding that the decision should ultimately be made by Palestinians and Israelis. But El-Sayed’s latest comments are part of a broader pattern of equivocation over Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish state. In a recent interview earlier this month with CBS’s “60 Minutes,” El-Sayed was asked directly whether Israel had a right to exist. He responded, “Yes, if there is a shared understanding,” before explaining that he would support either a two-state arrangement or a single shared state if both populations agreed. His answer contrasted with his unequivocal support for Palestinian statehood, raising questions about why Jewish sovereignty appears to require additional qualifications. Earlier this year, El-Sayed also told Jewish supporters that he struggled with the question of whether Israel should exist as a Jewish state, questioning how that designation could be consistent with liberal values. The remarks have drawn concern from Jewish community leaders, including Michigan Democrats who pressed him during the campaign to affirm Jewish sovereignty in Israel and more directly address antisemitism motivated by hostility toward the Jewish state. El-Sayed also dismissed concerns that his rhetoric could contribute to antisemitism, addressing the issue during Tuesday’s Atlantic appearance. Asked how he would respond to a Jewish American who said his criticism of Israel fueled fears of antisemitism, El-Sayed acknowledged those concerns but argued that discomfort over political criticism should be distinguished from threats to personal safety. “I’m sorry for your fear. Obviously, I don’t want to do anything that drives your fear,” he said. “At the end of the day, there’s a difference between safety or lack of safety and comfort.” He went on to argue that Jewish Americans uncomfortable with his rhetoric should instead be uncomfortable with what he described as injustices against Palestinians. El-Sayed also repeated his accusation that the United States had enabled genocide in Gaza, declaring, “We aided, armed, and abetted a genocide. Like, full stop.” He cited a figure of 70,000 Palestinian deaths, which he characterized as a minimum estimate, and accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of war crimes. Hamas-controlled health authorities in Gaza say over 70,000 Palestinians have been killed during the war with Israel since October 2023, although the figure doesn’t distinguish between civilians and combatants. It also doesn’t note who was killed by misfired Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad rockets, which are aimed at Israel but often fall short and land in Gaza. El-Sayed and others who accuse Israel of genocide generally do not acknowledge that Hamas conscripts children to serve in its armed forces and purposefully embeds its weapons and operation centers in civilian areas to increase the body count from Israeli strikes. The senator-elect’s remarks underscore the tensions surrounding his approach to Israel as he prepares to take his seat in the Senate. While he presents his position as a defense of universal equality and Palestinian self-determination, his insistence that Israel abandon its Jewish national identity raises a separate question: whether he recognizes the Jewish people’s right to exercise national self-determination in the same way he advocates for Palestinians.

articles.title: Palisades submits plan to encourage workers to report safety concerns
articles.description: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission required the plan after an inspection found a "chilled work environment" in two departments.
articles.content: The Palisades nuclear plant in Covert Township officially stopped operating in 2022. Now, with the help of a $1.5 billion loan from the federal government, the facility could be the first shuttered nuclear plant in the nation to be brought back online. (Dustin Dwyer / Michigan Public)Leaders at the Palisades nuclear plant in Southwest Michigan have submitted a plan to encourage more workers to report safety concerns.The plan comes in response to a Nuclear Regulatory Commission inspection that concluded Palisades had a “chilled work environment” in two departments.Holtec International, the owner of Palisades, was required to submit a plan for how to improve the work environment in the quality assurance and supply chain departments within 30 days.“We fully recognize the significance of the NRC's conclusion that employees within these departments may be reluctant to raise safety concerns through available avenues due to a perceived fear of retaliation,” wrote Palisades Chief Nuclear Officer Fadi Diya, in a letter accompanying the plan.Palisades said it had increased communication with employees in the two departments, holding town hall meetings, adding posters encouraging workers to report safety concerns and adding video and audio messages from senior staff. Palisades also created an independent assessment team to interview workers and formulate recommendations.“Evaluators will be independent of the affected departments and of decisions under review,” the plan submitted to the NRC said. “Any conflict will be resolved by replacement, recusal, or another documented control that preserves the independence of the work. Site personnel may provide coordination and records but will not control interview selection, participate in confidential employee interviews, or alter the team's findings.”The team will conduct interviews in December, issue a report in January and follow up with workers in February, according to the plan submitted to the NRC.The Palisades nuclear plant went into decommissioning in 2022, with plans to shut down. But Holtec has been working to re-open the plant instead. Palisades is currently in operating status, and nuclear fuel has been loaded into its reactors, but it is not generating power. Palisades would become the first nuclear plant in the U.S. to restart after going into decommissioning. The restart date has been pushed back a year as workers try to meet regulations.

articles.content: Michigan’s newest senator-elect and the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate talks about who belongs in America, his daughters, and what he can deliver on health care. In 1985, a 12-page flyer landed in mailboxes across Dearborn. The headline of the flyer read: “Let’s talk about the Arab problem.” It alleged that Arab families refused to assimilate. That they were abusing taxpayer money. If you were Arab and you opened your mailbox that week, the message was clear: you didn’t belong. The flyer came from Michael Guido’s campaign for mayor. He ultimately won his campaign. Now, 41 years later, Dearborn saw its highest voter turnout in decades. Some precincts even ran out of registration forms. Residents that night helped elect an Arab-American Muslim to the United States Senate. Dr. Abdul El-Sayed is the first Muslim ever elected to US Senate. He won after the president of the United States called him a jihadist. El-Sayed won by running on the platform of getting money out of politics, easing the costs of gas and groceries and pushing for Medicare for all. His win raised a question about who belongs, in his party and beyond. Could his work as a senator expand what it means to belong in America? Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) joined four of her congressional colleagues to decry what she described as “intimidation” and threats from the president and his allies against those speaking out against him. The press conference was hosted almost exactly one year after the group of legislators, all military veterans and former intelligence officers, posted a video reminding military servicemembers of their responsibility to refuse illegal orders. In the press conference Thursday afternoon, Slotkin recounted the past year of military and intelligence actions taken by President Donald Trump, including federal immigration enforcement deployments in Los Angeles, Chicago and Minneapolis, as well as the ongoing war in Iran and military strikes against boats in the Caribbean. “It was important for us to come together a year later to say: number one, we stand behind the video we made. Number two, we won’t be intimidated out of calling out threats to our democracy,” Slotkin said. “We stand behind our men and women in uniform for the amazing work that they do, and I think we feel strongly that if this is the thing we need to do to stand up for the country we love, we have no problem doing that.” Slotkin’s statements at the press conference come a week after a letter directed towards her was posted on X by Aaron Reitz, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas, alleging that her statements in a public podcast taping, which said that congressional oversight could send a “deterrence message” to those considering working in the Trump administration, were unconstitutional and potentially opening her up to a criminal investigation. “Your comments reflect soon-to-be-realized fantasies about weaponizing congressional investigations for the purpose of personal aggrandizement and punishment of people close to the President. In other words, your ’oversight’ plans seem to have no legitimate legislative purpose and may therefore be unlawful,” Reitz wrote in the letter. “The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action. Your stated intent to ‘deter’ Americans from associating with President Trump may run afoul of this constitutional right.” Slotkin responded Thursday with a letter of her own and a press release telling the Department of Justice to “bring it on.” Slotkin noted in a video posted to social media that, in addition to the constitutional freedom of speech rights that all Americans have, sitting senators enjoy further privileges and responsibilities for oversight that protect her and her colleagues in investigating Trump. “The Constitution’s Speech or Debate clause bars prosecution of a legislator for conducting an investigation or performing other legislative acts. As such, your threat of investigation is baseless, and you should withdraw your letter immediately,” Slotkin wrote in her letter. “Your public threats to prosecute a sitting Senator for speech and legislative oversight also violate Justice Department policy. Your breach of these rules — publicly posting your letter instead of providing it to me, my attorney, or Senate Legal Counsel — is evidence that your threat of investigation is more about publicity and your political ambitions than any sort of legitimate inquiry.” U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a radio interview in response to questions about Slotkin’s statements being potentially illegal, “what the senator said in and of itself is absolutely not a crime.” NBC News has also reported that Blanche said at a press conference last week that there were “no ongoing investigations, criminal investigations, into words that incoming senators or congressmen have said.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Slotkin referred, throughout her letter in response to Reitz and in Thursday’s press conference, to the result of an investigation into the video that was the subject of the press conference, and the failed criminal indictment from the federal government of Slotkin and her colleagues, as demonstrating that her speech is constitutionally protected. “It’s again similar, just going after someone for basic freedom of speech, and then on top of that, for speech and debate, for those of us who are legislators, we’re sort of doubly protected against that,” she said in the press conference. “It’s just a demonstration again that what began a year ago of the weaponization of the government continues.” U.S. Sen. Mark Kelly, a Democrat from Arizona, who was also featured in the 2025 video, similarly said at the press conference alongside Slotkin, “Donald Trump is trying to fundamentally change the nature of this country, it hasn’t worked on us. I will tell you that none of us are backing down.” “Just like the service members who have a duty to uphold the Constitution and refuse illegal orders, we have a duty in Congress to hold this president accountable and always stand up for the Constitution and the American people,” he continued. “That’s our job, and no amount of threats from Donald Trump or the people around him are going to stop us from doing that.”

(Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)As Democrats prepare to take control of the U.S. House in the next congressional term, caucus members are finalizing leadership roles, reelecting one Michigan representative to her role as head of the caucus’s communications and policy arm, and another to advocate on behalf of swing seat voters. The office of U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Ann Arbor) announced Thursday that she would once again serve as chair of the Democratic Policy and Communications Committee, continuing a tenure that began in 2024. “The most important work we will do with our new Democratic majority is pass policies that lower costs and help people who are hurting. But our work is unfinished if people never hear about it, cannot see how it changes their lives, or do not believe anyone in Washington is listening,” Dingell said in a statement. “That’s why it is critical Democratic leadership provides the support, resources, and tools our members need to effectively communicate with their distinct districts across the county. Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Bay City) also secured a position as House Democrats’ Battleground Leadership Representative, after making the case to her Democratic colleagues in a letter on Nov.5. McDonald Rivet represents Michigan’s 8th Congressional District, which was a key target for Democrats and Republicans alike during the 2024 election. She was recently elected to a second term, defeating retired GM engineer Thomas Smith, who dropped out of the Republican primary weeks before voters selected him to represent the party in the general election. “The American people have demanded real change that will actually make their lives better. They sent us an amazing class of members for the 120th Congress,” McDonald Rivet said in a statement. “It’s my honor to serve as this group’s representative to leadership. Now the work begins: to do everything we can to deliver on the opportunity we’ve been given.”

articles.description: Lawsuit: Over 99% of school system’s AI gun alerts were false positives.
articles.content: In October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home. It was then, in the lull of a moment any teen with after-school activities knows well, that the school’s AI gun detection system suddenly flagged one teen holding a bag of chips as a potential gunman. Within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat. They recognized the Doritos bag and canceled the alert, which notified not only other school officials but also the Baltimore County Police Department that no response was needed. articles.title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
articles.description: Jensen Huang has resigned from Nvidia following an affair, which could have ramifications for national security as the U.S. and China race to develop the most advanced AI infrastructure.
articles.content: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security. U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported. The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up. By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. Nvidia reported its quarterly earnings on Tuesday, which beat Wall Street expectations with $115.8 billion in revenue, up 103% year-over-year. Despite the unknowns the company faces without Huang involved, interim CEO Colette Kress said that full-year revenue is also on track to exceed expectations. The company also plans to raise its outlook for the 2028 fiscal year, indicating confidence that this unexpected leadership change won’t get in the way of its trajectory. “We have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap,” Kress said. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual. We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones affirmed that the company is not considering reinstating Huang. Kress also said that Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country. Jensen Huang posted his first public statement since he admitted to having an extramarital affair more than a week earlier. “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote. Many of Huang’s colleagues in the tech industry, including Elon Musk, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey, and Y Combinator President and CEO Garry Tan, have called for his return. Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an… More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia. Bloomberg reported that Huang looked “broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted” by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.” Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making. In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship with a purported Chinese spy. “Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang’s compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales,” the letter states. That same evening, Senator Tim Scott (R-SC) requested that Huang and Lutnick both testify before the Senate Banking Committee. “The American people deserve answers,” Scott wrote on X. After Huang was already ousted from Nvidia, we continued to learn more incriminating claims about the former CEO. According to Reuters, Huang had a third affair with an additional, unnamed employee of Nvidia. Nvidia said its board had accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress, will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang. Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993. Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26. “Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.” The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed. After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days. Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said. The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO. According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year. Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed. The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum. Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported. The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips. Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported. Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang. In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported. On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO. “I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said. When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia, Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.” Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.” “Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang wrote. Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day. Three Republican congressmen — Chairman John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Chairman Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Chairman Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence — sent a request to Huang for a closed-door joint briefing with their three committees. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People’s Republic of China]’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the chairmen wrote. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.” U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year when the New York Times broke the story in late October that the two executives also had a close relationship. An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.” U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, wa
