articles.content: The U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on April 18, 2024. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)WASHINGTON — Members of the U.S. Senate Homeland Security committee Thursday questioned the potential new head of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency about nationwide security disruptions that members of Congress said have left the American public on edge. Democrats also accused the Trump administration of trying to quickly confirm that nominee and others during the lame-duck session of Congress, before Democrats gain majority control of the Senate in January. Democrats are set to come in with 56 seats. Oklahoma Republican James Lankford, who is running to serve as the top GOP senator on the committee in the next Congress, defended President Donald Trump’s decision to make the nominations now. “The White House seemed to have followed the letter of the law,” Lankford said. “I’m not completely sure they followed the entire spirit of the law, but they have actually gone through the process that needs to be done to be able to put the nominees forward, to be able to have the input.” Trump nominated Michael LoSapio to be Director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, housed within the Department of Homeland Security. The agency handles election security and oversees protection of federal infrastructure from cyber attacks. Senators also questioned at length a nominee who has generated opposition among Democrats, Eric M. Ueland, whom Trump has tapped to be comptroller general of the U.S. Government Accountability Office, the top federal government watchdog agency. Scary tech outages Widespread technology outages have occurred for days across the United States, including tens of thousands of canceled flights, transaction problems at major banks and shut-down email services at the National Security Agency. Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a former national security federal government worker, grilled LoSapio about nationwide cyber outages. “American citizens are jittery,” she said. She raised concerns about the Trump administration’s decision to eliminate more than 1,000 positions at CISA. She asked LoSapio if he agreed with that decision and if he thinks CISA needs more funding. LoSapio said he couldn’t comment “on the current state of CISA,” because he was coming in from the private sector. LoSapio is Palantir Technology Inc.’s chief information security officer. LoSapio added that once he evaluates the agency, if he feels CISA needs more funding, he would ask Congress. “I’m going to get involved and understand where the gaps are, and I will come back to this committee with the gap analysis,” he said. Slotkin said she was not satisfied with his answer. “At the end of the day, every American knows that cyberattacks are going up, that the risks are going up,” she said. “You should be able to say clearly, ‘There’s increasing threat, therefore, we need increasing resources to deal with it.’” Connecticut Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal asked LoSapio about who won the 2020 presidential election, because CISA deals with election security. Trump has falsely claimed that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from him, and galvanized a mob of his supporters to stop the certification of the election by storming the U.S. Capitol. “I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” LoSapio said. Blumenthal said LoSapio should not be allowed to run CISA if he couldn’t answer that former President Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election. “You are disqualified from the position that you’ve been nominated to fill,” he said. He then asked LoSapio if the U.S. Capitol was attacked on Jan. 6, 2021. “I don’t believe it was an attack,” LoSapio said. Blumenthal asked LoSapio if he was “alive on the planet” during the Jan. 6 insurrection. LoSapio said he was. Impoundments GAO as the federal watchdog investigates fraud or violations of federal law. Ueland would serve for 15 years if confirmed by the Senate. He currently works at the Office of Management and Budget, which has come under scrutiny from GAO for violating the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, which occurs when federal funds approved by Congress are withheld without congressional consent. The Supreme Court last year allowed the Trump administration to move forward with withholding billions in foreign aid funding through what is called a pocket rescission, which means the president makes the request to cancel funds very late in the fiscal year. But the court stopped short of making a decision on the merits of the case and whether the president has the authority to unilaterally impound congressional appropriations. Michigan Democratic Sen. Gary Peters pressed Ueland about how GAO has found several times that OMB violated the federal impoundment law. He asked Ueland if he agreed with GAO’s conclusion. Ueland declined to reach a conclusion. “I’ve not had a chance to review those reports, and I took an affirmative decision not to because it was critical that if I am confirmed and have the privilege of serving as comptroller general, that I not prejudge or come to this committee with formed conclusions about what it is that GAO has rendered as advice to Congress,” Ueland said. “Instead, a clear commitment to continue to follow the process that GAO as comptroller general, is what I give to all of you.” The chair of the committee, Kentucky Republican Sen. Rand Paul, asked Ueland if he would ignore a request by the Trump administration to stop an investigation. Ueland said he would. “We will fully follow through on charges from Congress, and in the event of obstacles, figure out ways to proceed to try to elicit information,” he said. New Hampshire Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan questioned Ueland about the reaction to him leading the watchdog organization from his boss, OMB Director Russell Vought, who has publicly commented that GAO should not exist. Ueland said Vought didn’t say much. Hassan seemed skeptical. “You’ve been nominated to serve as a watchdog over … an agency that your boss thinks shouldn’t even exist, and now you are claiming to this committee that you only had a single passing conversation with your current boss about your nomination to lead that agency,” she said. “Is that correct?” Ueland said the most acknowledgment Vought gave was a head nod. Other nominees Senators also took up the nominations of: Michael Chamberlain to be director for the Office of Government Ethics Robert Steffens to be a governor for the United States Postal Service Jeffrey Zisk to be a commissioner for the Postal Regulatory Commission Maria D’Avanzo to be inspector general for the General Services Administration Mark Priebe to be inspector general for the U.S. Department of Education Dennis Kirk to be inspector general for the U.S. Department of the Interior Robert Steinau to be inspector general for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration Eric Glover, Fernando Campoamor-Sanchez, Roman Chaban, and Bernard Desrosiers to be associate judges for the Superior Court of the District of Columbia

articles.description: More states are seeing new cases of bird flu in cattle as state agricultural officials urge the federal government to prioritize approving vaccines for dairy cows. The virus, highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1, known commonly as bird flu, has been affecting poultry flocks for years. But in 2024, it was first detected in cows. Epidemiologists […]
articles.content: Cows from a non-suspect herd are seen at the Cornell Teaching Dairy Barn at Cornell University in 2024 in Ithaca, N.Y. States are seeing new cases of bird flu in cattle as state agricultural officials urge the federal government to prioritize approving vaccines for dairy cows. (Photo by Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)More states are seeing new cases of bird flu in cattle as state agricultural officials urge the federal government to prioritize approving vaccines for dairy cows. The virus, highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1, known commonly as bird flu, has been affecting poultry flocks for years. But in 2024, it was first detected in cows. Epidemiologists think cows initially contracted it via wild birds, and that the virus continued to spread between cattle via equipment and interstate transporting of asymptomatic dairy cattle. While cases peaked in 2024, states are still seeing new infections in cattle this year. The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service reported that there are cases in states this year that previously hadn’t seen infections among dairy herds: Last Saturday, Oklahoma saw its first case since the outbreaks among cows began that year, according to data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Oregon also detected its first diagnosis at a dairy herd last week, as did Indiana, earlier this month, bringing the total number of states where the virus has been detected in dairy cattle to 22. Colorado, Idaho, Texas and Washington state have also reported cases among cattle over the past month. This year so far, there have been at least 146 dairy cattle infected with the virus, with more than 1,200 cases among cattle since the outbreak began. On Nov. 6, the National Association of State Departments of Agriculture, which represents agricultural officials across all 50 states, and the National Assembly of State Animal Health Officials, wrote a letter to the USDA urging the agency to prioritize developing an emergency vaccination framework for cows, “to take additional action to control and ultimately eradicate” the virus in dairy cattle. Cattle can develop short-lived immunity to the virus but can get re-infected, the groups wrote. The USDA says it supports rapid development and timely approval of a vaccine for dairy cattle, and several are undergoing field trials or awaiting final approval for emergency use. Developing and approving a vaccine has its own regulatory structure, and that can make for slow testing and implementation. Bird flu in livestock “poses an urgent threat to public and animal health, national agricultural stability, international market access, and the economic viability of the dairy and poultry industries across the U.S.,” the associations wrote. “… Without a proactive, coordinated eradication strategy, H5N1 risks becoming an endemic disease in U.S. dairy cattle, requiring USDA, State Animal Health Officials and industry to manage the disease for years while continuing to respond to costly spillover events in poultry.” The risk to humans and the general public is low, but dairy workers who work closely with herds are at highest risk. Washington state has seen roughly three dozen new cases among cattle over the past month, and one dairy worker there died earlier this month, bringing the total deaths among humans contracting the virus to three nationwide. United Farm Workers, a workers union, said they think officials are undercounting cases among farmworkers in Washington state, and that immigration enforcement activity is hindering workers from interacting with public health systems. Last year, federal officials announced a $1 billion plan to fight the outbreak among poultry flocks in an effort to lower egg prices, with research into a vaccine for poultry as part of the plan. “Veterinary and state government leaders need every available tool to protect the agricultural economy in their states and empower their farmers in combating this virus to protect their dairy herds and poultry flocks. We are asking USDA for their support in helping our farmers,” Dr. Alex Hamberg, president of the National Assembly of State Animal Health Officials, said in a joint press release. articles.title: FEMA chief, US House members push for emergency management changes
articles.description: WASHINGTON — Federal Emergency Management Agency Administrator Cameron Hamilton testified before a U.S. House panel Thursday that he hopes to make significant alterations in the years ahead, though he didn’t share details. “The president’s vision is clear: Stronger states make a more capable, ready and resilient nation,” he said. “While FEMA is ready to meet […]
articles.content: The Federal Emergency Management Agency in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)WASHINGTON — Federal Emergency Management Agency Administrator Cameron Hamilton testified before a U.S. House panel Thursday that he hopes to make significant alterations in the years ahead, though he didn’t share details. “The president’s vision is clear: Stronger states make a more capable, ready and resilient nation,” he said. “While FEMA is ready to meet the current and future challenges, we must be reformed in an immediate, commonsense and lasting way.” A review council created by President Donald Trump released a report in May that called for local, state and tribal governments to “lead disaster response with the federal government in a supporting role,” but so far neither the administration nor Congress has taken action to implement the proposed changes. Alabama Republican Rep. Dale Strong, chairman of the Homeland Security Committee’s Emergency Management and Technology Subcommittee, said during the hearing “the need for meaningful reform has become increasingly clear.” “In recent years, we’ve seen the challenges that FEMA and the state governments face when responding to multiple major disasters,” he said. “In 2024, Hurricanes Helene and Milton struck within weeks of each other, followed by devastating wildfires in Southern California. These events underscored the importance of ensuring FEMA has the capacity and resources to respond effectively when communities need assistance most.” New York Democratic Rep. Tim Kennedy, ranking member on the panel, raised numerous grievances with how FEMA has managed counterterrorism grants and how it has responded to severe storms. “I want to say from the outset that I’m deeply concerned about the direction of FEMA under the Trump administration and your leadership,” he said. “Since January of 2025, you’ve helped set in motion a series of decisions that undermine the agency and weaken our nation’s disaster preparedness, making it harder for Americans to get help when they need it the most.” Kennedy said the administration “unlawfully shut down” the Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities, or BRIC, program that helps local and state governments prepare ahead of natural disasters. He mentioned that the agency gave U.S. Doge Services access to people’s information. And he said the agency was trying to move “disaster responsibilities onto states and local communities, even though FEMA’s own research shows that they lack the resources and capacity to manage them.” Despite a promise from Trump to restore counterterrorism funding to New York state, Kennedy said the administration still owed $87 million, hampering the city’s police and fire departments. “Without this funding, the NYPD’s counterterrorism and intelligence operatives will lose critical capabilities. FDNY will have to cut their hazmat team, their search and rescue team, and special operations command,” he said. “And it places into serious jeopardy emergency management for Erie and Niagara counties in western New York.” Hamilton testified during the hearing that FEMA planned to distribute the funding for fiscal year 2026, which concluded at the end of September, “shortly.” He said the amount the state would receive should be similar to previous levels. Katrina recovery ongoing Louisiana Democratic Rep. Troy Carter thanked Hamilton for approving a deadline extension “for several remaining Hurricane Katrina recovery projects, including the city of New Orleans Joint Infrastructure Recovery Request Program.” “This extension will allow the city to finish repairing some 10,000 blocks of streets and drainage systems damaged by catastrophic flooding,” he added. “Projects like these are critical for communities throughout south Louisiana, where the effects of Hurricane Katrina remain visible more than 20 years later.” Carter then asked Hamilton to commit to helping local and state officials move forward on about 20 other projects that are related to Hurricane Katrina, which struck in August 2005. Hamilton said he would “be happy to work with you in ways to ensure that these programs, which are awarded, can move forward in a successful manner.” Response based on governor’s party? Illinois Democratic Rep. Delia Ramirez didn’t receive such a commitment from Hamilton when she questioned him about why her home state was denied three times following a severe storm in 2025, but neighboring Indiana, which was struck by the same weather system, was approved for federal assistance from FEMA. “What I can tell you is, as a public servant, we support the decisions of the president,” Hamilton said. “The entirety of the Stafford Act declarations are at his discretion. The president is a very intelligent, very dynamic individual.” Ramirez then asked Hamilton to explain what “statutory criteria” Indiana met that Illinois hadn’t. He responded that FEMA had looked at “damages to roads, damages to power infrastructure, damages to fuel distribution centers, damages to corporate and public buildings.” Ramirez told Hamilton that Illinois was able to prove the state incurred similar damage three times, but was denied repeatedly. “What I’m really concerned about is that having a Republican governor seems to be a statutory requirement for getting FEMA assistance, not actually responding to emergencies that every state deserved to have a response to,” she said. Ramirez added that during the next Congress, when Democrats will take control of both chambers, there will be a significantly different approach to oversight of the Trump administration, including FEMA. “We are going to do a lot of oversight,” she said. “And one of the things that we have to do is to ensure that FEMA, (the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) and the Coast Guard are able to protect their mission and not be politicized.”

articles.title: Civil rights complaint filed against Cheboygan County officials over Islamophobic posts
articles.description: A Cheboygan County planning commissioner’s recent social media post, which called anyone who voted for a Muslim in the Nov. 3 election a “treasonous traitor,” has been referred to state civil rights officials and criticized as Islamophobic by the head of a prominent Muslim civil rights organization in Michigan. At least two complaints have been […]
articles.content: Michigan Department of Civil Rights office in Lansing. July 23, 2026 | Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceA Cheboygan County planning commissioner’s recent social media post, which called anyone who voted for a Muslim in the Nov. 3 election a “treasonous traitor,” has been referred to state civil rights officials and criticized as Islamophobic by the head of a prominent Muslim civil rights organization in Michigan. At least two complaints have been filed over the Nov. 5 Facebook post from Cheboygan County Planning Commissioner John Studer, which quoted another post from a community group unaffiliated with the county. The post was also liked by Cheboygan County Commissioner Tom Eustice, who shared a separate video of fitness influencer Jillian Michaels criticizing U.S. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and then offering an extremist interpretation of Sharia law. Studer responded to Eustice’s repost of Michaels’ video by saying, “So many are clueless!! This is a battle older than we can comprehend.” On Nov. 16, almost two weeks after El-Sayed’s election and following the post by Studer, a county resident filed a complaint that was sent to both the Cheboygan County administrator’s office and the Michigan Department of Civil Rights. “As you know, there is no religious test for public office under the United States Constitution,” the complaint said. “It is also unconstitutional, under the United States Constitution and the Constitution of Michigan, to discriminate against someone on the basis of race, ethnicity, or religion. I demand a full and independent investigation.” The complaint said that should the investigation determine that Studer made the post and that Eustice liked it, the full county Board of Commissioners should, at a minimum, censure Eustice and remove Studer from his appointed position as a planning commissioner. “This cannot and must not be tolerated by Cheboygan County,” the complaint added. Email and social media messages seeking comment from Studer and Eustice were not returned at the time of publication. Comments from either Studer or Eustice will be added to this article once they are received. What is Sharia law, and why is it so controversial in the United States? Tessa Roy, the public information officer for the Michigan Department of Civil Rights, confirmed for Michigan Advance that they had received the email complaint and that the department is evaluating the allegation, “as we would in any other similar situation.” “Since this matter is pending, we cannot comment on it any further,” Roy told the Advance. Cheboygan County Administrator Jeff Lawson, in an email to the Advance, also acknowledged the receipt of the complaint, but said there may be little that it can do officially because the comments were made on Studer’s and Eustice’s personal social media pages. “Cheboygan County takes any complaint alleging discrimination including, but not limited to, religious discrimination very seriously,” Lawson said, adding that the alleged statements in question were made on the individuals’ personal social media account, “outside of any official municipal meeting, event, activity, or communication.” Lawson added members of municipal boards and commissions, “like all individuals, retain the right to express personal opinions in their private capacity.” “Individuals’ personal statements do not necessarily reflect the views, policies, opinions or positions of Cheboygan County,” Lawson wrote. “Cheboygan County is committed to treating all individuals equally and with dignity and respect, regardless of their religious beliefs, ethnicity, national origin or affiliations. Cheboygan County firmly rejects all forms of discrimination including religious discrimination or intolerance.” Studer is a member of the Michigan Republican Party’s 1st Congressional District executive committee, and also ran for county sheriff in 2024. He serves on the county’s planning and zoning board, as well as the county Soil Conservation District Board. Several posts on Studer’s personal Facebook page contain anti-Muslim sentiments, along with criticisms of El-Sayed and other Muslim officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, that are focused on their religion. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE El-Sayed will become the nation’s first Muslim member of the U.S. Senate when he is sworn into office early next year. He was the most prominent Muslim candidate on the statewide Michigan ballot. Dawud Walid, director of the Michigan chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the nation’s largest Muslim civil rights and advocacy organization, has also called for an inquiry “into the bigoted post and the sharing of it by one of its planning commissioners, as well as one of its own members.” “Government officials, who were elected to serve residents and visitors irrespective of religious affiliation, should not be impugned as traitors for voting for fellow Americans that are Muslims,” Walid said in a statement. Meanwhile, CAIR-MI said it was also contacted by a concerned Cheboygan County resident, who is not Muslim, regarding the comment. Although a majority of Cheboygan County voters chose former Republican nominee Mike Rogers over El-Sayed, CAIR-MI did note that more than 2,300 county residents cast ballots for El-Sayed. El-Sayed defeated Rogers statewide by seven percentage points. While his election was historically significant, Walid said that there has been an increased amount of fearmongering and vitriol against Michigan’s Muslim population “due to millions of dollars recently poured into advertisements attempting to defeat Senator-elect El-Sayed in the 2026 midterm election.” CAIR’s latest civil rights report also documented more than 8,600 instances of anti-Muslim bias complaints last year, which was the highest number recorded of such incidents since CAIR began publishing its civil rights report in 1996.

articles.title: Anthropic’s IPO could deliver $156B to charity
articles.description: At a stock price of $95, the frontier lab's Public Benefit Foundation, its employee donations, and the company's match tot up to $156 billion.
articles.content: Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO has made quite a few people generationally wealthy, but it will also be an enormous windfall for the causes backed by the frontier lab and its employees. As you might expect from a company whose leadership emerged from the world of effective altruism (EA), Anthropic has multiple different avenues for cash raised in its market debut to be directed to philanthropy. First, the company’s Public Benefit Fund, or PBF (analogous to OpenAI’s foundation), was allotted 5% of the company’s shares, almost 850 million. At the current trading price of about $95, that will leave it with an endowment of $80 billion. And if the company continues its astonishing growth rate, Anthropic could add further 2% increases every time the company’s valuation grows more than 50% over the IPO price of $83, or about $124.50 per share for the next threshold. The PBF’s money will be focused on research and activities related to increasing the benefit of artificial intelligence to humanity. The first commitment of the PBF was $200 million to study the impact of AI on workers; Anthropic has said it will consider donations to philanthropic organizations or “direct distributions to specific populations” — perhaps a hint of future UBI plans. Anthropic also donated $50 million to the city of San Francisco last week. A company spokesperson tells TechCrunch the donation did not come from the PBF. Next, Anthropic’s employees have pledged shares to philanthropic causes of their choice, and the company will match those donations 3-to-1 for longer tenured employees and 1-to-1 for newer ones. In its S-1 filing, the company said that it had reserved more than 550 million shares to fulfill pledges made before September 30. Working backwards from that figure, and based on the disclosure that 84% of the shares were reserved for early employee matches, we can estimate that employees have pledged $23 billion of donations; the company’s match on those would be roughly $53 billion, depending on the stock price when those matches are delivered. All told, it adds up to $156 billion — a huge amount of potential philanthropy. For context, Americans donated $617 billion to charity in 2025; if all of the pledged funds resulting from today’s transactions get to do-gooders, that will be equal to about a quarter of all U.S. donations made last year. Employees will need to make good on their pledges for this to work out, and the value of the match will ultimately depend on when Anthropic makes its donation. The shares could also go to donor-advised funds, which would likely limit their initial impact. Interviews with employees and institutions suggest that donors are most likely to support EA-inflected charities like Longview Philanthropy, GiveWell, Coefficient Giving, Foresight Institute, and Giving What We Can. And it seems likely that significant funding will be allocated to AI safety research, given the concerns expressed about that subject by many Anthropic employees. Mamdani signs bill to ban horse-drawn carriages in New York City
articles.content: Animal rights activists back the new law while workers’ unions oppose the ban over concerns about lost livelihoods Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, has signed a bill that will bring the city’s horse-drawn carriage industry to an end by 1 June 2028. Known as Romanch’s Law, the legislation is named after 18-year-old Indian tourist, Romanch Mahajan, who was killed in June after being thrown from a carriage in Central Park when a horse became startled. The law marks the end of an industry that has operated in the city for more than a century. The legislation has been divisive, with workers’ unions opposing the ban over concerns about lost livelihoods, while animal rights activists have backed the move, citing longstanding concerns over horse welfare, including cases in which horses have died from exhaustion. During Thursday’s signing, Mamdani said: “For 150 years, horse-drawn carriages have been a fixture of Central Park. Today, we are bringing that chapter to a close. This industry will come to an end, and we have a responsibility to the workers whose livelihoods depend on it. We will work alongside them to ensure they have the financial support and career opportunities they need to build their next chapter.” Julie Menin, the New York city council’s speaker, also described the legislation as a historic milestone, saying: “This is a truly historic day for New York City, nearly two decades after the council first considered ending the horse-drawn carriage industry.” “Today, I’m thinking of Romanch Mahajan, who should still be with us and whose tragic, untimely death reminds us why this legislation was so urgently needed. This law will protect the welfare of horses while ensuring that the hard-working New Yorkers who depend on this industry have the support they need to transition to new employment opportunities,” Menin added. On Tuesday, the Mamdani administration announced a transition plan aimed at supporting about 200 affected workers, including medallion owners, carriage drivers and stable hands. The city, which will release a full transition plan by April 2027, said it plans to facilitate medallion buy-backs, as well as provide stipends and career assistance. City officials also said they would engage with the Transport Workers Union, which represents carriage industry workers. Mamdani’s administration said that city officials will establish a Horse Carriage Worker Industry Program offering job training, career counseling, entrepreneurship support, employer connections and tuition assistance. The city also said it would commission a feasibility study examining electric carriages and electric pedal-assist bicycles as potential alternatives in Central Park, as well as electric carriages along the park’s perimeter.

articles.description: Some models fare better, but all fail in similar ways.
articles.content: Many studies over the years have examined how people encounter climate science information. Some focused on the top results that Google surfaced (back when Google was still in the business of serving links), while others examined social media content or newspaper and TV news coverage. With large language models (LLMs) now forming a share of the public information diet, it's worth looking at how they handle climate change. But there’s no direct way for researchers to look at the information people have seen. It is served ephemerally to individual users, confined to their chat session. A study led by researchers from University College London and the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) tried to tackle this question from multiple angles, testing LLMs with different prompts and evaluating their output. They started with benchmarks of simple factual questions (benchmarks that might even be in models’ training data at this point) but also analyzed more complex interactions—including when users think they’re right to push back on an answer. CO2 Q&A LLM research often faces (no-true-Scotsman-tinged) criticism for focusing on a particular model rather than some other frontier model that may have been released after the experiment concluded. In this case, the study used 33 models, including multiple versions of the major frontier and open-weight models. The flagship frontier models used were Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Gemini 3.6 Flash, and GPT-5.6 Sol. (You can find the full list in the report.)Read full article Comments

articles.content: Google announced Android developer verification last year, and despite numerous objections from developers and users, the company is forging ahead. Google says it will start rolling out the requirement in all regions in January 2027, and it urges devs who still haven't registered their apps to do so soon. The apps you download from the Play Store all come from verified developers, and Google's new requirement expands that requirement to apps from third-party sources. articles.title: A state-level voting rights act is Michigan Democrats’ top priority
articles.description: Democrats in Lansing have tried but failed to pass the Michigan Voting Rights Act in each of the last two legislative sessions.
articles.content: This article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization covering local election administration and voting access. This story also appeared in Votebeat A proposal to protect minority voting rights in Michigan is coming back to the key swing state. Democrats in Lansing have tried but failed to pass the Michigan Voting Rights Act in each of the last two legislative sessions. But now that the party has regained full control of state government, the proposal might actually make it into law. Democratic Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson — who currently serves as Michigan’s top election official as secretary of state — has named the act as her top priority, saying on the campaign trail that it would be the first bill she would sign. And leaders in the House and Senate say they will work hard to pass it during next year’s legislative session, which starts Jan. 1. Speaker-elect Ranjeev Puri told Votebeat on Thursday that “there is a lot of interest and excitement amongst the Michigan House Democrats” to make sure the proposal passes, although he declined to give a specific timeline. Senate Majority Leader-elect Darrin Camilleri said in a statement that, as a lead sponsor of the act, “it is of course very high on my list of priorities when Democrats regain our trifecta in January.” At their core, the four bills that make up the Michigan Voting Rights Act aim to fill in the gaps of the federal Voting Rights Act, which has been chipped away at by court rulings in recent years. Several other states already have state-level voting rights acts, but Michigan would be the first true swing state to pass one, so its passage would mark an important milestone for voting rights advocates. The act would also add to the long list of ways the state has expanded voting rights over the past decade. But not everyone is excited about the proposed changes. What’s in the Michigan Voting Rights Act? It’s not clear if Democrats will modify the existing bills before reintroducing them when the session starts. But the 2027-2028 version of the Michigan Voting Rights Act is expected to be substantially similar to the two versions that have been introduced before. In past sessions, the first bill in the package proposed banning “discriminatory activity” in voting and established a legal framework for challenging it. It prohibited local governments from imposing prerequisites on voting or causing voting disparities between members of a protected class — including racial or language minority groups — “and other members of the electorate.” It also would introduce new requirements for notifying voters about changes to elections, including new polling places or precinct boundaries. The bill also would allow voters to sue municipalities over alleged violations of the act. It proposed granting courts the ability to appoint election monitors, have veto power over election-related changes such as moving polling places, and more — an echo of requirements that were once part of the federal Voting Rights Act before the Supreme Court struck them down in 2013. The second bill in the package proposed creating a “voting and elections database and institute” at at least one state university which would track and publish election data, such as precinct-level results and voter registration information. The third of the four bills would require jurisdictions to translate materials into another language if a significant number of voters speak that language and aren’t proficient in English. It also would establish thresholds for which communities needed to provide those translated materials and created an advisory council, with members appointed by the secretary of state, to suggest requirements. Language access is covered by Section 203 of the federal Voting Rights Act. Michigan’s proposal goes further and would set a lower bar for when ballots need to be translated and in which communities. The federal act, for example, does not include Arabic and related languages — which is relevant in Michigan’s case, since Arabic is the state’s third-most commonly spoken language. The final bill aimed to provide more conveniences for voters, including those with special concerns such as voters with disabilities. It would codify curbside voting, permit voters with language barriers to bring their own translators, and allow people to provide “food, warmth, or other necessities” to people in line to vote. It would also require governments to disclose when they made certain administrative changes, such as removing voters from the rolls or allowing voters to examine voting equipment. Why hasn’t the Michigan Voting Rights Act passed before? In past sessions, the Michigan Voting Rights Act simply wasn’t able to make it over the finish line. The package was first introduced in 2023, the last time Democrats controlled the Senate, House, and governor’s office all at once. During that session, though, the bills sat in committee for almost a year before the Senate passed them in September 2024, with just three months left in the session. Legislators tried to get them through the House as well — they even had a committee hearing in December — but the proposal ultimately died during a chaotic final month of the session when lame-duck Democrats struggled to move any legislation at all. Supporters tried again this year in the Senate, where the bills were re-introduced just a few weeks after the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in Louisiana v. Callais changed how race could be considered when redistricting, another blow to the federal Voting Rights Act. It passed the Senate in June. But the bill languished in the House, which had flipped to Republicans in the 2024 election. The divided Michigan Legislature has struggled to move any election-related legislation through both chambers this session; it took until June of this year for any voting legislation to earn the governor’s signature. How does the Michigan Voting Rights Act compare to other states? If the bills that make up the Michigan Voting Rights Act ultimately do pass, Michigan will be far from the only state with a voting rights act. The first passed in California in 2002, and the next came almost a decade later in Illinois in 2011. Since then, more states have looked at passing them, in large part as a response to the weakening of the federal Voting Rights Act. To date, 12 states — all controlled by Democrats — have enacted one. Michigan’s could be the most impactful one yet, though. As a swing state, Michigan has an outsized influence in federal elections, including for president. Marisa Wright, legal counsel for voting rights at the Campaign Legal Center, said the Michigan Voting Rights Act would position the state as a leader in voting rights across the U.S. “I know there are many important issues people care about, but I think we have seen, especially recently, the right to vote is our most critical fundamental right,” she told Votebeat. Sixty percent of voting-age Michiganders voted in the 2026 election, according to unofficial results — tied for the highest midterm turnout in state history. Experts say that is at least in part because voting has become more accessible in the state in the last decade. Since 2018, Michigan voters have approved ballot measures enacting automatic registration, no-excuse absentee voting, Election Day registration, early in-person voting, the right to permanent absentee ballots, and ballot drop boxes. The Michigan Voting Rights Act would continue that trend. By strengthening the rights of disabled voters, improving language access, and addressing discrimination, Wright said the act has the potential to protect voters in the sort of “meaningful” ways that no longer exist at the federal level. A state-level act is not a replacement for strong federal legislation, she said, but it can be an important start. Josh Douglas, an election law professor at the University of Kentucky, said that the strongest voting rights acts offer a state’s voters “robust voter protections,” such as the right to sue over alleged violations, and strict scrutiny for proposed voting restrictions — the exact kind of tools legislators are looking to implement with the Michigan Voting Rights Act. It will take more than just getting the bills to the governor’s desk, though, Douglas said. It also matters how state courts interpret the laws, which can be harder to predict. “Just passing the law is the first step, but it’s not the last,” he said. How do election officials feel about the Michigan Voting Rights Act? Voting rights advocates may be enthusiastic about the Michigan Voting Rights Act, but clerks — the people who actually run Michigan elections — have expressed reservations. When the act was first introduced, Michigan’s two major clerk groups had a hand in shaping its contents. But clerks said they were still concerned about being held responsible for violations of the act, even accidental ones. A number of them spoke out against the original proposals, and their groups issued neutral positions on the bills. “Although these bills are well intentioned, they have the potential of paralyzing clerks from making necessary ministerial decisions in the best interests of their voters, in fear of soliciting costly lawsuits further damaging public trust in our electoral process,” the Michigan Association of Municipal Clerks said in a statement in 2024. Individual clerks testified before the legislature and told Votebeat they felt the same way, both in 2024 and earlier this year. Chris Swope, the Lansing City Clerk, has testified multiple times about his concerns over the proposal. Like others, his concern was that punishing clerks would damage trust in elections rather than improve it. “As clerks, our whole job is to ensure the voting rights of individuals here in Michigan, so we take this very seriously,” Swope said during the May hearing. Swope told Votebeat on Tuesday that his conversations with lawmakers suggest that the 2027 version of the act may address some of those concerns. While he supports the concept of a state-level voting rights act, particularly the expansion of language access, he wants the version that is put into law to change how penalties for clerks are handled. In particular, he wanted to see the “public shaming” portion of the act — which would require the secretary of state’s office to publicly name communities that fail to issue required notices on time and keep that violation notice up for at least a year — to be removed. “We’re humans, and we make errors,” he said. “We train our election workers, but they make errors. Putting that on a secretary of state website doesn’t feel helpful or beneficial to the whole process.” He is cautiously optimistic about what the bills will say if and when they are signed into law. Swope said it was “pretty clear” the Michigan Voting Rights Act was finally going to pass next session, and at this point, he feels “pretty good” about that. “I’m a believer in voting rights,” he said. “I think we should make sure that people have full access.” Hayley Harding is a reporter for Votebeat based in Michigan. Contact Hayley at hharding@votebeat.org. Votebeat is a nonprofit news organization covering local election integrity and voting access. Sign up for their newsletters here.

Suspect nabbed in vape-shop robberies in Shelby, Chesterfield townships
articles.content: A man who robbed vape shops in Chesterfield and Shelby townships last weekend was arrested Wednesday after detectives worked together to identify and locate him, police said. The man was expected to be formally with armed robbery and weapons offenses for the alleged Saturday, Nov. 14, incident in Chesterfield and Sunday, Nov. 15, incident in Shelby, according to Chesterfield Township police. The suspect entered the Vapor Shoppe Smoke and Alternative Plus shop located at Gratiot Avenue and 24 Mile Road at about 10 p.m. Saturday and demanded an employee fill the duffle bag with expensive store merchandise, police said. The employee told police he feared for his safety as the suspect, who implied he was armed, threatened to hurt him if he didn’t comply, police said. The suspect fled with the duffle bag full of merchandise. Chesterfield Township detectives identified the suspect and determined he was armed from store security video, police said. Later during the investigation, Chesterfield Township detectives were contacted by Shelby Township detectives, who said the same suspect committed a similar offense Sunday at a vape shop in their township. After Chesterfield Township police obtained an arrest warrant for the suspect, Shelby Township detectives located him with the help of a Flock camera and arrested him at about 4:30 p.m. Wednesday during a traffic stop at 21 Mile Road and Gratiot Avenue in Chesterfield Township, police said. In addition to the robbery charge, which carries a maximum penalty of life in prison upon conviction, the warrant charges the suspect with felony firearm possession, carrying a concealed weapon and felony in possession of a firearm, police said. “I am extremely proud of the work our detectives put into this investigation,” said Brian Bassett, director of Public Safety and chief of police for Chesterfield Township. “Their professionalism, persistence, and commitment to holding those responsible accountable resulted in the apprehension of a dangerous suspect. I also want to thank the Shelby Township Police Department for their assistance and outstanding partnership throughout the investigation. This is a great example of how collaboration between law enforcement agencies strengthens our ability to keep our communities safe.” Anyone with more information about the suspect and/or the robberies is encouraged to contact Chesterfield Township police Det. Jason Kline at 586-949-3573.

articles.title: Mega-farms are booming in Michigan, drowning rivers in manure
articles.description: Industrial-scale livestock farms are increasing in Michigan. They generate 1,000 tanker trucks-worth of untreated waste a day, and the state’s efforts to better regulate them have faced lawsuits.
articles.content: Michigan rivers are suffering as the industrial-scale livestock industry expands in nearby communities The Pine River in Gratiot County is among the casualties, with fecal pollution levels that have skyrocketed in recent years State officials want to tighten manure pollution controls, but are caught in a yearslong legal battle with industry GRATIOT COUNTY — For generations in this agricultural region in the heart of Michigan’s Lower Peninsula, summertime revolved around fishing, boating and swimming in the tranquil Pine River. Not anymore. Bridge Listens: See how you can get involved What you should know Fecal-contaminated rivers expose Michiganders who swim, boat, or fish to bacteria, viruses and parasites from sewer overflows, farm runoff and failing septic systems. The contamination likely sickens thousands of people each year and can depress tourism and home values. Who's making public decisions The Michigan Legislature and EGLE hold the key authority over septic rules, farm manure regulation and enforcement, while local municipalities work to make sewer upgrades. Ways to participate Look up your state lawmakers on the state House Natural Resources and Tourism Committee →Contact state representatives who work on the environment. Look up your state lawmakers on the state Senate Energy and Environment Committee →Contact state senators dealing with environmental issues. Attend the Grand Traverse County Board of Public Works meeting →The board meets the second Thursday of the month at Garfield Township Hall, and its verified agenda includes well and water tank inspections, sewer pump station upgrades for several townships, and a state violation notice over a sewage overflow. Powered by Civic Action Toolbox One by one, residents have pulled docks, sold boats and stowed tackleboxes as much of the river has transformed into a feces-tainted mess, unsafe for swimming and often too weedy to navigate by boat. The situation is bleaker in some feeder creeks, where putrid brown water hardly harbors a frog or fish. “It’s enough to wake you up at night from the smell,” said 78-year-old Jane Jelenek, whose family has owned the same waterfront home for six decades.Donate The Pine is among some three-quarters of Michigan’s rivers and streams polluted by levels of human and animal waste that exceed state water quality standards and may sicken thousands of residents per year. Related: Pure Michigan has a poop problem: Dangerous fecal levels befoul 3 of 4 rivers Michigan has ignored faulty septic systems for decades. The bill is coming due Environmental groups blame pollution in the Pine on waste from ballooning livestock herds at concentrated animal feeding operations, or CAFOs. They have proliferated in Gratiot County and across Michigan since the turn of the millennium, replacing mom-and-pop farms with vast feedlots that raise livestock by the thousands. “Something has got to give, because what is clear is that the land cannot absorb the amount of waste that is being applied and sliding off into rivers, lakes and groundwater,” said Liz Kirkwood, strategic partnership officer for Flow Water Advocates, which is involved in a legal fight over Michigan’s efforts to regulate the operations. The industrial facilities achieve economies of scale to deliver low-cost meat, eggs and dairy to US consumers, who eat far more of it than the global average. And for farmers, who don’t control the price their product commands, growth is survival. “Smaller farms have less financial cushion to survive down cycles,” said David Ortega, an agricultural economist at Michigan State University. “The result is production increasingly concentrated in fewer, larger operations.” The byproduct of this consolidation: Staggering quantities of feces and urine — 420 million gallons annually in Gratiot County alone — which CAFOs dispose of by spreading it untreated onto nearby fields. Collectively, Michigan’s 272 largest CAFOs generate more waste than the state’s entire human population — 1.1 million solid tons and 3.93 billion liquid gallons in 2024, according to state records analyzed by Bridge. That’s enough to fill 1,000 tanker trucks a day. State officials acknowledge too much ends up in rivers across the state, fueling bacteria outbreaks, weed and algae overgrowth and oxygen-depleted water where fish can’t breathe. “That harm compounds with each passing month,” Assistant Attorney General Elizabeth Morrisseau wrote in a June legal filing on the topic. But regulators have struggled to curb the pollution amid a yearslong court battle with the farm industry. It contends stricter waste control could drive farms out of business. “Efforts to increase farmers’ red tape, paperwork, operational limitations, governmental reports and so forth will have no positive effect,” Michigan Farm Bureau lawyer Any Kok said in a statement last November. Alma College professor Murray Borrello has spent decades monitoring E. coli and other pollutants in the Pine River and its tributaries. The watershed’s health has declined in lockstep with the expansion of large livestock operations. (Kelly House/Bridge Michigan) Amid the debate, some along this river have begun to fear that by the time regulations catch up to the pollution, the Pine will be too far gone to recover. “Every year is worse than the one before,” said Jelenek, who no longer touches the water for fear of getting sick. “The rules are written for the CAFOs. They’re not written for the rest of us that live here.” ‘The watershed is dying’ Gratiot County is a hub of a statewide CAFO industry that has expanded threefold in the past quarter-century. There are now 272 regulated CAFOs in Michigan, each with a minimum of 1,000 cattle, 700 dairy cows, 80,000 laying hens or 2,500 pigs. More operations avoid regulation by staying just under those size thresholds. Unlike traditional farms where livestock graze in open pastures, CAFOs raise cattle, swine and poultry by the thousands in confined spaces, collecting their waste in sheds or lagoons before trucking it to nearby fields. They tend to crop up in clusters, concentrating vast quantities of waste in just a handful of communities. “Too much in one spot is part of the issue,” said Bruce Washburn, an environmental quality specialist within the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy Water Resources Division. Gratiot County has 24 CAFOs — more per square mile than anywhere in the state. Since the turn of the millennium, its cattle herd has more than doubled while hog counts have tripled. Other hubs include dairy operations in the Thumb, along the Ohio border and in the central-northern Lower Peninsula; hog farms in Mason and Oceana counties near the central Lake Michigan coast; and poultry and swine operations that fan out south of Grand Rapids. When applied judiciously, nitrogen and phosphorus in manure is a useful fertilizer. But research shows that today’s farms often apply more than crops can absorb. And CAFO waste often isn’t manure alone, but a slurry-like mix of feces, urine and wastewater. Waste and meltwater pool at the edge of a farm field after being applied to snow-covered ground that later thawed — an example of the pollution that can occur when CAFO waste is applied in wintertime. (Courtesy of EGLE) The resulting pollution has become a nationwide public health crisis, harming ecosystems and tainting drinking water near farms from Iowa to the Carolinas. Michigan is not alone in its struggle to address it. “Nobody adequately regulates these things,” said Bob Martin, a farm policy advocate who led the American Public Health Association’s call for a moratorium on CAFO expansions until stricter rules are in place. The state deems a waterway out of compliance for swimming if the number of E. coli — one of many potentially harmful germs found in feces — exceeds 300 per 100-millileters of water (just under a half-cup) in a single sample, or a mean of 130 E. coli across multiple samples during a 30-day period. The limit for paddling, wading and fishing is 1,000 E. coli. These days, almost nowhere in the Pine River basin consistently makes the grade. “The watershed is dying,” said Murray Borrello, an Alma College professor who has spent two decades monitoring its decline. Click on the images to see caption information When it rains, E. coli levels in creeks near CAFO waste application fields can spike to 10 times the limit for safe human contact, according to Borrello’s research. Much of the bacteria is antibiotic-resistant, which he attributed to regular antibiotic use to promote growth and suppress disease in cramped livestock pens. Levels of phosphorus — a nutrient found in feces — have also skyrocketed in the Pine, fueling thick weeds and algae in the once-clear water. Data from across the state shows similar trends in Michigan’s other livestock industry hotspots. The data shows these hotspots exceed state limits for fecal and/or nutrient pollution. Industry officials dispute CAFOs’ role in Michigan’s pollution and often point to other potential culprits, such as leaky septic systems. But data from the Pine River watershed casts doubt on those arguments. Water sampling data collected by Borrello and his students shows areas immediately upstream and downstream of the facilities can have dramatically different pollution levels. And when a CAFO closes, nearby water quality quickly improves. “The CAFO impact is so immense, it dwarfs any impact from other inputs,” Borrello said. Ray Hitsman baits a line for his grandkids, Brynlei Conner and Nolan Measel, as the group fish at the Pine River in Alma. Nearby, a sign warns visitors that the water has high levels of E. coli, one of many potentially harmful pathogens caused by feces in the water. (Kelly House/Bridge Michigan) CAFO owners say they’re doing their best to prevent pollution, but curtailing manure spreading would eat into thin margins. Renting a tanker to haul waste costs upwards of $300 an hour. If manure must be spread thinner, then CAFOs will face higher hauling costs and stiffer competition for available land. “You can chew up a lot of money in a hurry, going an extra mile or an extra two miles,” said John Crain, a feedlot owner in the village of Breckenridge. Bridge Michigan reached out repeatedly to industry representatives, including the Michigan Farm Bureau, local Farm Bureau offices, the Michigan Milk Producers Association, Michigan Pork Producers Association and lawyers representing the CAFO industry. None would comment for this story. In legal filings and past public comments, industry advocates have described CAFO owners as environmental stewards. Land-applying waste, they argue, is beneficial because it helps farmers avoid the use of synthetic fertilizers. “Our farmers have more interest than anyone in preserving the state’s ecosystem for the future,” the Farm Bureau’s Kok said during a public hearing last year. It’s not convincing to Dennis Kellogg, a sixth-generation farmer who has seen and smelled the difference between CAFOs and the dairy farm he grew up on. “Never in my life did my dad or I haul loaded manure spreaders through the streets of Ithaca, Michigan,” Kellogg said. A manure tanker travels down the road in rural Gratiot County. The tankers have become a common sight on local roads as a surging livestock population leads to more manure that is spread on local farms. (Kelly House/Bridge Michigan) On a recent afternoon just outside Ithaca, semi-sized CAFO waste tankers rumbled down t

articles.title: Michigan rivers befouled by sewage, as deadlines to fix problems come and go
articles.description: From Detroit and Lansing to Manistique, cities are slow to make upgrades to stop releasing billions of gallons of sewage in Michigan’s rivers. Money is mostly to blame, but so is political inaction.
articles.content: Despite progress, systems that serve one-third of Michigan still dump sewage into the state’s rivers Upgrades cost billions of dollars and often are delayed because of other priorities Other states have made progress, but deadlines repeatedly come and go in Michigan cities to fix the problem When Nicky Marcot bought land on the Rouge River for an urban farm in 2006, she imagined tending backyard crops while her children explored the wooded riverbank. Those dreams washed away the first time it rained and a flood of toilet water swamped her lawn. Even a brief shower can overwhelm Detroit’s sewers, sending a polluted mix of stormwater and sewage into the Rouge just upstream of Marcot’s house in Detroit’s Brightmoor neighborhood. The rains leave a stench that can linger long after the waters recede. “Who wants to eat a head of lettuce that got covered in sewer overflow?” Marcot asked, much less let their kids play in the river. Nicky Marcot and her daughters stand in their yard along the Rouge River. The family raises goats and chickens on the property and gardens on the higher ground, above where floodwater reaches. (Brayan Gutierrez for Bridge Michigan) Despite a decades-old legal obligation to stop using rivers as emergency waste conduits, Detroit and several other Michigan cities are slow to comply, missing deadlines as other priorities take precedence in the battle for scarce public funds. The contamination likely sickens thousands of people each year and can depress tourism and home values. Who's making public decisions The Michigan Legislature and EGLE hold the key authority over septic rules, farm manure regulation and enforcement, while local municipalities work to make sewer upgrades. Ways to participate Look up your state lawmakers on the state House Natural Resources and Tourism Committee →Contact state representatives who work on the environment. Look up your state lawmakers on the state Senate Energy and Environment Committee →Contact state senators dealing with environmental issues. Attend the Grand Traverse County Board of Public Works meeting →The board meets the second Thursday of the month at Garfield Township Hall, and its verified agenda includes well and water tank inspections, sewer pump station upgrades for several townships, and a state violation notice over a sewage overflow. See the DWSD’s upcoming meetings →The story names the DWSD. We do not list its meetings yet, so check its own schedule for the next one. Look up EGLE water quality reports → What to watch for next Watch whether state lawmakers take up a statewide septic code or stronger manure rules, and whether EGLE's ongoing E. coli testing leads to more waterways being listed as impaired. Are you taking action? Let us know. Submit Thank you! Your response has been recorded. Powered by Civic Action Toolbox Donate While most sewer overflow issues have been fixed, nearly a third of Michigan’s population — some 3 million people — are served by antiquated systems that still periodically overflow. In recent years, that’s dumped as much as 9 billions of gallons of untreated sewage into Michigan rivers. It’s part of a toxic stew that has made 75% of Michigan’s 300-plus rivers and streams unsafe for swimming, likely sickening thousands of residents. Other culprits include livestock farms and septic systems. Related: Pure Michigan has a poop problem: Dangerous fecal levels befoul 3 of 4 rivers Michigan has ignored faulty septic systems for decades. The bill is coming due Stopping Michigan’s spills may take billions of dollars. While Grand Rapids and other communities have borrowed money to get the job done on time, leaders of other water systems say residents struggle to afford new debt or higher water rates. “If we had all the money in the world, would we address all the outfalls? Of course,” said Navid Mehram, wastewater chief for the Great Lakes Water Authority, which manages regional sewers for dozens of southeast Michigan communities. With the state and federal governments offering limited help, Marcot and other residents are left to endure pollution with no clear end in sight. “It’s just such a flabbergasting issue to have in the 21st century,” she said. “You read about the sewage in London back in 1800 that was causing cholera. We’re not supposed to have to deal with issues like this anymore.” A sign written in Spanish and Arabic says “No swimming” along the Rouge River in Melvindale, where people kayak and fish. (Brayan Gutierrez for Bridge Michigan) While states throughout the northeast have struggled with similar problems, some of Michigan’s neighbors have made recent strides in addressing them. Indiana has reduced its sewage overflows by 71% since 2004 by diverting money for repairs and mandating system audits. In Ohio, a 2011 federal consent decree led to $2.4 billion in upgrades that have prevented 2 billion gallons of overflows a year from reaching Lake Erie. Fixing Michigan’s overflow problem is “totally doable,” said Donna Kashian, director of environmental science at Wayne State University. “It’s just the commitment.” Delay after delay Water runs out of a Grand River outfall in downtown Lansing, one of several Michigan cities that has struggled to eliminate sewer overflows amid funding woes. (Simon Schuster/Bridge Michigan) Modern sewer systems are built with two pipes: One that carries wastewater to treatment plants and another that whisks rainwater to the nearest river. But cities developed before the mid-1900s often have so-called combined sewers, which drain gutters and toilets into a single pipe that overflows into rivers when it rains. By the late 20th century, the resulting pollution shocked the state and federal governments into action. Cities were put on deadlines to stop the overflows. Among those that still have not finished the job: Lansing, which was supposed to separate its sewer and stormwater systems by 2020. It could take another 25 years. Detroit, where a 2022 deadline to eliminate high-priority outfalls has been repeatedly extended. With 55 outfalls remaining, officials are not sure the new 2037 deadline is feasible. Manistique, which is working to eliminate its final untreated outfall. Dearborn, which has five untreated outfalls on the Rouge River. Niles, which still has one on the St. Joseph River. St. Joseph, which aims to eliminate discharges from its three remaining outfalls by 2030. The Detroit suburbs, where a combined 13 outfalls await action. Michigan officials say they’re working as fast as funding allows. Federal grants have shrunk considerably since the 1970s, when they covered more than half of water infrastructure spending. Today, it’s about 7%, according to figures from the US Water Alliance. State funding for water projects is also limited, dwarfed by other priorities. For example, Michigan devotes just $200 million in non-federal funding to water infrastructure, compared to more than $5 billion for roads. “People see the roads every day and they know when roads are underfunded,” said Andy Kilpatrick, Lansing’s public services director. “But they don’t think about what’s under the ground.” Strategies to address overflows include installing modern separated sewers, building massive overflow retention basins or using “green infrastructure” to absorb rainfall before it can flow into gutters. Even with the missed deadlines, Michigan has made progress, said Charles Hill, a wastewater specialist at the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy. Since 1988, the number of uncontrolled outfalls statewide has plunged from 613 to 99, he said. “You’re usually knocking away the low-hanging fruit first,” he said, which means remaining overflows will be costly and complicated to fix. Statewide, Michigan communities are bracing for $15 billion in unfunded stormwater and wastewater infrastructure needs in the coming two decades, according to a 2022 congressional report. The state’s broader water infrastructure system needs $85 billion in investment over the same time period, according to a September report commissioned by the Great Lakes Water Authority, southeast Michigan’s regional water provider. A struggle to make fixes In Detroit, officials have spent more than $1.4 billion on overflow reduction efforts that first began in the 1990s, but cash shortages make it tough to finish the job. Efforts to raise new revenue – such as the fee dubbed the “rain tax” by some city residents – have not been popular. The city’s latest plan emphasizes green infrastructure such as rain gardens and engineered wetlands, which alleviate pressure on sewers by diverting water elsewhere. It’s often far cheaper than separating sewers or building treatment basins. But even so, it’s not clear the city will meet its 2037 deadline to eliminate high-priority outfalls. “The reality of it is, we haven’t identified the funding,” said Sam Smalley, deputy director of the Detroit Water and Sewerage Department. Many Detroit residents struggle to pay bills that fund water system upgrades, and overflow mitigation competes with a laundry list of other priorities, from replacing ancient water mains to eliminating lead drinking water lines. More efficient plumbing, suburban flight and industry loss have all exacerbated the crisis, leaving cities with fewer customers to pay the bills. Lansing, which has lost 17,500 residents and auto factories since its 1970s peak, was forced to pause sewer separations for several years as costs nearly bankrupted the city sewer fund. The city of 113,000 residents now spends $30 million annually on the project with help from a low-interest state loan. It faces a 2035 deadline to stop overflows, but officials acknowledge work may not be done until 2050. “There’s a political reality that if we raise our rates too much, there will be backlash,” said Kilpatrick, the city’s public services director. Michigan cities are not alone. Similar issues plague hundreds of communities nationwide, particularly older cities in the northeast and Great Lakes. Cities that have managed to eliminate combined sewer overflows have often issued large revenue bonds to finance the work, with ratepayers paying off the debt over decades. A cleaner Grand River runs through downtown Grand Rapids after efforts to clean up the region’s major waterway. (Kathy Kieliszewski/Bridge Michigan) Grand Rapids, for example, spent $400 million on a sewer separation project that wrapped up in 2015. Pressure from downstream communities, political will among local leaders and favorable borrowing terms prompted the investment, said city Utilities Director Wayne Jernberg. Sewer rates have gone up as a result. But a Grand Valley State University study commissioned by the city showed city residents have realized billions in returns from higher property values, cleaner beaches, reduced water treatment costs and other benefits. “It also opened up access to the river,” Jernberg said. He cited Canal Park, which is north of downtown. “When there were sewage issues in the past, not many people wanted to be down and around there,” Jernberg said. “Now this fall, the number of people down there fishing on the river was a ton. Part of that is, they know the river is a lot cleaner.” The ‘plastic wrap’ problem While municipalities struggle to come up with funding, climate change and continued sprawl are making the problem worse. Warmer air increases evaporation from the Earth’s surface while allowing the atmosphere to hold more of that moisture. The end result is intense storms that dump far more water at a time. In June and July of 2021, heavy rains caused severe flooding throughout the metro Detroit region. As extreme floods become more common, sewer overflow issues become harder to fix.

articles.title: Michigan has fixed polluted rivers before. Here are five ways to do it again
articles.description: Tougher regulations, infrastructure investment, more staffing and cultural changes are some of the solutions to riverways teeming with levels of feces.
articles.content: Michigan’s rivers are polluted by feces, but experts say the problem can be alleviated Proposed fixes include inspecting and fixing septic systems, reforming Michigan’s farm pollution regulations and funding sewer repairs Lawmakers are split on the best approach and in some cases, whether action is even necessary Fecal pollution has made a mess out of Michigan’s rivers and streams, but experts say tougher regulations, cultural changes and investment can begin to fix the problem. Look no further than history. Bridge Listens: See how you can get involved What you should know Fecal-contaminated rivers expose Michiganders who swim, boat, or fish to bacteria, viruses and parasites from sewer overflows, farm runoff and failing septic systems. The contamination likely sickens thousands of people each year and can depress tourism and home values. Who's making public decisions The Michigan Legislature and EGLE hold the key authority over septic rules, farm manure regulation and enforcement, while local municipalities work to make sewer upgrades. Ways to participate Look up your state lawmakers on the state House Natural Resources and Tourism Committee →Contact state representatives who work on the environment. Look up your state lawmakers on the state Senate Energy and Environment Committee →Contact state senators dealing with environmental issues. Attend the Grand Traverse County Board of Public Works meeting →The board meets the second Thursday of the month at Garfield Township Hall, and its verified agenda includes well and water tank inspections, sewer pump station upgrades for several townships, and a state violation notice over a sewage overflow. See the DWSD’s upcoming meetings →The story names the DWSD. We do not list its meetings yet, so check its own schedule for the next one. Look up EGLE water quality reports → What to watch for next Watch whether state lawmakers take up a statewide septic code or stronger manure rules, and whether EGLE's ongoing E. coli testing leads to more waterways being listed as impaired. Are you taking action? Let us know. Submit Thank you! Your response has been recorded. Powered by Civic Action Toolbox In the 1960s, the Rouge River was so polluted it caught fire and one stretch of the Clinton River could not support any fish. A decade earlier, the odor of industrial waste in the Kalamazoo River spurred officials to action. In more recent years, Michigan has curbed pollution from phosphate-based detergents and industrial PFAS discharges — and rivers and wildlife have bounced back. “Rivers are resilient…they just need a little bit of help,” said Robert Burns, who has served for more than 20 years as the Detroit riverkeeper. Donate “If you do your due diligence, you make that little effort to help clean things up and to reduce the influx (if pollution), the river will help clean itself up over time.” Related: Pure Michigan has a poop problem: Dangerous fecal levels befoul 3 of 4 rivers Michigan has ignored faulty septic systems for decades. The bill is coming due Now, with some 75% of Michigan rivers and streams containing fecal pollution that exceed limits meant to protect swimmers and anglers, experts say the time has come again for a concentrated push to protect the state’s waters. Bridge Michigan spoke to more than four dozen residents, experts, advocates and legislators about what needs to be done. Here are four actions legislators can take — and one for everyday people to do their part. Regulate septic systems Michigan is the only state in the nation without a uniform statewide sanitary code. It instead relies on a patchwork of inconsistent and often loosely-enforced local regulations. It’s a system that allows an estimated 330,000 failing septic systems to pollute with little oversight. Water advocates have long pushed for a statewide code that requires septic systems to be periodically inspected to ensure they’re working properly. The concept has garnered bipartisan support, but so far, bills to adopt a statewide code have floundered amid concerns about the cost of fixes and disagreement about when inspections should happen. “This is the type of legislation the next governor should run with and just say, “I did it,’” said Liz Kirkwood, strategic partnership officer at Flow Water Advocates. “Here you go. We’re the 50th state.” Bolster state oversight The Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy has more than 1,600 employees. Only one is charged with full-time monitoring of the state’s rivers and streams for E. coli, the gut bacteria that is an indicator of fecal pollution levels. Meanwhile, staffing to enforce manure pollution regulations at large livestock farms has remained largely unchanged in recent decades while the number of farms has tripled. Currently, seven people are devoted at least part-time to ensuring compliance. Environmental advocates argue such limited staffing limits the state’s ability to investigate pollution and keep tabs on industry to ensure rules are followed. However, contending EGLE’s regulatory approach is too heavy-handed, Republican lawmakers have recently pushed to reduce its staffing and cut its budget. Rethink farm pollution Agricultural runoff is the nation’s leading source of river pollution, according to the US Environmental Protection Agency. Michigan is no exception. Yet for the most part, the state and federal government don’t regulate it as closely as factories or water treatment plants, instead relying on voluntary efforts to curb the diffuse pollution that flows off farm fields. The largest livestock farms are a notable exception – the state requires them to obtain permits with terms meant to prevent pollution, but few believe the system is working well. Environmentalists and state regulators say permit terms are too weak. Farm groups have fought efforts to strengthen them, contending the changes are confusing, contradictory and onerous. All the while, Michigan’s manure pollution problem grows worse while some lawmakers do little to intervene. Eric Dennis, a research associate at the Citizens Research Council who has studied the issue, said Michigan should rethink its regulatory approach, rather than tweaking a permit system that only applies to a subset of farmers and is widely viewed as ineffective. “We need to find a better way to do this,” he said. Fund sewer fixes Cities across the state are under decades-old orders to update the antiquated “combined sewers” that overflow when it rains, but funding woes have kept them from finishing the job. Experts say part of the problem is that the federal government stopped chipping in much money to pay for water infrastructure upgrades, and the state never filled the gap. That left Michigan’s aging core cities to absorb more of the bill just as suburban flight, deindustrialization and improved water efficiency were cutting into their water system revenue. The state now devotes $200 million in non-federal dollars to water infrastructure per year — a fraction of the $5 billion spent on roads. Lawmakers for years have pondered proposals to boost funding, including a current bill that would impose a 25 cent-per-gallon royalty on bottled water companies to fund water initiatives. Scoop the poop Some of the hardest-to-tackle pollution comes from pet and waterfowl poop that escapes into waterways due to human actions. Michigan has 2.4 million dogs, and experts say not enough owners pick up their waste. Meanwhile, development that replaced wetland and forests with grassy waterfront lawns has created ideal habitat for geese and ducks to congregate, while making it easy for droppings to run off into the water. “I don’t know if people understand their personal relationship with the water or how connected they are to it,” said Rachel Cuschieri-Murray, executive director of the Eaton Conservation District. “Education is a big piece of the puzzle.” You can help by promptly picking up after your pet. If you live near the water, consider swapping the turfgrass for tall native grasses and shrubs. If your home has an illicit sewer connection or a malfunctioning septic system, getting it fixed will also shrink your fecal footprint.
