articles.title: Michigan regulators outline utility bill programs at Detroit energy affordability workshop
articles.description: Michigan’s utility regulator held a workshop Tuesday in Detroit to discuss the commission’s efforts to improve energy assistance efforts, and hear from residents about affordability challenges and barriers to accessing energy assistance and efficiency programs. The workshop comes as DTE Energy and Consumers Energy are requesting $474 million and $456 million electric rate hikes, respectively, […]
articles.content: Electric meters. | Sarah Vogelsong/States NewsroomMichigan’s utility regulator held a workshop Tuesday in Detroit to discuss the commission’s efforts to improve energy assistance efforts, and hear from residents about affordability challenges and barriers to accessing energy assistance and efficiency programs. The workshop comes as DTE Energy and Consumers Energy are requesting $474 million and $456 million electric rate hikes, respectively, and there’s growing concern over how Michigan’s data center buildout could impact ratepayers. Utility costs and data centers played a prominent role in November’s midterm election, with many candidates calling for stronger utility accountability and guardrails for data centers. The workshop at the Durfee Innovation Society was originally planned for Sept. 3, then rescheduled after strong storms knocked out power to hundreds of thousands of Metro Detroit utility customers. The Michigan Public Service Commission will use information from the workshop to make legislative recommendations to lawmakers and inform its work on reducing Michiganders’ energy burden, or percentage of gross household income spent on energy costs, MPSC Commissioner Katherine Peretick told Planet Detroit. The outreach events provide important context for the commission’s decisions, such as utility rate hike requests, although the information can’t be used as official testimony in those cases, Peretick said. During breakout sessions Tuesday night, the roughly 40 attendees discussed topics in small groups, including how to define affordable energy; utility cost control programs; and energy assistance programs. Residents submitted suggestions and questions to the commission. Rafael Mojica, resilience projects coordinator with the nonprofit Soulardarity, said during a question-and-answer session at the end of the workshop that he appreciated the back and forth with commissioners the event provided. “You don’t have to be an expert to be able to share real, life-impacting ideas with the people who at least have some power to do that,” he said. MPSC is changing what energy assistance looks like in Michigan The MPSC is moving the state from a one-size-fits-all model for energy assistance to customized programs for households with the goal of achieving a maximum 6% energy burden for both state and utility assistance programs, Peretick told workshop attendees. When a household experiences a high energy burden, it’s more likely to struggle to meet its energy needs, and may have to make dangerous tradeoffs between paying for energy or groceries, health care, and other essentials, Peretick said. The framework of energy assistance, energy waste reduction, and home weatherization programs is overwhelming, she said, showing a chart with over a dozen funding sources and programs. “This is not exactly easy to figure out or understand, even for people who are pretty familiar with this landscape,” Peretick said. She emphasized that ratepayers do not need to understand this complex maze of programs, and can find help by visiting the MPSC assistance webpage or calling 211. The commission is streamlining the assistance process by matching utility-supported programs with the Michigan Energy Assistance Program, or MEAP, which helps eligible low-income households — eliminating the need for a customer to determine the source of the assistance. Energy prices rising: MPSC chair Multiple factors are driving up U.S. energy costs, including federal tariffs and tax policy, an aging grid that requires significant investment, and general inflationary pressure, which has increased the cost of raw materials and labor, MPSC Chair Dan Scripps said Tuesday night. Rate increases for all investor-owned Michigan utilities — except Consumers Gas — fell below the overall U.S. inflation rate between 2020 and 2025, he said. Thirty-three percent of households nationally experienced energy insecurity in 2024, up from 27% in 2020, Scripps said, acknowledging that many Michiganders struggle to afford energy. In Michigan, 25% of households pay more than 6% of their income for energy, higher than the national average of 20%, he said. According to the Citizens Utility Board of Michigan’s 2025 Utility Performance Report, Michigan households pay more for energy as a percentage of state median income than those in nearby states like Minnesota, Wisconsin, Indiana, Illinois, and Ohio. On Aug. 10, the MPSC submitted recommendations for new legislation that encouraged lawmakers to give the commission authority to set multiyear rate plans tied to utility performance on reliability and affordability metrics, among other recommendations. Detroit City Council Member Denzel McCampbell said the MPSC doesn’t need a workshop to learn that Detroiters have unaffordable utility bills — while the commission continues to approve large rate increases. “I urge the MPSC to support legislation that already exists in the Legislature to untie their hands, regulate these billion-dollar monopolies, and make our energy more affordable,” McCampbell said in a statement released by the Michigan League of Conservation Voters. The Michigan League of Conservation Voters is urging lawmakers to pass the Ratepayer Bill of Rights legislation, which includes time-based outage payments for residential ratepayers, utility rates tied to performance, expanded assistance programs, and a ban on executive bonuses and travel paid for with customer funds. articles.title: U-M report predicts modest growth in Michigan, national economies
articles.description: relatively steady couple years could lie ahead for Michigan’s and the country’s economies. The University of Michigan Research Seminar in Quantitative Economics released its annual U.S. and Michigan forecasts Thursday morning.
articles.content: Steel and aluminum tariffs will affect auto manufacturing and other transportation equipment industries. That could cause job losses in that sector and even more in the wider Michigan economy.(Lester Graham / Michigan Public )A relatively steady couple years could lie ahead for Michigan’s and the country’s economies. The University of Michigan Research Seminar in Quantitative Economics released its annual U.S. and Michigan forecasts Thursday morning.In the big picture, researchers EXPECT per-capita income in Michigan to grow to about $74,200 by the end of 2028. The state could end that year with around 1.2% more jobs than pre-pandemic. U-M economist Gabriel Ehrlich said the labor market should be okay, though it’s a bit “fragile.”“At the moment, if you do have a job, it’s probably reasonably safe. But if you don’t have a job, YOU know if you’re on the outside of the labor market right now, it’s a really tough time to break in because hiring is low,” Ehrlich said.There are some sticking points within the positive job news. The report splits jobs into “cyclical” and “non-cyclical” industries.Cyclical industries include sectors related to manufacturing, construction, utilities, and professional services. Everything else falls under non-cyclical. Those cyclical industries could take a hit, losing around 16,100 jobs before this year ends, and another 3,300 jobs per year in 2027 and 2028.Federal policies could dictate what happens to Michigan. Uncertainty around tariffs, higher fuel costs, and high mortgage interest rates have all hit Michigan’s construction and manufacturing sectors. The non-cyclical industries, on the other hand, may keep padding Michigan’s job market, adding 17,100 jobs this year, and another possible 13,200 next year. Those gains could drastically drop in 2028. Ehrlich said upcoming federal cuts to health programs could hurt the state since the healthcare sector has helped drive Michigan’s job growth.“In the very long run we would expect people who would have otherwise worked in healthcare to be able to find jobs in other industries. But what we know in Michigan, if you think about the auto industry and the economic history of Michigan, we know that process can take a very long time,” he said.The report predicts a return to divided federal government next year could blunt some of the steepest healthcare cuts.Michigan’s unemployment could remain around five percent, a little higher than the national rate. Michigan’s aging workforce and slow population growth will also likely continue to haunt it.“The reality is Michigan’s demographics are increasingly going to be a speed limit on growth in the state. This is something we’ve been saying for a long time and now we’re finally here to where it really is a binding constraint,” Ehrlich said.The outlook suggests immigration might be Michigan’s only meaningful path to upping its population.Nationally, things look a bit better. The economy could grow at a steady 2% pace through 2028 as AI, productivity, and strong investment gains push things forward.Interest rates and inflation could also both slightly drop.As with Michigan's future, what the federal government does could decide the path nationally.

articles.title: Progressives grow sway in Lansing, push to tax the rich and corporations
articles.description: Progressive Democrats are growing their ranks in the Michigan Legislature and plan to push for ‘bold change.’ Several want to raise taxes on the rich and corporations to fund new initiatives.
articles.content: Roughly a dozen more progressive Democrats will join the Michigan Legislature next year, bringing ambitious policy goals with them With Democrats winning majorities in both chambers, legislators are optimistic there will be appetite for sweeping change New and returning lawmakers are pushing plans for single-payer healthcare, transparency reforms and targeted tax increases LANSING — In 2023, state Rep. Dylan Wegela stood alone. The Democratic Socialist was the only Democrat to oppose $1.5 billion in corporate business incentives backed by Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and leaders in his own party, who secured GOP support to pass it without his vote Three years later, Wegela and other progressives who have joined him are feeling emboldened after Democrats rode a populist economic message against special interests to sweeping, statewide victories. “More and more of my colleagues over the last couple years have, I think, been stepping into I guess their power, for lack of a better word, just to stand up and fight some of these fights,” Wegela told Bridge Michigan. The Garden City Democrat and like-minded lawmakers will have more company in the 2027 legislative class, with roughly a dozen additional progressives coming to Lansing, as identified by Bridge through public statements or policy positions. That includes another member of the Democratic Socialists of America, Chris Gilmer-Hill of Detroit. Related: Benson says Democrats have ‘mandate.’ How she plans to lead Q&A: Michigan’s next House speaker wants ‘transformational’ change Dems take full control of Michigan government. What to expect Their ranks are swelling to the point that they are considering forming a yet-to-be-named caucus to advocate for their shared values. “I think people are expecting us to have real, bold change,” Wegela said. “To do things that actually help their everyday existence and lives, and make life more affordable for them, but also clean up some of the corruption that has been going on.” He and other progressives will begin 2027 with ambitious goals, including an ongoing push to create a state-level Medicare for All-style healthcare system, aims for government ethics reforms and an openness to raising taxes on the rich and corporations. “I’m not proposing raising revenue just for revenue’s sake,” said state Rep. Natalie Price, who will join the Senate in January and told Bridge her top priority is to raise the state’s corporate income tax by 1.5 percentage points. Donate “The goal is to raise it to address these immediate needs in our communities and the crises that we’re facing.” Progressives are still outnumbered in Lansing, but a growing state Senate majority and a new House majority mean they’ll have greater influence. In 2023 and 2024, when Democrats last held both chambers, one defecting member in either chamber could kill party-line legislation. Progressives were repeatedly stymied, as they saw their priorities — issues like ethics reform and utility regulation — routinely dashed. “Michiganders aren’t going to have a lot of patience with us if we don’t show that we’re very serious about the power that they have given us,” said Rep. Betsy Coffia, who flipped her Traverse City district from Republican control in 2022. “We did not ask to inherit a corporate-controlled political culture, but we did, and it’s our job to make it better.” But next year, Democrats will have seven votes to spare in the House’s 63-member caucus and four more votes in the Senate than needed to break a tie. That’ll bring members some new freedoms, noted incoming Democratic Senate Majority Leader Darrin Camilleri. “We’ve got an opportunity here to again let people vote how they want to vote on certain items,” Camilleri, D-Trenton, told Bridge. “As long as we can still get the required number of votes to get a piece of legislation across the finish line, that’s all that matters.” More members, more problems? A 16-member majority in the state House doesn’t necessarily mean Democrats will be able to pass particularly progressive legislation. In some cases, a broad majority can actually present additional difficulties, as members may feel more freedom to diverge from party priorities or hold out for an ask in exchange for their support, said former House Speaker Tom Leonard. The DeWitt Republican knows those dynamics well. In 2017, Leonard’s aggressive push for an income tax cut fell apart when 12 of his GOP colleagues joined Democrats in opposing the measure. He had kept lawmakers in session into the wee hours of the morning in an attempt to extract votes. The proposal ultimately failed around 2 a.m. “With 63 seats, we’re going to definitely disagree on things,” said Rep.-elect Joanna Whaley, a progressive Democrat from Wayne County. She contends her election was part of a decadeslong shift among voters who are increasingly rejecting corporate influence in Michigan politics, and Lansing should reflect that, Whaley told Bridge. “People who run on a more progressive platform are probably listening to the people more than they’re listening to lobbyists and corporations, and that’s what voters want,” she said. “I really believe that the party is going to begin shifting more towards these types of leaders.” Incoming House Speaker Ranjeev Puri of Canton, viewed by some as a pragmatic progressive, will have to try to keep moderates and other factions happy but will have some room to spare on key votes. Puri intends to “spend a lot of time” ensuring all his members have a voice so “that we collectively reach an agenda that meets the needs of our caucus and this moment for the state of Michigan,” he recently told Bridge. Anti-corporate priorities While Wegela once stood apart from his colleagues on key issues, his message now sounds pretty similar to the one Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson hammered throughout her campaign. A day after the election, Benson held a press conference characterizing her nearly 11-percentage point victory as a “clear mandate” for Lansing to “work to lower our costs and raise our wages and end corruption.” And on those kitchen-table principles, there’s lots of overlap between Democrats’ left flank and their leadership. Rep. Jason Morgan, who represents Ann Arbor, noted most Democrats in the 2026 elections ran on “fundamental ideas of affordability, healthcare, education, infrastructure, money out of politics,” which he didn’t deem necessarily progressive. “It’s kind of pro-people, common sense stuff,” he added. But incoming progressives also have a long list of priorities they intend to center, too. Multiple left-wing candidates headed to Lansing framed Democrats’ fundamental split as not about ideology, but special interest influence. Gilmer-Hill, the Democratic Socialist who unseated Rep. Helena Scott in Detroit’s 2nd district, ran specifically on curtailing the influence of the electrical utility DTE Energy. Democrats’ last governing trifecta — when Scott chaired the House energy committee — was “dominated” by utility influence, Gilmer-Hill said in an interview with Bridge. He argued the 82% approval rate of Proposal 2, a measure to ban political spending by regulated utilities, shows that voters “will not tolerate a Democratic trifecta that just rolls over and ignores all of its promises to take on the utilities.” Multiple progressive legislators said they want to work on additional initiatives to reduce the influence of money in state politics and require more disclosure from lobbyists and political candidates beyond Proposal 2’s provisions. Several also backed the expansion of public records requests through the Freedom of Information Act — something Puri declined to specifically endorse in a recent interview with Bridge Michigan. Morgan, who partnered with other lawmakers on a stalled transparency package during Democrats’ last trifecta, said they plan to reintroduce the bills in the upcoming term, and “it seems clear to me that there’s much more appetite for tackling some of this work.” Regulating artificial intelligence and data centers is another interest of the incoming lawmakers. Wegela, who has long opposed the facilities, wants to move swiftly on a statewide moratorium and repeal the same tax breaks Democrats and Republicans alike championed only a few years ago. “Taking on AI and data centers needs to be of top priority, considering that the AI movement, I think, is threatening to take millions of working-class jobs,” he said. Incoming chamber leaders, Camilleri and Puri, have been more reticent about laying out specific objectives for the upcoming term. Affordability issues are “going to be our north star,” Camilleri told Bridge, but “I don’t have those policy prescriptions that we’re ready to announce today.” The members of his caucus, he said, “do not want to get into internal fights with each other.” “We’ve got people who come from all walks of life, from all areas of the state, and I know that we will come out unified with that agenda and start getting stuff done,” Camilleri said. Wegela and Gilmer-Hill, on the other hand, are unafraid to touch on something of a third rail in US politics: the prospect of creating new taxes to fund progressive government programs, with a focus on the wealthiest Michiganders and corporations. The state has a flat income tax, and raising taxes on the rich could require an amendment to the Michigan constitution and a statewide vote. Michigan also has a balanced budget requirement, and the possibility of looming funding shortfalls mean some progressive proposals would only be possible by raising new revenue. “I’m all for a corporate income tax increase. They already are paying not nearly enough of their fair share,” said Coffia. “I also think we should look at the highest earners. The DeVoses should be paying more of their fair share of taxes than people in that bracket.” The DeVoses, of Ada, routinely spend millions in Michigan elections to back their preferred candidates. Progressives instead intend to lean on some of the grassroots support they’ve cultivated to promote their priorities. “We are going to need pressure from below to make sure that lawmakers do the things that the people of Michigan want us to do,” Wegela said. State-level single-payer? In a year when universal, government-run health care was a central part of Abdul El-Sayed’s winning Senate campaign message, progressives in the Legislature want their constituents to know Lansing heard that message. Likely no lawmaker has championed the concept more than Rep. Carrie Rheingans, an Ann Arbor Democrat who has waged something of a lonely fight to create a state-level single-payer healthcare system. Over the last four years she’s held, by her count, 50 town halls “in every corner of the state of Michigan,” to promote the scaffolding of a plan she calls MIcare. She’s picked up some allies in the process, with El-Sayed joining her for one of the events earlier this year, and she said momentum is growing in the state Legislature. “We are going to, for the first time, break the bill up into multiple pieces so that multiple people can be the sponsor, and we’re going to introduce it in the House and the Senate,” Rheingans told Bridge. “We will have a robust team of legislative members working on this.” Rheingans, whose background is in public health, is convinced the US healthcare system is on the verge of collapse. “I want to make sure that Michiganders understand it’s not the Democratic trifecta or Gov. Benson who is causing the collapse of the healthcare system,” Rheingans said. “It’s the Republican trifecta in D.C. and tax cuts for billionaires.” Despite new Democratic majorities, Rheingans acknowledged her single-payer healthcare system is not likely to go far in Lansing, where legislative leaders have not backed it. articles.title: Amazon app warns New York of higher costs if Mamdani delivery law passes
articles.content: Amazon is taking its fight against a New York City delivery bill, which has been backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, to its shopping website and app. Some users who open the company's shopping app or website report being served with pop-ups and banners warning that the New York City Council "could add up to $5 per order" if it passes Intro 518, or the Delivery Protection Act. The bill would require Amazon to employ its army of third-party delivery companies directly, disrupting the contractor model it has relied on since 2018. Amazon uses a network of thousands of small companies, which often work solely for Amazon, to handle the last-mile portion of shipments, in an effort to speed up deliveries and control more of its logistics operations. "If this legislation passes, we'd no longer be able to work with them, and we'd be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city," Amazon's in-app message states. "That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees." The proposed legislation was introduced in February and is awaiting review by City Council Speaker Julie Menin. Amazon also posted a statement on its company website where it often publishes its policy positions. But rarely has the company used its valuable e-commerce site and app real estate to push its perspectives. Other tech companies including Uber and Lyft have similarly used their apps to advocate for or against legislation in the past. Amazon's pop-up notices and a stationary banner on its store homepage direct users to a form where they can "contact your council member to oppose Intro 518." According to Amazon, 20,000 customers sent emails to city council members in the first six hours that the pop-up appeared. Menin told CNBC in a statement that Amazon's claim it will need to raise prices due to the proposed legislation "defies logic." "We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs," Menin said. "If Amazon thinks this deceptive campaign will effectively threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council, they are dead wrong." Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement that the company put up the notices to be "transparent with our customers" about what the bill "would cause them if it passes as written." "If customers are concerned, one of the most impactful things they can do is contact their City Council member and ask them to oppose this bill," Nantel said. The Delivery Protection Act has received a swell of support from labor groups, including the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, which has sought to unionize Amazon delivery and warehouse workers. Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon's subcontractor model "leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets." He's argued the bill would lead to safer working conditions for drivers, and allow the city to "regulate last-mile operations." Amazon disputed Mamdani's claims, saying the bill would put Delivery Service Partner jobs "at risk without improving safety." It also argued that other businesses and governments use contractors in their operations, and said the DSP model has allowed it to meet growing customer demand. "It works because local entrepreneurs — people rooted in their communities — deliver a better experience," Amazon said. "They invest in their teams, their routes, and their neighborhoods. That's not a liability play." Amazon has lobbied heavily against the bill, while logistics and business groups have launched local advertising campaigns, and warned they may sue the city if the bill passes.

Now in charge, state Democrats plan climate agendas that focus on affordability
articles.description: Climate change was largely absent as a campaign topic during this year’s midterm elections. Democrats gained power in many states by focusing on issues such as the cost of living and healthcare. But many state lawmakers believe environmental policies will be key to delivering on those promises. Democrats want to use their newfound power to […]
articles.content: With newfound power in many state legislatures and governor’s offices, Democrats say their focus on climate and clean energy can deliver on their campaign promises to help residents with cost of living concerns. (Photo by Marga Buschbell-Steeger/Getty Images)Climate change was largely absent as a campaign topic during this year’s midterm elections. Democrats gained power in many states by focusing on issues such as the cost of living and healthcare. But many state lawmakers believe environmental policies will be key to delivering on those promises. Democrats want to use their newfound power to promote clean energy, rein in data centers and regulate utilities — priorities they believe could help with voters’ skyrocketing electricity bills. And they want to enact new safeguards for clean air and water, pointing to the healthcare burden caused by pollution. “Affordability absolutely does tie into our climate and energy agenda,” said Arizona state Sen. Priya Sundareshan, who will serve as Senate president next session after Democrats gained a majority. “I’m excited to see what we can do now that Republicans are no longer able to block any action.” Across the country, Democrats flipped control of 12 legislative chambers and six governorships. They will hold trifectas — controlling both chambers of the legislature as well as the governor’s mansion — in at least 22 states. And in several other states, the party will have newfound leverage with a majority in at least one legislative chamber or a Democratic governor. “Even though environment and climate did not reach the top level for most voters, they were deeply embedded in affordability conversations,” said Dylan McDowell, chief executive officer of the National Environmental Caucus, a collaborative forum for state lawmakers. “There is a higher sense of awareness around how energy and climate and environment are tied to kitchen table issues.” Tackling energy costs Lawmakers in newfound positions of power say they want to accelerate their states’ transition to clean energy — but with a message focused more on utility bills than carbon emissions. “Clean energy is more affordable and healthier,” said Pennsylvania state Sen. Carolyn Comitta, a Democrat who served as minority chair of the Environmental Resources and Energy Committee during the previous session. With Democrats now holding a trifecta in the state, Comitta expects lawmakers to craft an update to the state’s clean energy law to accelerate the buildout of renewable power. Other priorities include giving residents more access to rooftop, balcony and community solar projects, as well as promoting battery storage projects to bolster the electric grid. Comitta has also called for a moratorium on data centers amid concerns about rising energy costs. Some Republicans have sought to blame rising energy prices on Democratic climate policies. Pennsylvania state Sen. Gene Yaw, who will lose his chairmanship of the Environmental Resources and Energy Committee when the Democratic majority is sworn in, said during the campaign that the Biden administration’s pollution rules were driving up electricity bills. “Pennsylvania families should not be asked to sit in the dark so someone else’s climate timeline can be met on paper,” Yaw said in a statement at the time. In Georgia, Democratic state Rep. Eric Bell said lawmakers want to regulate electrical utilities to promote efficiency, instead of the current system where they earn returns from building costly infrastructure. One approach could include the use of grid-enhancing technologies, which allow more power to flow through existing infrastructure. As energy demand rises, Bell also said lawmakers will consider bills to regulate the power and water use of data centers to ensure they don’t drive up costs. Bell, who serves as Georgia’s state lead with the National Environmental Caucus, said he is also focused on restoring an electric vehicle tax credit, as gas prices remain high. While Democrats now control the Georgia governor’s office and state House, Republicans have a slim majority in the state Senate. In Arizona, where Democrats have a newfound trifecta, lawmakers are also looking at regulating utilities. Sundareshan, the incoming Senate president, wants to consider limiting utilities’ political spending. “We said we would be holding corporations accountable and lowering costs for people,” she said. “Is it appropriate to use ratepayer money for things like lobbying and campaign contributions?” Arizona Democrats will also focus on limiting data centers’ impact on energy bills and improving residents’ access to solar energy programs, she said. Utility spending was also a major issue in Michigan, where more than 81% of voters approved a ballot proposal to prevent electric and gas utilities from making campaign contributions. “We saw a real repudiation of utilities,” said Ben Poulson, state government affairs director with the Michigan League of Conservation Voters. “Michiganders are really concerned about rising energy bills, and they see those political contributions as standing in the way of reforms.” Environmental activists there are pushing Democrats, with a new trifecta in state government, to realign utilities’ investor incentives to be tied to reliability and bill savings rather than capital spending, while opening up more customer-owned generation such as community solar projects. Meanwhile, Michigan Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson has pledged to put a moratorium on data center construction until the state issues rules requiring them to pay for their own power and restricting their tax breaks. Michigan Democrats were able to retake control of the House from Republicans, who had argued that state climate policies were the real culprit in driving up energy costs. Republican state Rep. Pauline Wendzel, who will lose the chairmanship of the House Energy Committee, proposed legislation earlier this year that would have repealed the state’s clean energy mandates. “For too long, energy policy has focused on restricting what we can produce instead of making sure families have the power they need at a price they can afford,” Wendzel said in a statement last month. In Minnesota, lawmakers need to make sure the state is on track to meet its target of 100% clean electricity by 2040, said Democratic state Sen. Nick Frentz, who chairs the Energy, Utilities, Environment, and Climate Committee. He noted that severe weather caused by climate change is already driving up insurance bills. “Minnesotans are saying, ‘I can’t have my costs go up, but I do think it’s a priority to reduce carbon emissions,’” he said. “We’re spending billions of dollars right now on climate change through property insurance.” Frentz said Democrats may use their new trifecta to advance battery storage projects, facilities that can harness surplus electricity and redeploy it when demand is high. And in New Hampshire, Democrats now hold majorities in the House and Senate, while the governor’s office will continue to be held by Republican Kelly Ayotte. State Rep. Peter Bixby, a Democrat who serves on the Environment and Agriculture Committee, said lawmakers are likely to propose bills to increase solar access, battery storage and energy efficiency incentives. The legislature will also consider a moratorium on data centers, he said. Air and water protections Many lawmakers are also focused on air and water issues, from pollution to drought to flooding. “Voters were telling us that water is one of those top three to five priorities,” said Sundareshan, the Arizona lawmaker. “Water sustainability is really a concern for a state like Arizona.” She said legislators will seek to enact a new groundwater management plan for the state’s rural areas, where some residents have seen their wells run dry, while strengthening groundwater protections for urban areas. In Georgia, Democrats will seek to expand cleanup efforts for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, the “forever chemicals” commonly known as PFAS. Bell, the state legislator, said he was hopeful that priority will earn bipartisan support. “Whether you’re a Trumper or the president of Al Gore’s fan club, you don’t want to breathe dirty air or drink contaminated water,” he said. Bell also plans to advocate for an extended producer responsibility bill, an approach that forces manufacturers to take responsibility for the disposal and recycling of plastic packaging. Comitta, the Pennsylvania lawmaker, and Frentz, the Minnesota lawmaker, said state investments in pollution regulation programs have become increasingly important as President Donald Trump’s administration has rolled back federal rules for a variety of pollutants. “Pennsylvania has been that backstop protecting our citizens and we will continue and expand that work,” Comitta said. Minnesota lawmakers will likely consider a number of proposals to protect the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness, Frentz said, following congressional Republicans’ vote this year to rescind a mining ban in nearby national forest land. In Michigan, environmental advocates are pushing lawmakers to invest in water infrastructure. “We have a severe investment problem when it comes to all types of water infrastructure, whether it’s lead service line replacement, dam failure or old septic systems,” said Poulson, with the Michigan League of Conservation Voters. Meanwhile, New Hampshire lawmakers need to invest in dam repairs and flood protection, Bixby said. He’s also hoping to see bills supporting an extended producer responsibility program and PFAS cleanup. Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand, a Democrat, made water quality a major campaign issue, tying the state’s agricultural runoff and high levels of nitrates in drinking water to its fast-growing cancer rate. His proposals include investments in water quality monitors, manure management plans and restoring wetlands to harness their natural filtration benefits. McDowell, with the National Environmental Caucus, said voters are recognizing how environmental issues are linked to public health. “We’re not just saying this is bad for fish and wildlife, this is bad for people,” he said. “There’s very clear data and it’s scary. People are understanding the realities.” Stateline reporter Alex Brown can be reached at abrown@stateline.org. articles.title: East Lansing approves $472K federal grant with strings that conflict with sanctuary city policy
articles.description: East Lansing City Council members voted 3-1 at Tuesday’s meeting to accept a $472,000 grant from the U.S. Department of Justice, which would replace decade-old security cameras at municipal facilities, […]
articles.content: East Lansing City Council members voted 3-1 at Tuesday’s meeting to accept a $472,000 grant from the U.S. Department of Justice, which would replace decade-old security cameras at municipal facilities, despite residents’ concerns that strings attached to the federal funding could conflict with the city’s 2023 sanctuary city policies and expose immigrant communities to immigration enforcement. “This money is important for the city,” East Lansing Mayor Erik Altmann said. “We don’t have the luxury of half-million-dollar grants falling into our laps. We’re a city that doesn’t have two nickels to rub together and we spend an awful lot of time figuring out how to pay for the things we need. Now we have an opportunity to do that, and I think we should grab it.” East Lansing City Council members during a Nov. 17 meeting. Photo by Erick Díaz Veliz for City Pulse East Lansing City Council members during a Nov. 17 meeting. Photo by Erick Díaz Veliz for City Pulse East Lansing City Council members during a Nov. 17 meeting. Photo by Erick Díaz Veliz for City Pulse East Lansing City Council members during a Nov. 17 meeting. Photo by Erick Díaz Veliz for City Pulse East Lansing City Council members during a Nov. 17 meeting. Photo by Erick Díaz Veliz for City Pulse The grant will fund upgrades to about 350 cameras across 19 municipal buildings and facilities, including City Hall, the Hannah Community Center and parking structures. It was awarded through the DOJ’s Community-Oriented Policing Services (COPS) Technology and Equipment Program. But there are three controversial conditions: requiring the city not to restrict the sharing of information about individuals’ citizenship or immigration status with federal, state and local government agencies, including ICE; requiring the city to certify that it does not operate diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs requiring compliance with presidential memoranda and executive federal orders. Several residents said, during the Nov. 17 council meeting, that the change could require local cooperation with federal immigration authorities, including ICE, as well as conditions refuting certain DEI policies. Several residents urged officials to reject the funding or postpone the vote to a public hearing until they could review the federal conditions more thoroughly. City staff told council members that East Lansing had only until Nov. 20 to sign the grant agreement, leaving the city just three days after the meeting to finalize its decision. Karen Hoene, chair of the city’s Human Rights Commission, questioned why the grant had initially been placed on the consent agenda, which allows council members to approve multiple items together without separate discussion. It was later moved to the business agenda. Abbie Tykocki, a member of the East Lansing School Board who said she was speaking as a private citizen, warned that accepting the funding could transfer the consequences of a federal dispute to immigrant residents. “Elected officials are supposed to make difficult decisions and accept responsibility for the consequences, and I believe council members should be willing to take risks when those risks fall on themselves,” Tykocki said. “Don’t ask the immigrants to pay for city surveillance cameras with their safety. Don’t ask our most vulnerable residents to bear risks that you aren’t willing to bear yourselves.” MSU alum Cassidy Howard questioned the city’s decision to prioritize such a large sum of money, given the vulnerability of immigrant residents under federal conditions. “I believe you have been put in these seats to take care of us,” she said. “And not compromise our safety, especially, as stated, the many immigrants and international students who find a home here. I believe we deserve safety, and I believe our neighbors are worth more than $472,000.” City staff explained that the existing cameras were installed primarily in 2014 and 2016 and have exceeded their expected six-to-eight-year life cycle. Some equipment has been kept working only with repairs and replacement parts. The proposed cameras would be used for security and for reviewing incidents at municipal facilities, not for facial recognition, tracking individuals, or connecting to external databases, according to the city. Councilmember Mark Meadows argued that the federal conditions raised constitutional concerns and said accepting the grant did not require East Lansing to abandon its existing immigration policies. He said the city would formally notify the federal government that it intended to maintain its sanctuary city policies. Under the grant agreement, the DOJ could terminate the award or seek repayment if the city failed to comply with its conditions. Meadows acknowledged that challenging potential federal enforcement could result in expensive litigation but argued that the city should defend its established policies. Altmann, who introduced the motion to accept the agreement, supported moving forward, saying the funding was important for replacing critical infrastructure and that the city should not abandon its existing protections for immigrants. The motion passed with Mayor Altmann and council members Mark Meadows and Steven Whelan voting in favor. Mayor pro tem Chuck Grigsby voted against it. Councilmember Kerry Ebersole Singh was absent.

articles.title: Incoming Democratic Congress fuels hope of more federal dollars for elections
articles.description: The top elections official in Hardin County, Kentucky, is already bracing for 2028. The county south of Louisville, which includes Fort Knox, is growing as Ford builds a battery plant expected to bring thousands of jobs to an area that already boasts more than 110,000 residents. For Brian Smith, the Republican county clerk, more residents […]
articles.content: Election workers help voters cast their primary election ballot at the Historic Arkansas Museum in downtown Little Rock, Arkansas, on Tuesday, March 3, 2026. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)The top elections official in Hardin County, Kentucky, is already bracing for 2028. The county south of Louisville, which includes Fort Knox, is growing as Ford builds a battery plant expected to bring thousands of jobs to an area that already boasts more than 110,000 residents. For Brian Smith, the Republican county clerk, more residents mean more voters. “I am confident that by the 2028 presidential election, I (will) have huge equipment needs in order to have enough polling locations operating to serve the number of voters I have,” Smith said. Absent a major change, those costs will fall largely to the county. But the incoming Congress that begins in January is raising hopes among some election officials and election administration experts that more help — and more consistent help — could be on the way. Across the United States, election officials in recent years have sought more federal support as Congress has wavered on how much funding to provide. Over the past decade, lawmakers have approved more than $400 million some years in election security grants to states and zero in others. Billions of dollars in upgrades to the country’s election infrastructure are needed, experts say. Former President Joe Biden unsuccessfully proposed $10 billion over 10 years to bolster election security. Democrats who have called for substantial new federal investments in elections are poised to play influential roles over the next two years as the party takes control of the U.S. House and Senate. Democrats will lead the appropriations process, giving the party much more say over spending, though Republicans have also backed election aid in the past. The Senate’s 60-vote threshold for most legislation also could produce some friction with the new Democratic majority. In a preview of what could be ahead, California’s two Democratic senators — Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff — introduced legislation earlier this year to authorize $10 billion in federal aid for elections over three years. In the new Congress, Padilla will chair the Senate Rules & Administration Committee, which oversees federal elections policy. “Senator Padilla will continue to prioritize election administration and security funding and hopes to see bipartisan support for the issue going into the 2028 election cycle, especially if he becomes the Chairman of the Rules Committee in the 120th Congress,” Padilla spokesperson Danny Rodriguez said in a statement. Trump’s beef with commission President Donald Trump’s effort to assert control over the U.S. Election Assistance Commission may also encounter fresh resistance from Democrats. Trump fired two of the EAC’s commissioners in July and a third resigned, leaving the commission without any members. The EAC is the only federal agency dedicated solely to helping states and localities run smooth and secure elections, operating on a roughly $24 million budget — a drop in the ocean of federal spending. The bipartisan independent agency oversees the distribution of grants to states, develops voluntary security and design standards for voting machines and offers training to election officials. The EAC administers the Election Security Grants program, which was created in response to foreign interference in the 2016 election. The grants fund technology upgrades, including cybersecurity, physical security improvements at election sites and efforts to combat voter misinformation. States had spent about $343 million in election security grants on voting equipment and cybersecurity as of 2024, according to a report that year from the Bipartisan Policy Center to the EAC. Inconsistent funding Thomas Hicks, one of the two Democratic EAC commissioners fired by Trump, said in an interview that states don’t have adequate resources to continually upgrade voting equipment. Putting off improvements will only make the problem worse, he argued. “If we neglect doing this, we’re going to have some sort of catastrophic event where we say, oh, we should have put money in,” Hicks said. But Congress has funded the election security grants inconsistently. Funding peaked in the program’s early years, with $380 million in 2018 and $425 million in 2020. Election officials received an additional $400 million in pandemic relief aid that year as well. Over the past several years, the grants have been much smaller. Congress approved $75 million in 2022 and 2023, followed by $55 million in 2024 and just $15 million in 2025. That amount has risen slightly to $45 million for the past two years. “Even in the best of years, the federal government is paying a very small portion. But it’s an important piece,” Benjamin Hovland, the other fired Democratic EAC commissioner, said in an interview. Catch-up needed The Project for Election Infrastructure, a nonpartisan advocacy group, has called on Congress to provide $400 million a year. It released a letter in May signed by nearly 90 state and local election officials warning that inadequate funding can lead to long lines at the polls and delays in processing mail ballots. Each year’s grants are split between states and territories based on a formula. In practice, most receive the minimum amount. The 2026 grant of $45 million left most states with $819,000 each, along with a mandatory 20% match. The $45 million amount represents “pennies” for the needs of election workers and only scratches the surface, Sarah Hague, executive director of the Project for Election Infrastructure, said. “We have a lot of catch-up to do,” Hague said. In Washington state, Clark County Auditor Greg Kimsey asked county leadership in March for approval to spend nearly $900,000 on new mail sorting machines. In a state that conducts elections by mail, the machines are critical to processing ballot envelopes as they arrive. Kimsey, who oversees elections in an area that includes Vancouver, also purchased cameras to monitor the county’s ballot drop boxes after one was bombed in 2024, burning hundreds of ballots. He said in an interview the cameras cost about $600,000. A similar incident also occurred in nearby Portland, Oregon. Election officials recovered ballots from a ballot drop box targeted in an arson in Vancouver, Washington, on Oct. 28, 2024. Officials were able to identify voters for 488 damaged ballots. (Courtesy of Clark County Auditor) Until a few years ago, Kimsey said all of his office’s capital expenditures for elections were funded through grant dollars. “Looking forward, we made the assumption that these federal grant dollars were not going to be available,” Kimsey said. Congress’ appetite for funding boost While federal support for elections has received bipartisan support in the past, the Trump administration and some Republicans in Congress have pushed to make future funding contingent on adopting election security policies favored by the president. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security in July announced that to receive some DHS grant dollars, states would have to use a federal computer program to check the citizenship status of registered voters and meet other election-related requirements. A federal judge blocked the change in September. The Republican-controlled House Appropriations Committee in April approved a bill that would have cut the EAC’s salaries and expenses from $23.86 million to $17 million. It would have also reduced the election security grant program from $45 million to $15 million. And it included a provision prohibiting the use of funds to register noncitizens to vote, even though noncitizen voting was already illegal. Congress didn’t ultimately pass those reductions, instead opting to maintain spending for the EAC and the grant program at existing levels. The Senate also didn’t pass the SAVE America Act, Trump’s signature elections bill, which would have imposed a strict requirement that voters prove their citizenship. A spokesperson for Rep. Dave Joyce, an Ohio Republican who chairs the House Appropriations Financial Services and General Government Subcommittee, didn’t respond to a request to interview the congressman. The subcommittee oversees spending levels for the EAC and the election security grants. Several other returning members of Congress who serve on the subcommittee also didn’t respond to requests for interviews or declined to comment. A spokesperson for Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, a Washington Democrat, referred States Newsroom to her previous remarks about election funding. She represents the southwest corner of the state, including Clark County. “Last general election, my ballot boxes were firebombed. They have never caught the person who did it,” Gluesenkamp Perez said at a 2025 subcommittee meeting. “If you think this can’t happen all across the country, we are setting ourselves up for a very dangerous situation.” Independence at stake The White House didn’t respond to questions from States Newsroom about whether Trump continues to support linking grant funding to policies like requiring voters to show proof of citizenship — or whether the president intends to nominate new EAC commissioners. When Trump fired the EAC commissioners in July, the White House said in a statement that the administration had been working to “safeguard elections from fraud and abuse” and investing in “strong infrastructure” to sustain that mission. Tim Harper, a project lead focused on elections at the nonpartisan Center for Democracy & Technology, said Trump’s firing of the EAC commissioners threatens the independence of what is supposed to be a neutral agency providing nonpartisan guidance and help to election officials. The EAC’s independence allows states to trust that its recommendations aren’t influenced by partisan goals, Harper said. By contrast, Trump last year attempted to use the EAC to unilaterally require voters to offer proof of citizenship, though the move was blocked in federal court. “That independence is essential to its core mission,” Harper said. The Trump administration has argued that the president enjoys sweeping control over the executive branch and that Congress has limited power to place agencies beyond his control. The U.S. Supreme Court has at least partially affirmed that view, ruling in June that Trump could fire members of the Federal Trade Commission without cause. Hicks said that he’s still considering a legal challenge to his dismissal. He cautioned that if Trump is able to fire the commissioners, it opens the door to future presidents, including Democrats, also removing the EAC’s leadership. “It goes beyond this administration,” Hicks said.

UK government forced to disclose secret Apple backdoor order
articles.description: The U.K. tribunal's ruling rejected London's claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security.
articles.content: The U.K. government has been ordered to confirm that it issued a secret order demanding Apple to provide authorities with encrypted customer information. The Thursday ruling from the U.K.’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal, an independent court that allows citizens to challenge government surveillance orders, is a rare rebuke for the government, which sought to keep the encryption backdoor order a state secret. The tribunal’s ruling rejected the Home Office’s claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security. The ruling comes a year after the U.K. government reportedly demanded that Apple build a backdoor to allow U.K. authorities access to customer data anywhere in the world. Details of the so-called “technical capabilities notice,” which are issued under strict non-disclosure rules, leaked to the media, which drew ire from White House officials and U.S. lawmakers who criticized the effort, arguing that the U.K. order would put Americans’ privacy at risk. California-based Apple refused the order, and blocked U.K. users from switching on its Advanced Data Protection data-encryption feature for iCloud, rather than comply with the demand. The U.K.’s secret order was later narrowed to allow access to British nationals’ data stored in Apple’s encrypted cloud, and Apple also challenged this second order. Prior to the ruling, Apple was legally barred from disclosing the order, even after details leaked. When reached for comment, Apple told TechCrunch that it welcomes the decision to make public the fact that the U.K. Home Office issued a technical capability notice. Apple previously said that it has “never built a backdoor or master key” to any of its products or services and “never will.” A spokesperson for the U.K. Home Office, which has yet to confirm the existence of a notice, did not respond to a request for comment. Rights group Liberty International, which brought the legal challenge on behalf of two individuals, said that this is the first known time that the government has been compelled to confirm the existence of a secret technical order. A final hearing on what specific order details can be released is anticipated next year. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. Jocelyn Benson promises Michigan Voting Rights Act. What would it do?
articles.description: Democratic Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson has said the Michigan Voting Rights Act will be the first bill she signs into law. What you need to know about the plan.
articles.content: This article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization covering local election administration and voting access. Sign up for Votebeat Michigan’s free newsletter here. A proposal to protect minority voting rights in Michigan is coming back to the key swing state. Democrats in Lansing have tried but failed to pass the Michigan Voting Rights Act in each of the last two legislative sessions. But now that the party has regained full control of state government, the proposal might actually make it into law. Democratic Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson — who currently serves as Michigan’s top election official as secretary of state — has named the act as her top priority, saying on the campaign trail that it would be the first bill she would sign. And leaders in the House and Senate say they will work hard to pass it during next year’s legislative session, which starts Jan. 1. RELATED STORIES: Benson says Democrats have ‘mandate.’ How she plans to lead Q&A: Michigan’s next House speaker wants ‘transformational’ change Dems take full control of Michigan government. What to expect Speaker-elect Ranjeev Puri told Votebeat on Thursday that “there is a lot of interest and excitement amongst the Michigan House Democrats” to make sure the proposal passes, although he declined to give a specific timeline. Senate Majority Leader-elect Darrin Camilleri said in a statement that, as a lead sponsor of the act, “it is of course very high on my list of priorities when Democrats regain our trifecta in January.” At their core, the four bills that make up the Michigan Voting Rights Act aim to fill in the gaps of the federal Voting Rights Act, which has been chipped away at by court rulings in recent years. Several other states already have state-level voting rights acts, but Michigan would be the first true swing state to pass one, so its passage would mark an important milestone for voting rights advocates. The act would also add to the long list of ways the state has expanded voting rights over the past decade. But not everyone is excited about the proposed changes. What’s in the Michigan Voting Rights Act? It’s not clear if Democrats will modify the existing bills before reintroducing them when the session starts. But the 2027-2028 version of the Michigan Voting Rights Act is expected to be substantially similar to the two versions that have been introduced before.Donate In past sessions, the first bill in the package proposed banning “discriminatory activity” in voting and established a legal framework for challenging it. It prohibited local governments from imposing prerequisites on voting or causing voting disparities between members of a protected class — including racial or language minority groups — “and other members of the electorate.” It also would introduce new requirements for notifying voters about changes to elections, including new polling places or precinct boundaries. The bill also would allow voters to sue municipalities over alleged violations of the act. It proposed granting courts the ability to appoint election monitors, have veto power over election-related changes such as moving polling places, and more — an echo of requirements that were once part of the federal Voting Rights Act before the Supreme Court struck them down in 2013. The second bill in the package proposed creating a “voting and elections database and institute” at at least one state university which would track and publish election data, such as precinct-level results and voter registration information. The third of the four bills would require jurisdictions to translate materials into another language if a significant number of voters speak that language and aren’t proficient in English. It also would establish thresholds for which communities needed to provide those translated materials and created an advisory council, with members appointed by the secretary of state, to suggest requirements. Language access is covered by Section 203 of the federal Voting Rights Act. Michigan’s proposal goes further and would set a lower bar for when ballots need to be translated and in which communities. The federal act, for example, does not include Arabic and related languages — which is relevant in Michigan’s case, since Arabic is the state’s third-most commonly spoken language. The final bill aimed to provide more conveniences for voters, including those with special concerns such as voters with disabilities. It would codify curbside voting, permit voters with language barriers to bring their own translators, and allow people to provide “food, warmth, or other necessities” to people in line to vote. It would also require governments to disclose when they made certain administrative changes, such as removing voters from the rolls or allowing voters to examine voting equipment. Why hasn’t the Michigan Voting Rights Act passed before? In past sessions, the Michigan Voting Rights Act simply wasn’t able to make it over the finish line. The package was first introduced in 2023, the last time Democrats controlled the Senate, House, and governor’s office all at once. During that session, though, the bills sat in committee for almost a year before the Senate passed them in September 2024, with just three months left in the session. Legislators tried to get them through the House as well — they even had a committee hearing in December — but the proposal ultimately died during a chaotic final month of the session when lame-duck Democrats struggled to move any legislation at all. Supporters tried again this year in the Senate, where the bills were re-introduced just a few weeks after the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in Louisiana v. Callais changed how race could be considered when redistricting, another blow to the federal Voting Rights Act. It passed the Senate in June. But the bill languished in the House, which had flipped to Republicans in the 2024 election. The divided Michigan Legislature has struggled to move any election-related legislation through both chambers this session; it took until June of this year for any voting legislation to earn the governor’s signature. How does the Michigan Voting Rights Act compare to other states? If the bills that make up the Michigan Voting Rights Act ultimately do pass, Michigan will be far from the only state with a voting rights act. The first passed in California in 2002, and the next came almost a decade later in Illinois in 2011. Since then, more states have looked at passing them, in large part as a response to the weakening of the federal Voting Rights Act. To date, 12 states — all controlled by Democrats — have enacted one. Michigan’s could be the most impactful one yet, though. As a swing state, Michigan has an outsized influence in federal elections, including for president. Marisa Wright, legal counsel for voting rights at the Campaign Legal Center, said the Michigan Voting Rights Act would position the state as a leader in voting rights across the U.S. “I know there are many important issues people care about, but I think we have seen, especially recently, the right to vote is our most critical fundamental right,” she told Votebeat. Sixty percent of voting-age Michiganders voted in the 2026 election, according to unofficial results — tied for the highest midterm turnout in state history. Experts say that is at least in part because voting has become more accessible in the state in the last decade. Since 2018, Michigan voters have approved ballot measures enacting automatic registration, no-excuse absentee voting, Election Day registration, early in-person voting, the right to permanent absentee ballots, and ballot drop boxes. The Michigan Voting Rights Act would continue that trend. By strengthening the rights of disabled voters, improving language access, and addressing discrimination, Wright said the act has the potential to protect voters in the sort of “meaningful” ways that no longer exist at the federal level. A state-level act is not a replacement for strong federal legislation, she said, but it can be an important start. Josh Douglas, an election law professor at the University of Kentucky, said that the strongest voting rights acts offer a state’s voters “robust voter protections,” such as the right to sue over alleged violations, and strict scrutiny for proposed voting restrictions — the exact kind of tools legislators are looking to implement with the Michigan Voting Rights Act. It will take more than just getting the bills to the governor’s desk, though, Douglas said. It also matters how state courts interpret the laws, which can be harder to predict. “Just passing the law is the first step, but it’s not the last,” he said. How do election officials feel about the Michigan Voting Rights Act? Voting rights advocates may be enthusiastic about the Michigan Voting Rights Act, but clerks — the people who actually run Michigan elections — have expressed reservations. When the act was first introduced, Michigan’s two major clerk groups had a hand in shaping its contents. But clerks said they were still concerned about being held responsible for violations of the act, even accidental ones. A number of them spoke out against the original proposals, and their groups issued neutral positions on the bills. “Although these bills are well intentioned, they have the potential of paralyzing clerks from making necessary ministerial decisions in the best interests of their voters, in fear of soliciting costly lawsuits further damaging public trust in our electoral process,” the Michigan Association of Municipal Clerks said in a statement in 2024. Individual clerks testified before the legislature and told Votebeat they felt the same way, both in 2024 and earlier this year. Chris Swope, the Lansing City Clerk, has testified multiple times about his concerns over the proposal. Like others, his concern was that punishing clerks would damage trust in elections rather than improve it. “As clerks, our whole job is to ensure the voting rights of individuals here in Michigan, so we take this very seriously,” Swope said during the May hearing. Swope told Votebeat on Tuesday that his conversations with lawmakers suggest that the 2027 version of the act may address some of those concerns. While he supports the concept of a state-level voting rights act, particularly the expansion of language access, he wants the version that is put into law to change how penalties for clerks are handled. In particular, he wanted to see the “public shaming” portion of the act — which would require the secretary of state’s office to publicly name communities that fail to issue required notices on time and keep that violation notice up for at least a year — to be removed. “We’re humans, and we make errors,” he said. “We train our election workers, but they make errors. Putting that on a secretary of state website doesn’t feel helpful or beneficial to the whole process.” He is cautiously optimistic about what the bills will say if and when they are signed into law. Swope said it was “pretty clear” the Michigan Voting Rights Act was finally going to pass next session, and at this point, he feels “pretty good” about that. “I’m a believer in voting rights,” he said. “I think we should make sure that people have full access.” Hayley Harding is a reporter for Votebeat based in Michigan. Contact Hayley at hharding@votebeat.org.

Here are 6 issues the new Detroit school board will face
articles.description: The Detroit school board will swear in five members in January, a new majority that will help make pivotal decisions for the city’s school district.
articles.content: This story also appeared in Chalkbeat Detroit This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters. The Detroit school board will swear in five members in January, a new majority that will help make pivotal decisions for the city’s school district. The Detroit Public Schools Community District’s seven-member board must consider funding priorities as the money from a federal “right to read” lawsuit comes to an end. As parents and community members push the district to make quicker progress improving students’ academic performance, board members will weigh whether to continue current strategies or vote to change curriculum. And perhaps the largest decision the board could face in the coming year is whether to keep Superintendent Nikolai Vitti at the helm. In November, voters elected four new members — Georgia Lemmons, Jameel Smith, LaMar Lemmons, and Aliya Moore — plus incumbent Bessie Harris to the board out of a crowded field of candidates. The incoming board members bring different levels of experience in education and history with the district. “This is a crucial moment for the district all around,” said Imani Foster of educational equity nonprofit 482Forward. Below are some of the big issues the new board will face. Will the board’s direction prompt leadership changes? Most of the loudest candidates calling for Vitti’s departure were not elected. But the district could still be in store for new leadership. Vitti has not yet commented on the outcome of the election or how it may affect his future in the district. Many of the board members-elect told Chalkbeat they need time to review information and data before they decide if Vitti should remain. Though the board can vote to terminate the superintendent’s contract, it must be approved by the Detroit Financial Review Commission. If the board majority clashes too often with Vitti and his cabinet, it is possible Vitti will decide to leave on his own. Vitti’s current contract expires June 30, 2028. His nine-year tenure is among the longest in districts similar to DPSCD across the country. He raised the possibility of his exit from the district for the first time when negotiating the contract in 2024. How will the board define DPSCD’s funding priorities? The new board may have to make difficult decisions during the 2027 budget season. The $94.4 million settlement from the “right to read” lawsuit,which was used to hire hundreds of academic interventionists to help catch up struggling students, will run out at the end of this school year. The 2016 federal lawsuit alleged long-time state education funding inequities led to unsafe conditions in Detroit schools, which denied children in the city “access to the most basic building block of education: literacy.” Vitti has said he wants to keep the interventionists after the money is gone. Most of the newly elected board members said during their campaigns that they want to prioritize early literacy after the settlement funds have been depleted. Other priorities of the members-elect include wraparound services, music education, better transportation options, stronger tutoring services, and retaining highly qualified teachers. Maintaining libraries after bringing them back to schools The current board is expected to vote on an $8.7 million plan to return libraries to 89 schools. The costs would only cover the initial set up, including up to 4,000 books per school, a new cataloging system, furniture, and displays. In the short term, Vitti said at November’s board meeting the district plans to negotiate with the teachers union for interventionists to open and run the libraries around three periods a day and after school next fall. If the plan is approved, Vitti said it would cost an estimated $10 million to $12 million each year to staff certified librarians at the schools. The new board will likely have to find ways to cover the recurring costs, encourage teachers to get certified as librarians, or recruit librarians outside of DPSCD. If teachers do move into full-time librarian roles, the district will also need to consider how to fill vacancies. The board would also vote on new policies for the libraries, including on book selection. Will the board continue current strategies or adopt new curriculum? Even though the district has sustained long-term improvements on state standardized tests, many parents and community members say it’s not enough. Some board members agree. In recent months, board members have said they want to make changes to curriculum, particularly in early literacy. During their campaigns, members-elect suggested they were interested in a range of changes, including adopting new curriculum, reducing class sizes, ensuring the same curriculum is used across the district, and strengthening support for “the whole child.” Some want more emphasis on the sciences and to bring back wood shop and home economics classes. Deciding the fate of small schools with high costs In the coming years, the board will have a say in the future of schools with low enrollment that don’t generate enough funding to cover operational costs. The issue is an emotional one for many in the city because of the effects of widespread closings that occurred under the former Detroit Public Schools. In 2025-26, the district accelerated the closures of four such schools and another, Thurgood Marshall Elementary School, will close at the end of this school year. There are another 17 school buildings that the district identified as having few students and high costs. (Vitti has said that appearing on the list does not mean a school is being considered for closure, however). With enrollment remaining largely flat in recent years and many costly infrastructure needs in school buildings, the new board will likely be faced with difficult decisions. Harris and Georgia and LaMar Lemmons have taken a hard line against closing more schools. Moore said some should be consolidated. Smith said she would consider “school boundary adjustments, combining grade configurations, and merging schools.” The board will develop a new strategic plan for DPSCD With the expiration of the district’s current four-year strategic plan at the end of this school year, the new board will have to adopt a new one. The strategic plan lays out specific goals for the district, including attendance rates, increasing enrollment, student proficiency in core subjects, graduation rates, and growth in language comprehension for English learners. Those target goals are used to evaluate the superintendent’s performance. Updates on the goals are also given at monthly meetings for the board and the community to gauge the district’s progress. Hannah Dellinger covers Detroit schools for Chalkbeat Detroit. You can reach her at hdellinger@chalkbeat.org.

articles.title: With the biggest IPO of all time, Anthropic’s ‘good guy’ reputation is on the line
articles.description: Today is a new beginning for Anthropic: a years-in-the-making IPO that beat out SpaceX for most valuable of all time, having raised $81.3 billion and set an important precedent for the other public AI lab debuts to come.
