articles.content: Today is a new beginning for Anthropic: a years-in-the-making IPO that beat out SpaceX for most valuable of all time, having raised $81.3 billion and set an important precedent for the other public AI lab debuts to come. But it’s not simply a financial milestone. Anthropic was founded on the idea that it prioritized safety more than other labs; its founders had left executive research positions at OpenAI. As the AI race has accelerated, though, its executives have emphasized that Anthropic can only fulfill this mission by coming in first place, requiring lots of money and compute. Unsurprisingly, thoughtful, safe, and intentional AI development can conflict with the kind of sheer speed that winning this race requires. Adding in an initial public offering only complicates things further, and Anthropic’s leadership can pursue it more or less unilaterally. That’s thanks to a corporate structure focused on insulating the company from shareholder pressure to turn a profit — but one that also removes typical checks on its power. One former Anthropic employee, who left ahead of the IPO, said he and others at Anthropic have increasingly been feeling that the current pace of AI development is “untenable under normal market structures,” particularly with the mismatched incentives at play in a powerful industry with little to no oversight. Anthropic has spent years billing itself as different from, and more careful than, other AI companies. In theory, this extends to its plan for going public. It’s registered as a Public Benefit Corporation, which means Anthropic’s board has a responsibility to balance its mission against shareholder wealth maximization. As my colleague Robert Hart has discussed before, it has also developed a highly unusual power structure. Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), introduced in 2023, and its founders have controlling voting rights, meaning they’d never be able to be voted out by shareholders even as a public company. A special class of stock, Class T, allows a small group of trustees — the members of the LTBT — the “authority to select and remove a portion of” Anthropic’s board. They exist outside typical shareholder pressure and theoretically are a check for the founders, tasked with a mission to “balance the financial interests of our stockholders and our public benefit purpose at key junctures where we expect the consequences of our decisions to reach far beyond Anthropic.” The reality is significantly more complicated. The LTBT technically chooses four members of Anthropic’s seven-person board, for instance, but one of those four effectively needs to be approved by Anthropic’s founders, leaving the trust short of straightforward majority control. There are also stipulations about nominating or removing a director: the LTBT must provide its decision with 30 days’ notice to the company’s “nominating and corporate governance committee,” which consists of three members: co-founder Daniela Amodei (who is chair of the committee), Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings, and Anthropic investor Yasmin Razavi. Though the LTBT members are “financially disinterested” in the company, there’s also nothing stopping Anthropic from hypothetically hiring away a trustee and paying them a lot of money to work for the company. Mariano-Florentino Cuéllar (a former trustee) joined Anthropic in August as its Chief Global Affairs Officer, and OpenAI has in the past hired a former board member, Fidji Simo, to an executive position within the company. One could imagine a scenario in which, if a trustee was “looking a little bit too activist-y or something, they could just make that trustee an offer with millions of dollars in effective compensation that would entail stepping down from the trust, and that’s one way that they could have some oversight over this,” said Tyler Johnston, founder of The Midas Project, a nonprofit AI industry watchdog. Although the LTBT is billed as a way to check Anthropic’s leadership, to some outside observers, the fine print looks shaky. “The trust, since it doesn’t have a financial interest in Anthropic, could theoretically use its power with three slash four directors to keep the company on mission,” says Ann Lipton, law professor at the University of Colorado Law School and an expert in corporate governance. “One might question how likely that is to occur.” Moreover, Lipton questions whether the trust would know enough to gauge when to hit the brakes on a company plan or product even if they did have such authority. The four listed LTBT members aren’t known to be AI experts: they include former Fed Chair Ben Bernanke, foreign policy analyst Richard Fontaine, experimental physicist Christopher Stubbs, and former GiveWell executive Neil Buddy Shah, who is chair of the LTBT. “I’m not convinced that the trustees or the directors that they appoint have the insight into AI and AI development to be able to make these choices,” Lipton says. “They’re very prestigious people, but what does Ben Bernanke know about AI?” Several experts compared Anthropic’s LTBT to OpenAI’s nonprofit board before Altman’s ouster: “The powers, or lack thereof, of the Long-Term Benefit Trust … [are] analogous in some ways to the powers that the OpenAI nonprofit has,” said The Midas Project’s Johnston. Of course, that board’s decision to oust OpenAI CEO Sam Altman ended up leading, days later, to Altman’s return as CEO and the majority of the board’s resignation and replacement. But there’s a notable difference between that and the LTBT. Before OpenAI’s restructuring, its nonprofit board had the ability to step in and guide day-to-day decisions at the company when deemed necessary, and even after its restructuring, they retained that ability for safety and security matters, such as delaying or stopping a model release. Anthropic’s Form S-1 suggests that the LTBT, with its main duty being appointing (and potentially removing) certain board members, does not have either of those levels of authority. Instead, Anthropic’s structure looks more like the kind of founder-centric setup that Silicon Valley favors — like Mark Zuckerberg with Meta, and Elon Musk with SpaceX. Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment. “Neither the Trust or the trustees have any decisionmaking authority … over day to day decisions,” said Hamza Chaudhry, who leads AI and national security at the Future of Life Institute. “So I do not have strong hopes for the LTBT being a key mechanism for governance after they go public.” The former Anthropic employee said that Anthropic’s founders are essentially the only ones with any real decisionmaking power: “I would be surprised if you could find anyone who knows the founders, knows the Long-Term Benefit Trust, understands how decisions get made, and thinks the Long-Term Benefit Trust has any meaningful power,” he said. The employee added that the trustees were both “poorly equipped to provide meaningful oversight” to the founders and also selected on purpose to not rock the boat. Anthropic as a public company will face more pressure than ever before to secure capital, whether via driving more revenue or fundraising. That means that, as has been a trend in the industry for years, it will likely be more difficult to justify expensive AI safety initiatives, and there will inevitably be more pressure to speed up product releases and commercialization. “This trust and the founders together are the ones who actually have governance power,” Lipton said. “So you either trust that they are going to balance the interests of society appropriately, or you don’t. Either way, the real constraint on whatever societal impulses they have is going to be the fact that Anthropic needs money.” Anthropic has been open about the fact that it’s in extreme need of cold, hard cash, particularly to buy more compute and speed up its AI advancement. “Compute is the deepest business dilemma that the company faces,” Amodei said last Friday in a livestreamed conversation with JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon. “If you buy too much, of course you can financially overextend yourself. If you buy too little, then you can’t support inference for customers, and even more importantly … you can’t do the R&D.” Anthropic’s website summarizes the company’s raison d’être as one thing: “AI research and products that put safety at the frontier.” But it’s also been clear that for that safety pledge to matter, Anthropic needs vast resources to remain a viable business. Like other labs, it’s been pursuing recursive self-improvement, a controversial and potentially dangerous industry milestone denoting AI systems that can autonomously improve and create advanced versions of themselves. “You can’t do safety from second place,” said Anthropic policy chief Sarah Heck in September. This explanation hasn’t satisfied everyone, including some Anthropic employees. Anthropic’s head of safeguards research departed in February alleging that “the world is in peril”; one of its researchers, Jacob Coxon, made headlines in September for claiming that both Anthropic and OpenAI are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”; and that same month, an Anthropic safety researcher departed for a job at nonprofit third-party AI auditor METR, writing that “AI companies are on track to impose an unprecedented level of risk on society” and that “while Anthropic hasn’t had as severe an incident as the HuggingFace attack [by OpenAI agents], I think that’s partly a matter of luck.” --- Are you a current or former Anthropic employee? Contact me via Signal at haydenfield.11 on a non-work device with tips. --- On Wednesday, a new statement from the Center for AI Safety, with prominent industry signatories from Hugging Face, Harvard University, and more, alleged that Anthropic is “not a safe AI company” and that it attempts to “amass power in the name of the greater good.” It stated, “Anthropic warns that recursively self-improving AI could concentrate power and escape human control, yet races to build it first. The company uses safety branding to court investors, employees, and the public—even as it has quietly weakened its safety pledges and lobbied for self-serving regulation.” The former Anthropic employee said he felt he had initially “drunk the Kool-Aid” about Anthropic needing to come in first place in the AI race for a safe outcome but then grew disillusioned, realizing that the race to the top did not “warrant the cost imposed” — namely, that one company should not be able to “unilaterally” decide to pursue RSI. (Amodei has stated publicly that “left unchecked, [RSI] could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems, and so must be pursued very carefully, if at all.”) “It’s pretty ridiculous that private companies are building a new form of intelligence on track to be more powerful and influential on the planet than humans and are doing that with less oversight, in many ways, than taco trucks currently have,” the former employee said. Anthropic’s website states that “at the end of the day, the mission is what we’re all here for. It gives us a shared purpose and allows us to act swiftly together, rather than being pulled in multiple directions by competing goals. It engenders trust and collaboration, and is the final arbiter in our decisions.” The question is whether, and how, the interpretation of Anthropic’s mission may shift — once it’s facing more pressure than ever before to justify a fully diluted market cap of about $1.5 trillion.

articles.title: JD Vance called Abdul El-Sayed "very, very evil." Now they're preparing to meet.
articles.content: Vice President JD Vance and Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed are preparing to meet, El-Sayed and the White House said, after a bitter campaign in which Vance called the Democrat "very, very evil."It's not clear what the meeting will look like or who asked for it. The two sides gave different accounts. El-Sayed said in a Tuesday interview on MS NOW that Vance's office contacted his team. Vance's office said Wednesday it reached out after being told El-Sayed wanted time with the vice president.Vance will preside over El-Sayed's swearing-in Jan. 3. In his victory speech after the Nov. 3 election, El-Sayed addressed Vance as "habibi," an Arabic term of endearment, and said, "Wolverine one, Buckeye zero," a nod to the Michigan-Ohio State rivalry. Vance is an Ohio State graduate. El-Sayed is a Michigan alumnus.Both men have said in recent days that they're open to finding common ground, on their own terms."If Abdul El-Sayed wants to work with me and the president to make people's lives better, he's going to find us very much a willing partner," Vance said Monday on Fox News Channel."If he wants to work with us to get money out of politics, put money in pockets and pass Medicare for All, which is what I ran on, I'm a willing partner," El-Sayed said on MS NOW.It's not clear how they could cooperate. Medicare for All, El-Sayed's chief policy goal, has been dismissed by the Trump administration, including Vance.Vance's "very, very evil" remark came in August while he was campaigning for Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers in the Detroit area. In October, he called El-Sayed a "weasel" who should "shut his mouth," and said at a rally in Monroe that El-Sayed "doesn't love this community." El-Sayed said the remarks were meant "to raise questions about my commitment to America."The talk of a meeting comes after Republicans lost their majorities in both chambers of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, and as Vance nears a decision on whether to seek the Republican presidential nomination in 2028. At an October town hall in Michigan, Vance said he hadn't decided whether to run and acknowledged there's a chance he won't.El-Sayed, who defeated Rogers, will be the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate.

articles.title: Schneider Electric warns high power costs could push AI investment out of Europe
articles.content: High electricity prices in Europe could push AI investment to other regions, Peter Weckesser, chief digital officer of Schneider Electric, told Reuters in Gdansk on Nov. 19 [1]. He said energy costs feed directly into the cost of computing, and that high power prices, insufficient grid investment and fragmented regulation across the European Union could slow the region's AI data center expansion [1]. Reuters reported that the United States is clearly ahead in data center construction, followed by China, while Europe lags and regions including the Middle East are expanding faster [1]. Weckesser said Europe needs major grid investment and a more consistent regulatory framework [1]. On calls for European control of the AI supply chain, Weckesser said full control is unrealistic and would raise costs. "I think it's much smarter to think about which parts of the supply chain you really need to own" and "which ones you are able to source from the outside," he said [1]. Schneider, which sells power distribution, cooling and control equipment to data center builders, set out its view of the region's power needs in a November 2025 study. It modeled European AI electricity demand of 45 TWh in a constrained scenario, 90 TWh in a coordinated one and 145 TWh under unchecked expansion by 2030, called for grid capacity to be built ahead of demand, and said Europe holds less than 5% of the world's computing infrastructure [2]. Schneider is the lead energy infrastructure partner on a SoftBank-led plan for up to 5 GW of AI data center capacity in France [3]. articles.title: Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things
articles.description: Watching fights wasn't as good as practical experience, but it got the mice halfway there.
articles.content: Credit: J.M. Iravedra-Garcia et al., 2026 Credit: J.M. Iravedra-Garcia et al., 2026 There's something about watching violent events that broadly appeals to us, whether it's the latest John Wick movie, a video game, or a live UFC bout. Scientists have debated whether watching violent things could make us more aggressive, but it could also be an adaptive survival strategy. Male mice, for instance, who watched other mice fighting learned enough about how to fight to better protect themselves (compared to mice who didn't watch fights) when pitted against stronger, more aggressive opponents, according to a paper published in the journal Nature. The team randomly assigned male mice to three groups—fighters, spectators, or novices—and then subjected each group to eight days of training with three 10-minute sessions per day. The novices played with stuffed mice in isolation, while the spectators watched various pairs of fighter mice battle from a raised platform behind a transparent barrier—a set-up chosen to let them smell and listen to the fights as well as observe them. The ninth day was "fight night," when all the mice had to face a daunting opponent in three 4-minute rounds. Each fight was filmed from above so that the mouse behavior could be analyzed. To monitor corresponding changes in brain activity, the team engineered the rodents' excitatory brain cells to glow green whenever they were activated, while inhibitory brain cells glowed red. They also implanted tiny optical fibers into 12 interconnected brain regions so they could track changing activity in every brain region simultaneously.Read full article Comments

articles.title: Federal judge considers rare review of grand jury proceedings in U-M protest case
articles.description: A federal judge in Michigan may take the rare step of opening secretive grand jury testimony to determine if the panel was given the full and accurate account of a raid on a home that led to additional charges being filed against Zainab Hakim, one of 12 current and former University of Michigan students charged with crimes related to pro-Palestinian protests over the last several years.
articles.content:
Zainab Hakim, left, and her attorney, Amanda Bashi, exit the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026 in downtown Ann Arbor, Mich. Hakim was in court for a revocation of bail hearing
(Ben Solis / Michigan Advance)A federal judge in Michigan may take the rare step of opening secretive grand jury testimony to determine if the panel was given the full and accurate account of a raid on a home that led to additional charges being filed against Zainab Hakim, one of 12 current and former University of Michigan students charged with crimes related to pro-Palestinian protests over the last several years.Hakim, along with 11 others, has been charged in federal court on allegations of protests, graffiti and property damage at the offices and homes of weapons developers, political organizations and U-M officials related to actions in support of Palestine. She appeared in court on Wednesday for a hearing to determine if she would be jailed before her trial in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan due to new charges of evidence tampering, which her defense denies took place.Hakim was not taken into custody on Wednesday and will be back in court on Dec. 2 as there were questions of whether the grand jury that brought the new charges — and made up the basis for the government to revoke her initial bond — was given the full scope of evidence on the raid that led to the request to revoke bail.Hakim’s defense believed that the grand jury was not given an accurate picture of the raid, or the evidence of alleged tampering, and is asking U.S. District Judge Judith Levy to review the grand jury testimony to determine if prosecutors had presented misleading testimony or whether irregularities in the proceeding undermined the grand jury’s decision to bring the charges.Levy entertained that idea and adjourned the bail hearing to do her own research on whether she had authority to do so. Levy also asked the government and Hakim’s defense attorney, Amanda Bashi, to file additional briefing on the issue.Levy was clear, however, that there was limited precedent allowing judges to unseal grand jury proceedings, and Bashi only read off a handful of cases that helped her position.State charges against the group were dropped last year, but the federal government pursued the case and charged Hakim and others for allegedly conspiring “to transmit threats in interstate and foreign commerce” against individuals who they deemed connected to or supporting Israel’s war in Gaza against Hamas.The federal government has alleged that the group did so outside the bounds of the First Amendment and constituted criminal acts in support of Hamas.In October, the FBI arrested Henry David Mackeen-Shapiro, one of the co-defendants, and then raided the home where Hakim and Mackeen-Shapiro live to execute an additional search warrant. In that raid, agents said they uncovered a laptop that they believed was dumped into a bath of either salt water or fresh water in an alleged attempt to tamper with or destroy evidence. However, the complaint didn’t specify if it had been dumped in water or just kept in a wet bag. The government has claimed that the laptop was found in Hakim’s bedroom, and not in the room of its owner, Mackeen-Shapiro.In court on Wednesday, Bashi said the public complaint filed with the court, in her view, contained so many inconsistencies that it appeared as there were two diametrically opposed accounts of what happened during the raid, and that the government’s account amounted to a misrepresentation to the court. During the bond hearing, federal prosecutors had to correct themselves multiple times before Levy as to the veracity of the statements in the complaint.That led Bashi to believe that, potentially, the grand jury which brought additional evidence tampering charges against Hakim hadn’t been told the whole story, or an incorrect version of events.A timeline of the raid, along with body-worn camera images, showed that Hakim and others appeared to have cooperated with FBI agents and made themselves present at their front door. It also indicated agents had not congregated inside the home. Statements from defense witnesses also showed that agents had commended the home’s residents, including Hakim, who had cooperated with agents during the raid.The federal government said it is still actively restoring the laptop in question, and that it had not been chemically tested prior to the grand jury presentation to show whether it had been dumped in salt water or fresh water in an attempt to destroy it.Federal prosecutors, however, did not quarrel with Bashi’s alleged timeline of the events.Bashi noted that neither the laptop’s surroundings nor Hakim were wet when agents obtained the laptop, and that earlier insinuations that the laptop was found in a bag of wet clothes — as a way to destroy it — were inaccurate; the wet bag had been found on top of the laptop during the raid.The laptop belonging to Mackeen-Shapiro, Bashi added, was in poor condition that showed it was heavily used and possibly damaged by Mackeen-Shapiro well before the raid and the alleged attempt to destroy it.Bashi posited that it was more likely that Mackeen-Shapiro “was a slob” and failed to take care of the laptop, leading to its dilapidated condition, which was not evidence of material destruction.Federal prosecutors characterized Bashi’s attempts to poke holes in the grand jury testimony as a delay tactic, but Levy was open to the idea of at least peeking behind the curtain — if she was allowed to do so under legal precedent — to gauge the official account of the raid to what was presented to the grand jury.Briefs on the matter are due next week from both Bashi and federal prosecutors while Levy researches the matter.Meanwhile, Hakim was able to remain free on Wednesday. She had a crowd of supporters with her, including her parents, in the courtroom, as well as another group holding a small solidarity rally for her outside.It was also Hakim’s birthday and her friends and allies presented her with a cake and sang to her on the courthouse steps following the proceedings.November 19, 20264:45 amThis story was updated to more accurately reflect the charges filed in the case.Michigan Advance is part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity. U-M experts: Michigan economy at ‘cruising altitude’ despite plummeting labor rate
articles.description: University of Michigan economists are ‘relatively upbeat’ about the state’s economic outlook in coming years despite a shrinking labor participation rate that has some worried.
articles.content: Michigan’s economy will remain resilient in the coming years in spite of labor market strain, volatile trade policy and high energy prices Michigan’s aging population remains a “major risk” for the state, according to a new economic outlook from U-M researchers That said, the state may still need to cut $1.5B from the state budget in the 2027 fiscal year due to tax changes as part a new roads deal LANSING — Despite high interest rates, volatile trade policy and high energy prices, University of Michigan economists say the state economy is poised to remain resilient and suggest news of a cratering labor force should be taken “with a large grain of salt.” While they are “relatively upbeat,” the experts warn in a new report that Michigan’s aging population may be a significant constraint on economic growth in the future, and that “tepid population growth poses a major risk to the state’s longer-run economic and demographic outlook.” More immediately, two big issues loom over the state’s economy: “The future direction of tariffs and international trade policy, and the ongoing war in Iran,” the U-M economists wrote in a forecast released Tuesday. They project Michigan will add 1,000 payroll jobs this year and that growth will accelerate to 9,600 jobs next year before the state loses 2,200 jobs in 2028 as federal “healthcare funding cuts bite.” Michigan’s unemployment rate is also anticipated to hover in the 4.9% to 5% percent range through the end of 2028 — higher than the projected national unemployment rate of 4.1 percent through 2028, economists note. Related: Michigan is old and aging. Experts warn of looming consequences Report: Aging crisis to cause Michigan to lose out on economic boom Michigan population steady at 10.1M. Detroit, Grand Rapids up slightly In late October, data released from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics showed that Michigan’s labor force participation rate fell to just 58.5% in September—a record low outside of the pandemic years. Some saw that as a big warning sign for Michigan, but U-M economists said they are “skeptical of the extent to which this decline reflects underlying labor market conditions, particularly in the period since the federal government shutdown in 2025.” Still, the economists do project that the state’s labor force participation rate “will continue declining” through 2028, with a smaller share of the population either working or actively looking for work. That’s partly due to Michigan’s aging population. Members of the baby boom generation are continuing to retire, and federal immigration policies are restraining labor force growth. Donate By the end of 2028, economists say the state’s labor force participation rate will likely edge down to 57.8%, well below the historic low of 59.1% in the first half of 2021. Michigan is projected to lose jobs this year in cyclical industries such as manufacturing, trade and transportation, but U-M economists predict other job gains will more than offset those losses. “Our assessment of the incoming data is that Michigan’s economy is roughly at cruising altitude,” economists note, “and we forecast it to remain there over the next two years.” State budget outlook The new economic projections for Michigan come as Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson and Democratic legislative majorities prepare to take over state government in January. Officials will likely meet that same month to agree on revenue estimates that Benson will use to craft her first state budget proposal, but the new U-M report provides an early preview. After a year of “solid” growth, state revenues are expected to decline by 1.4% in the 2027 fiscal year that began in October before growing again by 4.2% in fiscal year 2028, the economists wrote. The pending decline is due, in part, to broad forces, they wrote: weaker state tax collections and a “suite of legislative changes enacted” in late 2025, most notably the elimination of the state’s 6% sales tax on fuel, which was a key component of Whitmer’s road funding deal. New deductions for qualified tips and overtime are also expected to reduce state revenues. The economists also noted Benson could pursue other tax code changes after taking office next year, and “unified Democratic control of state government could provide” her with the latitude to do so. “Her emphasis on affordability, including a pledge not to raise taxes on middle-class residents and proposals for targeted tax credits, suggests that tax relief could feature in the new administration’s agenda,” they wrote. That’s uncertain, however. And “in keeping with our traditional practice, our forecast of Michigan revenues reflects the state’s current tax code,” they wrote.

NYC Mayor Mamdani signs bill banning horse carriage industry into law
articles.content: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed the horse carriage ban into law Thursday as workers vow to legally challenge it. The mayor signed Romanch's Law at 9:30 a.m. at City Hall. In October, the City Council passed the bill, which sets a June 2028 deadline to phase out horse carriages.Horse-drawn carriages have been a fixture in Central Park for more than 160 years."Our city has changed. Now it is time for our laws to change too," Mamdani said. The legislation is named after 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, a tourist from India who was killed after a horse became startled and threw him from a carriage in Central Park. "This is a truly historic day for New York City, nearly two decades after the Council first considered ending the horse-drawn carriage industry," said Speaker Julie Menin. "Today, I'm thinking of Romanch Mahajan, who should still be with us and whose tragic, untimely death reminds us why this legislation was so urgently needed."There was jubilation at City Hall as Mamdani signed the legislation that will mean the death knell for the horse carriage industry in New York. "This is a new day for our city. One that will make the crown jewel of Manhattan's parks safer, while also recognizing the lasting legacy and contributions the horse carriage industry has made in our city," Mamdani said. "One thing became abundantly clear," Menin said. "Unless we act, and unless we act with urgency, unless we do something to prevent another fatality from happening in our great Central Park, this would continue." Efforts to ban the industry have gone on for decades. Bill de Blasio made it a key plank in his 2013 campaign for mayor. "I think the tragedy brought it home to a lot of New Yorkers very emotionally, very humanly," de Blasio said. But will it survive a court challenge from those who oppose it? Immediately after the bill was signed, the Transport Workers Union filed a lawsuit against the city. Union leaders, attorneys and carriage workers gathered outside the federal courthouse in Manhattan at noon to outline their legal challenge, claiming the ban is unconstitutional. "There are alternatives to putting 300 people out of work. There are alternatives to destroying $20 million worth of medallions. There are alternatives the city has not considered," attorney Arthur Schwartz said. Christine Hansen is a driver who owns five horses. "This is a national disgrace today about what is happening to the Central Park horse carriages," she said. "Let me tell you, I am so tired of watching my fellow carriage drivers and my friends be bullied, harassed and accused of horrible things when they are the most gentle and good-spirited and loving people that I have met in this city. Their priority is the care of their horses, and they've devoted their lives to working alongside them," said carriage driver Danielle Slott. City Councilmember Christopher Marte, who sponsored the bill, pledged the drivers will be taken care of. "We look forward to working with the TWU and all the independent contractors to make sure they get a fair compensation and they get the jobs that they want," Marte said. Mamdani said the city will work with the drivers to develop a compensation plan and to help them find other work. He also ordered a feasibility study to see if electric carriages and pedal-assist bicycles can replace the horses.

articles.title: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage
articles.description: When everything goes down, don’t assume it’s a cyberattack.
articles.content: Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US. Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking, this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence. Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.Read full article Comments

The Michigan Voting Rights Act could finally become law in 2027. Here’s everything you need to know.
articles.description: This article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization reporting on voting access and election administration across the U.S. Sign up for Votebeat Michigan’s free newsletter here. A proposal to protect minority voting rights in Michigan is coming back to the key swing state. Democrats in Lansing have tried but failed to pass […]
articles.content: Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson spoke to reporters the morning after winning the gubernatorial election, telling reporters that her agenda for the first 100 days would be rolled out soon. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)This article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization reporting on voting access and election administration across the U.S. Sign up for Votebeat Michigan’s free newsletter here. A proposal to protect minority voting rights in Michigan is coming back to the key swing state. Democrats in Lansing have tried but failed to pass the Michigan Voting Rights Act in each of the last two legislative sessions. But now that the party has regained full control of state government, the proposal might actually make it into law. Democratic Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson — who currently serves as Michigan’s top election official as secretary of state — has named the act as her top priority, saying on the campaign trail that it would be the first bill she would sign. And leaders in the House and Senate say they will work hard to pass it during next year’s legislative session, which starts Jan. 1. Speaker-elect Ranjeev Puri told Votebeat on Thursday that “there is a lot of interest and excitement amongst the Michigan House Democrats” to make sure the proposal passes, although he declined to give a specific timeline. Senate Majority Leader-elect Darrin Camilleri said in a statement that, as a lead sponsor of the act, “it is of course very high on my list of priorities when Democrats regain our trifecta in January.” At their core, the four bills that make up the Michigan Voting Rights Act aim to fill in the gaps of the federal Voting Rights Act, which has been chipped away at by court rulings in recent years. Several other states already have state-level voting rights acts, but Michigan would be the first true swing state to pass one, so its passage would mark an important milestone for voting rights advocates. The act would also add to the long list of ways the state has expanded voting rights over the past decade. But not everyone is excited about the proposed changes. What’s in the Michigan Voting Rights Act? It’s not clear if Democrats will modify the existing bills before reintroducing them when the session starts. But the 2027-2028 version of the Michigan Voting Rights Act is expected to be substantially similar to the two versions that have been introduced before. In past sessions, the first bill in the package proposed banning “discriminatory activity” in voting and established a legal framework for challenging it. It prohibited local governments from imposing prerequisites on voting or causing voting disparities between members of a protected class — including racial or language minority groups — “and other members of the electorate.” It also would introduce new requirements for notifying voters about changes to elections, including new polling places or precinct boundaries. The bill also would allow voters to sue municipalities over alleged violations of the act. It proposed granting courts the ability to appoint election monitors, have veto power over election-related changes such as moving polling places, and more — an echo of requirements that were once part of the federal Voting Rights Act before the Supreme Court struck them down in 2013. The second bill in the package proposed creating a “voting and elections database and institute” at at least one state university which would track and publish election data, such as precinct-level results and voter registration information. The third of the four bills would require jurisdictions to translate materials into another language if a significant number of voters speak that language and aren’t proficient in English. It also would establish thresholds for which communities needed to provide those translated materials and created an advisory council, with members appointed by the secretary of state, to suggest requirements. Language access is covered by Section 203 of the federal Voting Rights Act. Michigan’s proposal goes further and would set a lower bar for when ballots need to be translated and in which communities. The federal act, for example, does not include Arabic and related languages — which is relevant in Michigan’s case, since Arabic is the state’s third-most commonly spoken language. The final bill aimed to provide more conveniences for voters, including those with special concerns such as voters with disabilities. It would codify curbside voting, permit voters with language barriers to bring their own translators, and allow people to provide “food, warmth, or other necessities” to people in line to vote. It would also require governments to disclose when they made certain administrative changes, such as removing voters from the rolls or allowing voters to examine voting equipment. Why hasn’t the Michigan Voting Rights Act passed before? In past sessions, the Michigan Voting Rights Act simply wasn’t able to make it over the finish line. The package was first introduced in 2023, the last time Democrats controlled the Senate, House, and governor’s office all at once. During that session, though, the bills sat in committee for almost a year before the Senate passed them in September 2024, with just three months left in the session. Legislators tried to get them through the House as well — they even had a committee hearing in December — but the proposal ultimately died during a chaotic final month of the session when lame-duck Democrats struggled to move any legislation at all. Supporters tried again this year in the Senate, where the bills were re-introduced just a few weeks after the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in Louisiana v. Callais changed how race could be considered when redistricting, another blow to the federal Voting Rights Act. It passed the Senate in June. But the bill languished in the House, which had flipped to Republicans in the 2024 election. The divided Michigan Legislature has struggled to move any election-related legislation through both chambers this session; it took until June of this year for any voting legislation to earn the governor’s signature. How does the Michigan Voting Rights Act compare to other states? If the bills that make up the Michigan Voting Rights Act ultimately do pass, Michigan will be far from the only state with a voting rights act. The first passed in California in 2002, and the next came almost a decade later in Illinois in 2011. Since then, more states have looked at passing them, in large part as a response to the weakening of the federal Voting Rights Act. To date, 12 states — all controlled by Democrats — have enacted one. Michigan’s could be the most impactful one yet, though. As a swing state, Michigan has an outsized influence in federal elections, including for president. Marisa Wright, legal counsel for voting rights at the Campaign Legal Center, said the Michigan Voting Rights Act would position the state as a leader in voting rights across the U.S. “I know there are many important issues people care about, but I think we have seen, especially recently, the right to vote is our most critical fundamental right,” she told Votebeat. Sixty percent of voting-age Michiganders voted in the 2026 election, according to unofficial results — tied for the highest midterm turnout in state history. Experts say that is at least in part because voting has become more accessible in the state in the last decade. Since 2018, Michigan voters have approved ballot measures enacting automatic registration, no-excuse absentee voting, Election Day registration, early in-person voting, the right to permanent absentee ballots, and ballot drop boxes. The Michigan Voting Rights Act would continue that trend. By strengthening the rights of disabled voters, improving language access, and addressing discrimination, Wright said the act has the potential to protect voters in the sort of “meaningful” ways that no longer exist at the federal level. A state-level act is not a replacement for strong federal legislation, she said, but it can be an important start. Josh Douglas, an election law professor at the University of Kentucky, said that the strongest voting rights acts offer a state’s voters “robust voter protections,” such as the right to sue over alleged violations, and strict scrutiny for proposed voting restrictions — the exact kind of tools legislators are looking to implement with the Michigan Voting Rights Act. It will take more than just getting the bills to the governor’s desk, though, Douglas said. It also matters how state courts interpret the laws, which can be harder to predict. “Just passing the law is the first step, but it’s not the last,” he said. How do election officials feel about the Michigan Voting Rights Act? Voting rights advocates may be enthusiastic about the Michigan Voting Rights Act, but clerks — the people who actually run Michigan elections — have expressed reservations. When the act was first introduced, Michigan’s two major clerk groups had a hand in shaping its contents. But clerks said they were still concerned about being held responsible for violations of the act, even accidental ones. A number of them spoke out against the original proposals, and their groups issued neutral positions on the bills. “Although these bills are well intentioned, they have the potential of paralyzing clerks from making necessary ministerial decisions in the best interests of their voters, in fear of soliciting costly lawsuits further damaging public trust in our electoral process,” the Michigan Association of Municipal Clerks said in a statement in 2024. Individual clerks testified before the legislature and told Votebeat they felt the same way, both in 2024 and earlier this year. Chris Swope, the Lansing City Clerk, has testified multiple times about his concerns over the proposal. Like others, his concern was that punishing clerks would damage trust in elections rather than improve it. “As clerks, our whole job is to ensure the voting rights of individuals here in Michigan, so we take this very seriously,” Swope said during the May hearing. Swope told Votebeat on Tuesday that his conversations with lawmakers suggest that the 2027 version of the act may address some of those concerns. While he supports the concept of a state-level voting rights act, particularly the expansion of language access, he wants the version that is put into law to change how penalties for clerks are handled. In particular, he wanted to see the “public shaming” portion of the act — which would require the secretary of state’s office to publicly name communities that fail to issue required notices on time and keep that violation notice up for at least a year — to be removed. “We’re humans, and we make errors,” he said. “We train our election workers, but they make errors. Putting that on a secretary of state website doesn’t feel helpful or beneficial to the whole process.” He is cautiously optimistic about what the bills will say if and when they are signed into law. Swope said it was “pretty clear” the Michigan Voting Rights Act was finally going to pass next session, and at this point, he feels “pretty good” about that. “I’m a believer in voting rights,” he said. “I think we should make sure that people have full access.” Hayley Harding is a reporter for Votebeat based in Michigan. Michigan Court of Appeals affirms unconstitutionality of abortion limitations
articles.description: In a ruling issued Tuesday, a panel of judges on the Michigan Court of Appeals unanimously ruled that limitations on abortion procedures within Michigan’s public health code are unconstitutional, a decision that was celebrated by reproductive rights advocates. The specific mandated limitations in question are a 24-hour mandatory waiting period, uniform informed consent requirements, a […]
articles.content: A sign at the Michigan Pride rally in Lansing on June 26, 2022. (Photo by Laina G. Stebbins/Michigan Advance)In a ruling issued Tuesday, a panel of judges on the Michigan Court of Appeals unanimously ruled that limitations on abortion procedures within Michigan’s public health code are unconstitutional, a decision that was celebrated by reproductive rights advocates. The specific mandated limitations in question are a 24-hour mandatory waiting period, uniform informed consent requirements, a physician participation mandate and mandatory screening for coercion. The suit, which was first heard in the Court of Claims, was brought by the Northland Family Planning Center, alleged that these provisions in the law “unconstitutionally burdened the right to abortion without serving the limited compelling purpose of protecting the health of an individual seeking care, that each provision was inconsistent with accepted clinical standards of practice and evidence-based medicine, that the provisions imposed requirements that intruded on the autonomous decision making of patients, and that the provisions discriminated in the protection and enforcement of the right to reproductive freedom.” In the decision from the Court of Claims, which was issued in May 2025, the court decided that the mandatory 24-hour waiting period, the uniform mandatory consent requirement and the physician mandate were unconstitutional and issued a permanent injunction enjoining enforcement of those provisions. Planned Parenthood of Michigan to close three clinics after funding cuts However, the lower court did not rule that the mandatory screening for coercion was unconstitutional, arguing that it is neutral on the face of the law. The Court of Appeals, on the other hand, ruled that because the statute prohibits only coercion to abort, not coercion to become pregnant or continue a pregnancy, it “risks operating in a manner that discriminates against individuals who seek to exercise the full range of reproductive choices guaranteed by our Constitution.” The decision goes on to say that the Court of Claims did not fully interrogate the question at hand, “namely, whether the law, as applied, impermissibly discriminates in the enforcement of reproductive rights by creating a disparate impact on those who do not wish to continue a pregnancy, or who are coerced to become pregnant. The absence of such analysis renders the lower court’s decision incomplete with respect to the constitutional issues presented.” As such the court remanded the decision to the Court of Claims, which “must determine whether the statutory framework, both in its language and in its application, comports with the constitutional mandate of equal protection in the enforcement of the right to reproductive freedom” and must complete “a searching examination not only of the statutory text, but also of the real-world consequences of its enforcement.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Reproductive rights advocates, including Planned Parenthood of Michigan President and CEO Paula Thornton Greear, welcomed the decision. “Michigan voters decided that decisions about pregnancy belong to the person who is pregnant, and this ruling holds the state to that,” Thornton Greear said in a press release issued Wednesday. “These laws had nothing to do with patient health, because they delayed care, forced people to read state-written material no clinician would hand a patient for any other kind of care, and limited who could provide that care — and now the courts have said so twice.” Thornton Greear also encouraged the incoming Democratic-controlled Legislature, which will convene in January, to update the laws in statute, instead of relying on court decisions to prevent the enforcement of the limitations — a priority that she has previously called on legislators to take up in the new legislative session.

articles.title: APEC serves as a backdrop as big power politics eclipse talk of open trade, AI
articles.description: APEC serves as a backdrop as big power politics eclipse talk of open trade, AI AP News Futuristic Shenzhen Shows Trump the Difficulty of Stopping China Bloomberg.com Xi Jinping rallies against protectionism as he welcomes Trump to Apec summit The Guardian Behind the scenes at the APEC Summit Reuters In Choosing Shenzhen for Trump-Putin Summit, Xi Shows Off His Tech Ambitions WSJ
articles.content: SHENZHEN, China (AP) — Countries must unite in keeping trade and technology development open, Chinese President Xi Jinping told fellow leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit Thursday in the skyscraper-studded financial hub of Shenzhen. The APEC extravaganza of meetings of Pacific Rim economies has showcased China’s leadership in artificial intelligence and other 21st-century marvels. But it is being overshadowed by big power politics. Xi, U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin were meeting later in an unprecedented trilateral summit. The annual APEC summit has followed the usual traditions of formal arrivals, a gala dinner, scores of bilateral meetings on the sidelines, and a formal group photo. This year, the portrait featured business attire and wide red or blue scarves draped over the leaders’ shoulders. The venue, in China’s showcase technology hub, resplendent with its lightshows and robots, has drawn somewhat more attention than usual for a grouping moving ever so slowly toward its longstanding goal of establishing a free trade zone around the Pacific Rim, while keeping its members talking through wars, trade disputes and economic crises. The meeting between Xi, Trump and Putin was expected to focus on a wider array of issues, including nuclear arms and the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East. As the historic trilateral meeting started on Thursday, Trump said that “too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements. No problems are ever solved by refusing to talk about it.” “Let’s see if we can get something done,” Trump said. Earlier in the day, in opening the APEC leaders’ meeting, Xi urged fellow leaders of the 21 APEC economies to unite behind their shared interests in open trade and technology development. “APEC members are like passengers riding the same boat,” he said to the dozens of officials arrayed in a big circle at the lavish venue. “To weather the winds and waves of the Pacific, we should join forces and watch out for one another and strengthen the bonds of shared interests.” Putin is attending an APEC summit for the first time in nine years. He echoed Xi in saying that “APEC must set a tone of unity and develop a constructive agenda for cooperation.” In his brief remarks, Trump boasted about the U.S. economy and said that he expected to be signing more trade agreements in the near future. He asserted he has helped bring in trillions of dollars of new investment into the U.S. and helped to create trillions in new wealth. He also vowed to oppose “globalist” efforts to regulate or stifle AI, which he calls “super intelligence.” Still, U.S. efforts to restrict Chinese access to the most advanced computer chips and other components used for AI are a perennial sore point for Beijing, an issue highlighted in the recent scandal over Nvidia founder and former CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with a Chinese technology executive. Xi and other Asian leaders have emphasized that it’s imperative for AI technology to be fairly shared and regulated to ensure financial stability, cybersecurity and equitable growth. Earlier this week, Washington tightened restrictions on remote access to such technology in a move that experts say has eliminated a significant loophole that facilitated access for China to billions of dollars worth of the most advanced Nvidia chips used for AI. More broadly, AI is having a “material impact” on global growth, helping to offset the blow from energy shocks from war in the Middle East, Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, told the APEC leaders. The APEC region’s economies, which account for more than half of all global business activity, are growing at a 3.4% annual pace, slightly faster than global growth of 3.1%, she said. And global trade has been expanding at a rate of 4.6%, in large share thanks to the AI investment boom. “While the energy shock will eventually dissipate, AI is forever, the most significant factor for medium-term competitiveness, productivity, and growth,” Georgieva said. “This is the fastest transformation in human history,” she added. “And to put it very simply, you snooze, you lose.” Associated Press journalists around the world contributed to this report.

Wreck of Australia’s first warship built at home found 128 years after sinking
articles.description: Wreck of Australia’s first warship built at home found 128 years after sinking AP News Wreck of First Australian-Built Warship Is Revealed 128 Years After It Sank The New York Times Wreck of first Australian-built warship found off Far North Queensland coast ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation Wreck of Australia's First Home-Built Warship Discovered The Maritime Executive Australian Navy’s Firs
articles.content: MELBOURNE, Australia (AP) — The wreck of the first Australian warship built in the country, HMCS Spitfire, was found 128 years to the day after it sank off the north coast of what is now Queensland state, officials said Thursday. The 19-meter (62-foot) schooner was launched in Sydney in 1855 to fight a potential Russian invasion. But Spitfire had been operating as a fishing boat four decades later when it sprung a leak and foundered on Aug. 21, 1898, off Piper Island, documents show. A Royal Australian Navy mine hunter vessel found and exposed 16 meters (52 feet) of the wreck nearly three months ago, also on Aug. 21, after a monthlong search using a dive team and remotely operated vehicles, a joint statement from multiple agencies said. “It is remarkable luck that Spitfire was discovered on the 128th anniversary of its sinking,” Queensland heritage officer Celeste Jordan said in the statement. The discovery was not announced sooner because of reporting processes between government agencies required under laws designed to protect shipwrecks, the Defense Department explained Thursday. Bearing the designation of HMCS, meaning Her Majesty’s Colonial Schooner, Spitfire was commissioned in 1855 during the Crimean War when the British colonial government of New South Wales in Sydney feared the Russian Pacific Fleet would invade, Australian National Maritime Museum archaeologist James Hunter said. Britain was at war with Russia in a conflict centered on Ukraine’s Crimean Peninsula. Gold had recently been discovered in New South Wales and the neighboring colony of Victoria, making them lucrative targets for conquest. The Australian colonies then relied on Britain’s navy for defense and British warships were rare in the most distant reaches of the empire. The Crimean War ended in 1856 without the Australian two-mast sailing vessel ever being used in battle. Spitfire became a pilot vessel in 1857 at Moreton Bay in what would soon become the Colony of Queensland, but was then still part of New South Wales, documents show. The Queensland government sold Spitfire in 1885 into private ownership for use as a fishing boat. Shipbuilder John Cuthbert delivered Spitfire two months after winning the contract. The speed suggested the warship’s construction already had been underway for a different purpose, Hunter said. It was built from native timbers including an ironbark keel, blackbutt frames and kauri planking. The ship had copper sheathing below the waterline. Russia’s Pacific Fleet at the time was mostly iron-hulled, steam-powered and “armed to the teeth warships,” Hunter told Australian Broadcasting Corp. Spitfire was armed with a single cannon that fired 32-pound (14.5-kilogram) iron cannonballs. “Would that have bounced off the side of one of those larger, Russian iron-hulled warships? Probably,” Hunter said. There are no plans to salvage the wreck, which is largely buried in seabed sand. Authorities have not revealed Spitfire’s exact location because it lies at a depth that can be reached by scuba divers. The ship is protected by federal and state law. Vice Admiral Matthew Buckley, chief of the Australian navy, said Spitfire represents the beginning of the service’s continuing story. “Spitfire occupies a unique place in Australia’s naval history as the first warship built in Australia for Australian service,” Buckley said.
